Separately, we investigate stationary squeezing in a reduced five-mode model with fixed pump amplitudes, including a parasitic single-pump spontaneous four-wave-mixing channel. Within this model, the parasitic channel reduces the achievable squeezing and shifts the instability threshold to lower pump amplitudes. These results provide a compact framework for estimating the validity range of the undepleted-pump approximation and for analyzing transient squeezing dynamics in nonlinear microresonators.

title: Reconstructing Interacting Blood Flow and Wall Interface Deformation from Noisy Flow Data Using PirateNets
abstract: Blood flow and elastic vessel-wall motion interact with each other: fluid stress drives wall deformation, while the moving wall changes the domain in which blood flows. Given noisy flow images, we study the inverse problem of reconstructing the coupled, unsteady three-dimensional motions. We solve the reconstruction through Gauss--Seidel-type alternating fluid and geometry updates. For the fluid, we use physics-informed networks to recover velocity and pressure by fitting the observations while enforcing the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations on the moving domain, which is described by an arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) map. For the geometry, a reference-domain correction and sequential registration recover the vessel shape and wall displacement. Interface traction continuity and an elastic momentum equation regularize the registration so that the recovered displacement is also physics-informed. The networks evaluate fields and physical residuals at sampled space--time points without remeshing the moving domain. Experiments on a converging channel and a patient-like aorta demonstrate reconstruction of flow and wall motion from noisy data. Ablation and parameter-sensitivity studies examine the role of structure regularization and imperfect physical coefficients. A further experiment with a three-element Windkessel outlet condition demonstrates how the framework accommodates a more physiologically realistic boundary setting.

title: SRA: Spatial Reasoning Adapter via Evolving Social Interaction Graphs for Trajectory Prediction
abstract: Predicting where multiple agents will move next is fundamental to autonomous driving, robotics, and any system that must share space with people safely. Modern stochastic predictors read off inter-agent interactions once from the observed past and keep that view fixed throughout the generative rollout, so the reciprocal geometric constraints that emerge as the joint future sharpens are not re-examined. We address this gap with SRA (Spatial Reasoning Adapter), a modular graph denoiser that is integrated into existing diffusion and flow-matching predictors without redesigning their generative cores. At every reverse step, SRA reads the host's current future estimate, builds a sparse Euclidean interaction graph on the predicted trajectories, and returns a residual correction to the host's decoding path. Our adapter consists of three core components: a sparse neighborhood retrieved with a learned query-key score and a geometric bias, a future-conditioned relational feature recomputed on the evolving prediction, and uncertainty-weighted message passing where confident agents act as anchors for uncertain ones. We instantiate SRA on three structurally different hosts (LED, MID, and MoFlow) across four multi-agent benchmarks: SDD, NBA, Soccer, and Football. SRA improves ADE for every host on every dataset, with average gains of 5.8% in ADE and 7.0% in FDE. A cumulative ablation shows that the three components act as one mechanism: only together do they improve every host on every sports dataset, indicating that spatial reasoning over the model's own evolving future, weighted by how far that future can be trusted, is broadly useful across denoising architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/Jaewoo97/SRA.

title: Thouless pumping and Haldane-model topology in a driven extended SSH chain
abstract: Thouless pumping provides a powerful route for probing Chern topology through quantized motion in one-dimensional lattices. We investigate such a topological pump in an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model with tunable next-nearest-neighbor hoppings. A graphical representation in Bloch space is used to construct pumping schemes. In this framework, the Bloch vector traces a closed loop that evolves in time. The Chern number of the synthetic band is then determined by the motion of this loop. Quantum pumping phenomena are demonstrated for a filled band and for a bosonic wave packet driven by Bloch oscillations. We further show that the Haldane model can be mapped to the driven extended SSH chain by replacing a quasimomentum by the pumping time. The quantized charge pump indicates that the Chern number of a two-dimensional model can be read out from a one-dimensional pumping protocol, offering an accessible route for detecting higher-dimensional topology, such as in photonic and cold-atom platforms.

title: Imperfectly Imperfect: Evaluating Graded Cognitive Diversity in LLM Persona Simulations
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as synthetic participants in social, behavioural, and decision-making research, yet it remains unclear whether they can express graded cognitive diversity as assigned when engaging in simulated behaviour. We introduce a cognition-suite evaluation that tests whether simulated populations reproduce human variation in reasoning, self-reported traits, their associations, and downstream behaviour. Agents conditioned on synthetic or human-derived profiles of cognitive reflection, Need for Cognition, and Big Five personality answer the same suite as a cohort of 473 adults: two newly assembled tests, a Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) and a Behavioural Reflection Test (BRT) whose decision scenarios measure reflection in behaviour, alongside an established CRT and the two trait questionnaires. Across seven full-battery simulation runs of four models, agents recover Need for Cognition and Big Five trait distributions on self-report questionnaires, but fall short on simulating diversity of cognitive task performance and downstream behaviours. In the four Claude Sonnet 4.6 runs, every agent scores full marks on both CRTs, whatever reflection level its persona was assigned. In the other three runs agents make intuitive-lure errors (the tempting wrong answers CRT items invite), but 49 to 85% score full marks, against under 10% in the human sample. Claude Sonnet 5 comes closest to people's item-by-item pattern of lures; the other two runs give fewer lures and vary less between items. In the BRT scenarios, every run over-produces 8 to 11 of 15 coded behaviours by at least 20 percentage points, and people's links between reflection and behaviour carry over only in part. Useful synthetic populations must preserve not only trait descriptors but the structured variation in reasoning, error type, and behaviour those descriptors are meant to organise.

title: Scaling Optimization-Oriented Hypernetworks for Implicit Neural Representations
abstract: We present a hypernetwork that generates the parameters of an implicit neural representation (INR) for a given signal in a single forward pass, without test-time optimization. Existing hypernetworks for this problem either ignore the chain-rule structure of the test-time optimization that produces an INR or, when they preserve it, instantiate the structure with MLPs whose parameter count grows quartically in target-network width. Our central contribution is to show that this parameter-count cost is structural to the MLP instantiation, not to the optimization-oriented principle of preserving chain-rule structure, and to resolve it by replacing the MLP body with attention. The resulting hypernetwork combines three design choices: an output-neuron-centric tokenization that aligns the token axis with each layer's output-neuron axis; an information-flow consistency rule that fixes the role of every cross-attention module from the representation its output should occupy; and a token-space iterative rollout that realizes the five quantities one optimization step on the target INR computes as five cross-attention modules with parameter count independent of target-network width. Across five 2D and 3D INR generation benchmarks, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art single-pass and optimization-oriented baselines; scales to target-network widths at which the MLP-based optimization-oriented paradigm exhausts GPU memory; and produces the highest result on NeRF generation without ground-truth INR weights supervision.

title: ReSkill: Selective Self-Improvement for Robot Manipulation
abstract: Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. We present ReSkill, a selective self-improvement framework that concentrates revision on capability gaps. A coding agent constructs an object-centric task graph from an instruction and a skill library, then uses node-level execution records to locate failures. At the task level, it revises stage organization, hand-off conditions, and recovery routes; at the skill level, it strengthens perception, motion, manipulation, and verification capabilities that repeatedly fail. Candidate revisions undergo full-task evaluation and paired comparisons before adoption, allowing local changes to accumulate into validated skills and an independently executable policy. The agent participates only during development; the deployed policy calls the retained skills without invoking the agent at run time. On the same development set, average success across ten RoboDojo tasks rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2% for the final adopted programs; retained programs achieve 83.6% in recorded robustness and model-selection evaluations. Across eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 rebuilt-simulation trials and 62 of 80 real-robot trials (77.5%). The median revision changes only three functions, approximately 0.5% of a program, while 39% of task-specific functions in later-added tasks directly reuse existing implementations. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks.

title: CALFA-KV: Joint Calibration and Fisher-Guided Anchors for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression
abstract: 1-bit key-value (KV) cache compression can combine quantizer calibration with selective high-precision storage to reduce reconstruction error. We propose Calibration and Fisher-guided Anchors for KV cache compression (CALFA-KV). Offline, we jointly fit a key center, radial normalization parameters, and K/V vector codebooks to match the frozen model's projected attention output. We also estimate channel-wise Fisher-type sensitivities from squared gradients of a reference next-token cross-entropy loss. Online, we use these sensitivities to weight the squared reconstruction errors of each KV state. Here, a KV state is one token's key-value pair within one layer and KV head. We retain the highest-scoring states at high precision under a per-layer, per-KV-head budget. Under exact restoration, we bound the excess risk of score-based anchor selection relative to the optimum at the same anchor budget, where risk is the conditional mean square of the first-order loss change. With a budget of 56 additional FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, CALFA-KV (d8b8) outperforms all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on the mean score across seven benchmarks for each of the three models. At the same anchor budget, CALFA-KV (d8b10) uses a nominal index rate of 1.25 bits per channel and narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90--2.01 points on the same metric.

title: Quartet ferromagnetism in the small-exchange limit
abstract: Rare-earth magnets are often regarded as classical owing to their large angular momentum J, but this picture breaks down when exchange is smaller than the crystalline electric-field (CEF) energy scale, allowing the degeneracy of low-lying CEF manifolds to dictate the emergent quantum phases. Here, we uncover such a regime in the RV6Sn6 (R = rare-earth) kagome metals with strong magnetic anisotropy. Thermodynamic and neutron-diffraction measurements reveal successive axial and tilted ferromagnetic (FM) phases in DyV6Sn6, arising from independent ordering of the axial Mz and transverse Mx dipolar components enabled by a rare quasi-quartet ground state. On the other hand, HoV6Sn6 has a similar tilted magnetic anisotropy, but remains axial down to 0.03 K. This discrepancy can be traced back to the non-Kramers nature of Ho3+ where the CEF lifts the quartet degeneracy, leaving a quasi-triplet ground state. Unlike quartets or higher multiplets, we find that the effective spin-1 triplet does not allow independent dipolar ordering without strong quadrupolar (nematic) interactions that act to break rotational symmetry, revealing an essential multipolar prerequisite for tilted magnetic ground states. These results establish a quartet CEF manifold as the minimal degeneracy required for dipolar-driven independent ordering. Mapping the surrounding CEF parameter space further reveals competing magnetic, non-magnetic singlet, and potential quadrupolar phases, driven by multifold ground state degeneracies. These results establish CEF tuning as a versatile route to unconventional quantum phases across the broader RT6X6 (T = transition metal; X = Sn, Ge) family.

title: Dipolar Exchange and Emergent Electric-Dipole-Carrying Quasiparticles in Electronic Ferroelectrics
abstract: Electronic correlations underpin diverse spontaneously ordered states in matter, whose collective excitations emerge as quasiparticles that encode the underlying order. While spin exchange interactions give rise to magnetic order and its quasiparticle excitations known as magnons, their counterparts in electronic ferroelectrics remain poorly understood. Here, we derive an analogous quantum dipolar-pseudospin exchange model for electronic ferroelectricity and identify the associated bosonic quasiparticles that carry intrinsic electric dipole moments. Unlike ferrons in conventional lattice-based ferroelectrics, these dipolar quasiparticles arise entirely from collective electronic dynamics without involving lattice vibrations. Their excitation spectrum exhibits a linear Stark shift under a static electric field, while coupling to an oscillating electric field enables their coherent excitation, leading to colossal, resonantly enhanced second-harmonic generation and optical rectification in the terahertz regime. These dipolar quasiparticles offer promising opportunities for electrically tunable nonlinear optics and open a route toward extending the paradigm of transport in electronic systems beyond conventional charge currents to electric dipole currents.

title: FADE: Fractional Anomalous Dynamics Extrapolation for Training-Free Diffusion Transformers Acceleration
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have established themselves as the preeminent paradigm for high-fidelity generative modeling across various modalities, yet their practical deployment is hindered by the severe computational overhead of iterative sampling. While recent feature-caching methods mitigate this latency through feature reuse or forecasting based on integer-order operators, they remain limited in adapting to the non-stationary and highly curved dynamics of DiT latent trajectories. In this work, we reveal that DiT feature evolution exhibits anomalous diffusion characteristics and a certain degree of spatiotemporal heterogeneity, rendering static, integer-order forecasting operators inadequate and prone to error accumulation. To address this, we propose Fractional Anomalous Dynamics Extrapolation (FADE), a unified framework for training-free diffusion transformers acceleration. FADE models DiT feature evolution via anomalous diffusion and employs a Mittag--Leffler fractional operator to better adapt to high-curvature and non-linear latent trajectories of DiTs. Leveraging the empirical observation that these complex dynamics maintain cross-sample stability, we further construct a Look-Up Table with multiple dimensions through offline profiling. This enables negligible LUT-retrieval overhead, spatiotemporally adaptive parameter retrieval during online inference. Extensive evaluations across diverse architectures and modalities demonstrate that FADE achieves state-of-the-art acceleration, preserving exceptional generation fidelity under aggressive skip intervals with negligible latency overhead. Our project page is available at https://youngkinlon.github.io/fade-project-page/.

title: A General Statistical Framework for Attention and Manipulation Checks
abstract: Attention and manipulation checks are widely used in survey experiments to assess respondents' attentiveness and engagement with treatment, respectively. Yet these checks are subject to measurement error, which may itself depend on treatment when checks are administered after treatment exposure. Restricting analyses to respondents who pass these checks can therefore introduce substantial bias. We propose a general statistical framework for analyzing survey experiments with pre- or post-treatment attention and manipulation checks while accounting for measurement error. We show that three separate checks suffice to identify the proportion of respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment, provided that the checks are conditionally independent among treated respondents given their true, unobserved attentiveness or manipulation status and pre-treatment covariates. Under additional mild assumptions, this result also identifies the average treatment effect among respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment. Building on these identification results, we propose an estimator that allows flexible covariate modeling and establish its asymptotic normality. Applications to framing and digital media literacy experiments demonstrate how accounting for measurement error yields treatment effect estimates that are substantively different from those obtained using conventional approaches.

title: An Overview on Multimodal Wireless and Visual Sensing for Environment Reconstruction: Opportunities and Challenges
abstract: Physical-scene reconstruction through visual sensing and channel knowledge map (CKM) reconstruction through wireless sensing have attracted growing research interest but have largely evolved independently within the computer vision and wireless communications communities, respectively. When applied to the same physical environment, the two sensing modalities provide complementary observations. Visual sensing captures detailed scene geometry and appearance but is constrained by occlusion and poor lighting. Wireless sensing can provide information beyond visual line of sight regardless of lighting conditions, but its measurements are often sparse and difficult to associate with scene structures. These complementary strengths motivate a unified multimodal approach to physical-scene and CKM reconstruction. This paper provides an overview of such unified environment reconstruction through wireless and visual sensing. We first compare the capabilities and limitations of the two modalities and discuss potential applications that benefit from jointly reconstructing both targets. We then review two complementary research directions, namely wireless-assisted physical-scene reconstruction and vision-assisted CKM reconstruction, highlighting how each modality supports the reconstruction task associated with the other. Building on these perspectives, we discuss design principles for a joint representation that supports both targets and identify mutual refinement, in which each modality helps improve the reconstruction associated with the other. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future research directions, offering insights into developing site-specific environment models for sixth-generation (6G) and beyond networks.

title: Spatiotemporal Energy Consistency Enables Reliable Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics from Diffusion Models
abstract: Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) extends molecular simulations to length and time scales inaccessible to atomistic models, but building thermodynamically faithful CG potentials remains a longstanding challenge. Energy-based diffusion models (EBDMs) provide a promising route for learning CG potentials through their zero-time energy. However, CGMD driven by diffusion-learned potentials can produce equilibrium ensembles that deviate substantially from the target distribution. We show that the zero-time distribution error is bounded by the sum of the spatial score error and temporal energy-derivative error, whereas conventional diffusion objectives directly supervise only the spatial component. Based on this finding, we introduce Spatiotemporal Energy Consistency (STEC) supervision, which complements spatial score matching by explicitly constraining temporal energy derivatives. We derive an exact and tractable objective for this temporal component, avoiding the substantial computational overhead associated with previous regularization schemes. Across peptide and fast-folding protein systems, STEC-trained EBDMs accurately reproduce equilibrium distributions with free-energy errors within chemical accuracy, while supporting stable long-time simulations that recover key metastable transition patterns. On held-out octapeptides, STEC reduces free-energy errors by more than 5-fold relative to the strongest competing baseline, while achieving a median production-cost reduction of approximately 1,700-fold relative to atomistic molecular dynamics under a defined structural-coverage benchmark. These results establish STEC as a scalable framework for learning thermodynamically reliable CG force fields for increasingly complex biomolecular systems.

title: Beyond Row Alignment: Virtual-Camera-Aware Online Stereo Rectification
abstract: Stereo matchers estimate depth by comparing the left and right images from a stereo camera pair, but they assume that the two cameras are accurately calibrated and rectified. In real deployments, small physical shifts after calibration, caused by camera motion, mechanical drift, vibration, or installation changes, can break this assumption and degrade depth estimation. Online stereo rectification is therefore needed to correct the image pair during operation and recover a stereo geometry where standard stereo matching can work reliably. Recent online rectification methods mainly optimize row alignment, making the left and right views of the same scene point fall on the same image row. We show that this target, while necessary, is insufficient for deployable stereo depth estimation. A rectifier may make a small set of matched points look well row-aligned, but still distort the full images in ways that hurt stereo matching: useful image regions may be cut off, large blank areas may appear, objects may be stretched or squeezed, or image scale may change unevenly across the view. We propose VirtualRect, an online stereo rectification method designed for reliable real-world deployment. Rather than treating rectification as simply making the left and right image rows line up, this method estimates a rectified virtual stereo camera and combines image-wide supervision of image warp behavior. This makes the rectified images and the camera parameters come from the same geometry, so the images used for matching and the model used for depth computation remain consistent. Experiments on multiple datasets show that, compared with the prior state-of-the-art online rectifier, VirtualRect reduces vertical flow error by 17% on Carla-Flowguided and 7% on Semi-Truck Highway, and lowers depth MAE by 30-41% on Carla-Flowguided across three downstream stereo matchers.

title: On naturality of cohomological support for small quantum groups
abstract: We apply the theory of hypersurface support by Negron and Pevtsova to prove the naturality of cohomological support of the small quantum Borel groups, with respect to restriction to Levi subalgebras. This in turn implies naturality of cohomological support of the small quantum groups for modules that lift to Lusztig's big quantum group, for instance tilting modules. This allows us to make the recent conditional classification of tensor ideals of abelian type in the category of such tilting modules unconditional.

title: Error Estimates and Convergence Analysis for Learning Mechanism--AI Coupled Dynamical Systems
abstract: Mechanism--AI coupled dynamical systems retain known mechanisms while learning unknown dynamics from data. We study how neural approximation, numerical integration, finite observations, and optimization jointly affect the accuracy of this learning process. For time-dependent learned terms in a fixed compact admissible class, we derive a four-component objective error bound within an optimal control formulation. Explicit estimates are obtained for constrained ReLU approximation and Euler integration, with deterministic quadrature and random sampling treated separately. Under joint refinement, we establish $Γ$-convergence of the approximate objectives and show that approximate minimizers approach the continuous optimal set when the global optimization gaps vanish. We also derive conditional stability estimates for state-dependent learned terms. Numerical experiments with a susceptible--infected--recovered (SIR) model illustrate the analysis and show how solver resolution affects continuous-trajectory accuracy even when training losses are similar.

title: TimeHF 2.0: Multimodal, Multivariate, and Multi-Region Collaborative Forecasting for Large-Scale Retail Supply Chains
abstract: Large-scale retail supply chains need sales forecasts for specified products, future dates or planning windows, and regions under the conditions available at the forecast origin. Regional sparsity, changing environments, volatile sales, and unfamiliar business situations make these dimensions difficult to model together. We introduce TimeHF 2.0, a multimodal, multivariate, and multi-region collaborative forecasting framework that makes flexibly expressed business knowledge usable in numerical prediction. A coverage-aware directed encoder integrates regional sales and applicable covariates. A semantic alignment module transfers language-model hidden representations of natural-language plans and domain experience into target-specific forecasting context. Learning against sales observations connects these meanings to numerical evidence, allowing business users to supply experience, future plans, and changing circumstances without defining a new numerical feature for each description. Text-conditioned future queries and shared/routed experts adapt prediction to the supplied context. An ordered-distribution head allocates fine resolution to routine fluctuations and coarse resolution to extreme sales movements, while daily/window learning connects forecasts to cumulative planning quantities. Online parallel forecasting at JD yields relative accuracy improvements of 18.25% and 17.94% for national daily and planning-window sales, and 19.44% and 18.99% for DC daily and planning-window sales, over the original production deep learning baseline. Component comparisons, loss-design results, and product-type analyses examine the roles of regional information, covariates, business knowledge, context-dependent processing, and robust planning-oriented learning.

title: Geometric classification of Noether invariants of the Time-Dependent damped Duffing Oscillator
abstract: We present a systematic geometric classification of the Noether point symmetries of time-dependent conformal Lagrangians of the form $L = A(t)\left(\frac{1}{2}g_{ij}\dot{x}^{i}\dot{x}^{j} - V(x)\right)$, whose Euler--Lagrange equations describe dynamical systems with time-dependent linear damping. The classification is carried out by coupling the temporal parameters of the conformal factor $A(t)$ with the homothetic algebra of the kinetic metric $g_{ij}$ through a set of compatibility and integrability conditions. The central result is a main theorem which determines the Noether generators, the associated gauge functions and the resulting invariants. The theorem splits naturally into two cases according to whether the quantity $D - 2ψ$ is non-zero or zero, with further subcases depending on whether the homothetic vectors are gradient or non-gradient. The theorem imposes no restrictions on $A(t)$, $g_{ij}$ or $V(x)$, and is therefore fully general and covariant. We apply the theorem to the time-dependent damped Duffing oscillator (DDO) in Euclidean space $E^{3}$ with $A(t) = e^{γt}$ and potential $V = \frac{1}{2}a\,r^{2} + \frac{% λ}{4}r^{4}$. For the damped harmonic oscillator ($λ= 0$) the theorem reproduces the classical Bateman invariant as a special case. For the anharmonic case we obtain a new exact time-dependent quadratic invariant, valid when the linear stiffness satisfies $a = 2γ^{2}/9$. Each invariant is verified explicitly by direct differentiation along the equations of motion. The new invariant provides a rare example of a global conservation law for a fully nonlinear dissipative system, and can be used for the integration and quantization of the DDO.

title: Action Transfer Across Character Body Plans in Latent-Action World Models: An Empirical Study of Animated Characters
abstract: Latent-action world models learn actions from video without labels, and recent methods aim to share these actions across bodies. Transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored. In this paper, we study whether an action learned from one character can make a character with a different body perform the same action. A cat, a blob and a human can all jump, but each moves its body in its own way. The usual transfer gain mixes body motion with screen movement and can assign a perfect score to a model that ignores its action. To address this, we introduce a transfer score that compares the correct action with wrong ones from the same source. We test five training objectives on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D. With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models. In contrast, with a camera that follows the body, the best model reaches only 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans. With this camera, a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%). The learned actions therefore retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character.

title: Delta-Corrected Shot Reduction for Bypassing Optimization Plateaus in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
abstract: The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) remains a cornerstone hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for quantum simulation, yet its scalability is fundamentally constrained by heavy measurement overheads. While strategies such as variance-preserved shot reduction (VPSR) mitigates this cost, they suffer from convergence instability and optimization stagnation caused by finite-sample bias in limited pilot shots. To overcome this limitation, we introduce delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), an analytically enhanced shot allocation strategy that rigorously mitigates finite-sample instability. Utilizing the multivariate delta method, we derive explicit higher-order bias correction terms for the empirical reduction factor. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that incorporating higher-order statistical moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, provides the gradient resolution necessary to bypass noise-induced barren plateaus. DSCR significantly accelerates convergence compared to standard VPSR across diverse noise and resource regimes while matching or decreasing cumulative measurement costs, establishing a mathematically rigorous framework for variance-stabilized shot allocation on near-term hardware.

title: Polarization Signatures of Magnetic Reconnection Bubbles near Black Holes
abstract: Motivated by the observed horizon-scale polarization variability in multi-epoch Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) data, we develop a time-dependent general relativistic polarized ray-tracing framework to study how localized magnetic reconnection near a black hole imprints itself on synchrotron polarization. We model the reconnection phenomenologically as a transient magnetic bubble. While keeping the underlying spacetime, emission prescription, and polarization transport scheme unchanged, the bubble weakens the local ordered field, reorganizes its geometry, induces a conservative local kinematic response, and relaxes through a finite magnetic-memory prescription. We explore how the key bubble parameters control the recovery of the magnetic-field strength, the spatial spreading of the disturbed region, the persistence of the post-reconnection imprint, and the resulting polarization signatures. Perturbations dominated by different magnetic-field components produce distinct polarized morphologies, EVPA evolution, and Stokes-(Q, U) trajectories: azimuthal perturbations favor outward EVPA shifts, radial perturbations favor inward shifts, and vertical perturbations mainly suppress the polarized intensity. For the illustrative M87^*-like cases, the phase evolution of the β_2 polarization coefficient further traces how localized magnetic reconfiguration contributes to the global EVPA twist of the ring. These results show that horizon-scale polarization variability can provide a sensitive diagnostic of localized magnetic restructuring and that the present framework offers a physically transparent way to interpret time-dependent polarimetric signatures in future EHT observations.

title: On the structural aspects of Convex Subhyperlattices under different orders
abstract: Nayak et al. (2025) introduced the concept of convex subhyperlattices of a strong join hyperlattice $\mathfrak{L}$ and demonstrated that the collection of all convex subhyperlattices, $\operatorname{CS}(\mathfrak{L})$, together with empty set, forms a lattice. In particular, for $P$-hyperlattices and Nakano hyperlattices, they obtained a unique representation of convex subhyperlattices in terms of hyperideals and hyperfilters. In the present work, we extend these studies by proving that $\operatorname{CS}(\mathfrak{L}) \cup \{\emptyset\}$, under set inclusion, forms an algebraic lattice. Moreover, we introduce two new orders on $\operatorname{CS}(\mathfrak{L})$ and examine their properties, including conditions for equivalence of these orders. In the class of $P$-hyperlattices, we characterize convex subhyperlattices in terms of initial and final segments, providing a structural insight into their formation. When convexity is extended to arbitrary join hyperlattices, many results known for $P$-hyperlattices and Nakano hyperlattices fail to hold. To address these limitations of convexity in arbitrary hyperlattices, we introduce the notion of strongly convex sets, denoted $\operatorname{SC}(\mathfrak{L})$, which naturally generalizes the concept while preserving its fundamental properties and extends the applicability of results to a wider setting. We establish several results for $\operatorname{SC}(\mathfrak{L})$ that do not hold for $\operatorname{CS}(\mathfrak{L})$.

title: QAOA Inside ADMM: Subproblem Wins Do Not Become Decomposition Wins at Matched Budgets
abstract: We benchmark the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) as the binary subproblem solver in a two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for mixed-binary problems against classical solvers under matched budgets. With 23 optimizer evaluations per subproblem, scoring determines the comparison: on its final readout, the optimized QAOA loses to random search at $n=12$ and 16 binary variables (inconclusive at 20; exploratory and post hoc tests). When credited with its best sample, it wins. In a noiseless 12-qubit simulation, transferred-angle depth-2 QAOA finds the exact optimum of 97.3\% of planted-family subproblems, against 50.6\%--67.4\% for the four strongest local heuristics (100\% against 90.4\%--94.4\% crediting the four best bitstrings) and a not significantly different 96.5\% for semidefinite rounding with local search (SDP+LS). Under our evaluation-counting convention, its time to solution there is a factor of three to five below the local heuristics' but grows with a larger exponent; it is ten times that of SDP+LS and, in seconds, 54 times that of tabu search with restarts. For the benchmark class, an unconstrained binary quadratic problem in disguise, ADMM's binary step is a proximal step on the reduced problem: at unit penalty ADMM re-solves it, and for larger penalties exact solutions increasingly stall. On two families that do not reduce to one, less accurate solvers found the problem optimum more often at unit and larger penalties. No family gave QAOA a better ADMM outcome than the best classical solver and penalty. The benchmark includes a correctness gate and a log of its hypothesis tests.

title: PrivMark: Pixel-Space Steering against Privacy Leakage in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) routinely disclose soft-biometric attributes such as age, gender, and race in their text outputs, exposing demographic information from uploaded images to any downstream API user. Existing privacy defenses do not fit this setting: face de-identification leaves distributed soft-biometric cues intact, classifier-targeted adversarial perturbations do not transfer to open-ended generation, and stronger VLM-specific methods require retraining or runtime activation access unavailable to downstream APIs. We propose PrivMark, a framework that suppresses biometric leakage at the image level. By analyzing VLM activations, we identify two weakly aligned steering vector directions in hidden-state space, each tied to a distinct leakage behavior --- one corresponding to incidental attribute disclosure under open-ended descriptions, the other to compliance with direct biometric probes instead of refusal --- and encode both directions into a single bounded pixel perturbation, so the protected image alone enforces privacy with no invasive access to model internals at deployment. To support evaluation, we assemble BioleakBench, $1{,}600$ VQA pairs covering biometric privacy attributes under both free-form description and direct-probe protocols. Across three white-box source models, PrivMark achieves up to $85.9\%$ biometric suppression while retaining $75\%$ of clean OK-VQA utility, up to $1.4\times$ the privacy-utility tradeoff of the strongest pixel-only baseline. The same one-shot perturbations transfer consistently to seven unseen VLMs including closed-source APIs.

title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
abstract: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

title: Mismeasuring the Life of a Line of Code: Lessons Learned the Hard Way
abstract: Studies of how long lines of code live, including lines written by AI agents, rest on choices that look technical: when a line counts as gone, what to do with lines still alive, whether to pool projects, and how to evaluate a model. We studied 32.5 million line births in 120 TypeScript repositories and got several of these choices wrong at first. For ten of them, we compare the result as we first computed it, or as commonly done, with the result after correction. All ten change conclusions, or would have. Six were our own mistakes. Counting moved and rewritten lines as dead shortens a line's median life from 3.0 years to 1.3. Counting any change as a death hides an outcome that can be predicted: within-project concordance falls from 0.71 to 0.56. Regressing observed lifetimes discards three quarters of the lines. Keeping rewritten lines at risk makes protective effects grow with age. Lines are born and removed together, so treating them as independent misleads twice: nine of fifteen effects look significant only under that assumption, and a split by file makes a barely predictable outcome look good (within-project concordance 0.71 instead of 0.61). After the corrections, removal depends on a line's age and project, but our models could barely rank it within a project. Local revision they could rank (0.71). Obvious cases aside, the top 1% of a project's new lines are revised at 2.3 times the base rate. Each pitfall leaves a symptom; we give a checklist.

title: Comonotonic and moment matching approximations for sums of lognormal random variables II
abstract: In this paper, based on the concept of step-weighted distribution, we introduce a minimum-deformation approach to constructing comonotonic and moment-matching approximations for sums of lognormal random variables. The proposed approach aims to minimize the Pearson deformation of a starting comonotonic approximation subject to moment-matching constraints. We establish several results concerning the existence and uniqueness of minimum-deformation comonotonic approximations and propose a method for determining the step quantiles and weights. In particular, when the number of steps is one greater than the moment-matching order, we show that the joint optimization problem can be reduced to an optimization problem involving only the partition points. The proposed framework accommodates moment matching of any prescribed finite order, and numerical experiments demonstrate its application to approximations matching the first five moments of the original sum. The numerical results also show that minimizing the Pearson deformation does not necessarily improve the approximation accuracy of risk measures, which depends on both the starting comonotonic approximation and the choice of partition points and correction weights.

title: An exact Kähler form on $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ without a global SYZ fibration
abstract: We construct an explicit exact Kähler form on \((\mathbb C^*)^2\) admitting no almost-toric fibration and hence no smooth Lagrangian torus fibration. For the logarithmic holomorphic volume form, we also rule out any special Lagrangian fibrations with compact fibers and dense regular locus, even when arbitrary compact connected singular fibers are allowed. For higher dimensions, taking products also yields explicit exact Kähler forms on \((\mathbb C^*)^n\), for every \(n\ge2\), admitting no smooth proper Lagrangian torus fibration.

title: Local regularity and p-harmonic approximation for weak inverse mean curvature flow
abstract: We prove local Lipschitz regularity for locally bounded $BV$ solutions of the calibration equations for inverse mean curvature flow. We also approximate every prescribed variational weak flow locally by Moser's logarithmic transforms of positive $p$-harmonic functions. On a fixed smooth domain, with the trace of a calibrated Lipschitz solution prescribed, both the uniform error and the absolute difference of total variations are $O((p-1)^{1/3})$ as $p\downarrow1$. In particular, the approximations converge strictly in $BV$.

title: Coupled plasmonic Fabry-Perot resonances modulating electromagnetic enhancement at a silver nanowire-nanoparticle junction proved by surface-enhanced fluorescence spectroscopy
abstract: We investigated the surface-enhanced fluorescence (SEF), which is the broad background spectrum underlying the surface-enhanced resonant Raman scattering of dye molecules, emitted from junctions between silver nanoparticles (NPs) and nanowires (NWs). We found that the electromagnetic enhancement factors (FR) derived from the SEF exhibited spectral modulation, such as complicated oscillatory structures. This property became clearer when the emission polarization was perpendicular to the long axis of the NWs. The FR spectra of the long and short NWs exhibit fine and broad oscillatory structures, respectively, when the NPs are positioned near the NW centers. When the NPs were near the NW ends, a combination of fine and broad structures was observed. Numerical calculations of the position-dependent FR spectra successfully reproduced these properties, indicating that the spectral properties originated from the interaction between two plasmonic Fabry-Perot (FP) resonators within the NW, separated by a NP. Based on this result, an analytical model of coupled FP resonators was developed to evaluate these spectral features using experimentally measured NW lengths and NP positions while varying the inter-resonator coupling efficiency. This analysis revealed that the interference and superposition of the two FP resonances resulted in these complex spectra, the energy of which was radiated by the localized plasmons of the NPs.

title: Positive sectional curvature on all smooth 13-spheres
abstract: Every smooth homotopy $13$-sphere admits a Riemannian metric of strictly positive sectional curvature. We construct a special $S^3$--$S^3$ bundle over $S^{13}$ whose star quotient represents the nonzero class $\pmα_1β_1\inΘ_{13}\cong\mathbb Z/3$. The defining equivariant map factors through the Blakers--Massey map by a smooth Hopf construction representing an unstable $J$-generator. This factorisation retains the prescribed base representation and makes Schultz's plumbing composition formula applicable; a normal-invariant computation in smoothing theory then identifies the smooth structure. On the quotient we implement the compatible-disk strategy with complete curvature estimates on arbitrary two-planes, matching boundary metrics, and a strictly positive sum of outward second fundamental forms. A direct smoothing argument completes the metric construction. Orientation reversal gives the remaining nonzero class in $Θ_{13}$.

title: In Search of Lost Time: Temporal Competence in Large Language Models
abstract: Today's large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with time: AI agents schedule tasks, coordinate with people and other AI systems, and even decide how long to think. Yet LLMs only ever encounter time secondhand---in descriptions rather than experience. Does this hinder their reasoning and decisions that involve time? Our paper traces this question from a model's knowledge to its actions through four successive evaluations. We find that models know the rules of time, which can be read, but struggle to predict durations, which must be lived; while they are highly accurate (92.0-97.5\%) on a collection of questions built from the theorems of various time-related literatures, they underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5\% and fail to identify which tasks will take them longer to run. And while they are better at estimating durations of human tasks, their duration judgments change based on how an event is worded, magnifying similar human biases by up to 1.3$\times$. Moving from estimation to action, we find that some LLMs disregard time costs completely when answering user queries, ignoring a 1,200-fold increase in wait time entirely. Together, our experiments reveal new challenges posed to LLMs as they navigate a dimension they cannot directly perceive, and highlight how their blind spots can even be simple cognitive abilities that humans take for granted.

title: Formal Proof of an Anisotropic Calderón Uniqueness Theorem
abstract: We announce a Lean~4 formal proof of a special case of the smooth anisotropic Calderón uniqueness theorem released by OpenAI on October 6, 2026. We consider smooth Riemannian metrics on the three-dimensional unit ball, with full boundary measurements and Euclidean extensions outside the ball. OpenAI's release did not include a Lean proof of their uniqueness result. Our formalization uses results from Mathlib and Tau Ceti, and it is given as a solution to a Lean comparator challenge whose check permits only the standard axioms of Lean. The Lean proof is not a line-by-line translation of the OpenAI manuscript.

title: Close and Sort: Exact Maximum-Likelihood Aggregation of Cyclic Rank-Two Preferences
abstract: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in general. Known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize this likelihood. We show that the weighted problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix $W_{ij}=\log(p_{ij}/p_{ji})$ has rank two, including when the induced preferences contain cycles. Writing $W_{ij}=\det(h_i,h_j)$ and adding the closing vector $h_0=-\sum_i h_i$ turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. This geometry yields CloseSort, which polar-sorts the $n+1$ edge vectors, cuts after $h_0$, and returns a global maximum-likelihood order in $O(n\log n)$ time from the factors. The same geometry identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate beyond exact rank two. When the smallest determinant $δ$ of two consecutive edges in the closed angular cycle is positive, it is exactly the best-to-runner-up log-likelihood gap. For $W=W_0+E$, the CloseSort order of $W_0$ has regret at most $\sum_{i<j}|E_{ij}|$ on $W$ and remains optimal whenever this sum is below $δ$, a worst-case tight threshold. In 5,120 determinant-logit simulations, increasing the observations per pair from 4 to 64 raises the fraction on which rank-two projection outperforms the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles drawn from 63 systems and ten judges, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles containing a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda and improves the mean normalized objective over each of eight baselines. With factors supplied, it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings.

title: Shallow-water black holes and lattice superradiance
abstract: Rotating black holes can amplify waves that scatter off them, a process known as superradiance that fluid analogues bring into the laboratory. Separating the horizon's role from dissipation in the surrounding fluid remains difficult. Here we realise a rotating analogue black hole in a lattice fluid: a shallow-water vortex whose horizon is set by a topographic sill, so that the only sink lies behind a supercritical layer that lets nothing out. We measure superradiance as energy extraction: the flux at the horizon is outward for co-rotating waves whose pattern rotates more slowly than the horizon, and inward for faster waves, counter-rotating waves and a non-rotating hole. A scan over three lattice viscosities separates the extraction at the horizon, which is inviscid, from that of the viscous fluid inside the corotation radius: well below the band edge the horizon is the absorber; near the edge the viscous share is half at the operating viscosity and vanishes at the lowest. A drain-anchored horizon, as in water-tank experiments, gives the same signs. Our analysis gives insight into the mechanism of superradiance and offers a cheap, flexible platform for designing analogue-gravity experiments.

title: Engineering a digital acoustic black hole
abstract: We show how to design and build an analogue black hole as a synchronous digital circuit. We define the sound speed, the flow and the horizon of such a circuit in terms of its own logic, and realise one on a field-programmable gate array, where the black hole is probed electrically with a signal generator and an oscilloscope. We measure the stability of the horizon, its causal cone, the ringdown and rotational superradiance. A single flipped bit inside the horizon leaks out by an amount that falls exponentially with depth. Digital circuits thus form a reconfigurable class of gravitational analogues and realise an analogue black hole as a cellular automaton.

title: AFVE-Bench: Measuring Abandoned-Frame Verbalization Errors in Multi-Turn LLM Revision
abstract: Multi-turn revision often asks a model to replace an earlier organizing frame while preserving still-valid facts and artifact requirements. Existing instruction-following evaluations mainly assess the latest target and may therefore score an artifact as successful even when it adopts the new frame but exposes the superseded one. We call this failure an abandoned-frame verbalization error (AFVE). AFVE-Bench evaluates silent frame replacement in English and Chinese using 192 matched four-turn dialogues across eight writing domains. Each seed has zero, one, or two pre-target user requests to generate under the source frame. AFVE eligibility depends on the user-request history and applies to the one- and two-request conditions; the zero-request condition serves as a frame-bearing baseline. Eleven model configurations yielded 4,224 expected post-target response units. Two annotators independently scored 4,204 scorable responses for target adoption, source-frame verbalization, and direct usability; model and condition metadata were hidden, and disagreements were adjudicated. AFVE occurs in 25.54% (715/2,799) of history-conditioned responses. Of 2,388 target-passing history-conditioned responses, 472 (19.77%) still expose the abandoned source frame, most often through contrastive framing (423/472). For these standalone revision tasks, target adoption does not ensure source-frame silence.

title: When Experience Becomes a Backdoor: Poisoning Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Failure-Aware Task Optimization
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly improve themselves through self-evolution, distilling execution experience into persistent, reusable skills. However, this persistence creates a new attack surface: malicious rules implanted into skills can compromise subsequent agent behavior. Existing skill backdoor attacks typically assume direct manipulation of the victim's skills, which is impractical when skills are constructed internally by a trusted evolver. In this paper, we study a novel problem of task-level backdoor attacks, where the attacker can only inject poisoned evolution tasks, inducing the agent to implant backdoors into its own skills. Since the attacker controls neither skill induction nor downstream execution, a natural approach is to iteratively optimize poisoned tasks based on attack success. However, our preliminary analysis reveals two key challenges: (i) failures at different stages of skill evolution and downstream execution can produce indistinguishable outcomes, providing little guidance for targeted poisoned-task updates; and (ii) unsuccessful updates may undermine earlier progress, while simply discarding them may lead to repeated ineffective updates. To address these challenges, we propose BadEvolve, a failure-aware task-poisoning framework against self-evolving LLM agents. BadEvolve diagnoses attack failures across four stages, i.e., Induction, Activation, Following, and Effect, and directs updates toward the failing stage. It further employs rollback to preserve earlier progress and failure memory to avoid repeating ineffective updates. Extensive experiments across diverse self-evolution frameworks, benchmarks, and backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of BadEvolve. Our code is available at https://github.com/ventr1c/BadEvolve.

title: Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation: Evaluating Hierarchical Policies from Non-Hierarchical Data
abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the expected return of a target policy from previously collected data without additional environment interaction. While OPE methods for flat Markovian policies are well studied, little work has addressed evaluating hierarchical policies in which a high-level policy selects temporally extended options that generate primitive actions until a termination condition is met. The primary existing approach applies per-decision importance sampling at the option level, but requires option-annotated trajectories and exhibits variance that still grows with the horizon. For non-hierarchical policies, fitted Q-evaluation (FQE) typically achieves lower error than importance sampling by leveraging the classic Bellman equation for policy evaluation; however, a naive extension of FQE to hierarchical policies results in a biased policy value estimate. In this paper, we introduce Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation (IO-FQE), which estimates a value function in the augmented state-option space; this approach enables OPE of hierarchical policies even when we lack annotations of what option was run in the data. We develop two continuous-action instantiations of IO-FQE and show on long-horizon hierarchical continuous control tasks (AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation) that IO-FQE eliminates the bias incurred by a naive application of FQE to hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared-error compared to option-level importance sampling.

title: Compact Quantum Channel Attention for Static ASL Recognition: A Controlled Study with Parameter-Matched Baselines
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report good accuracy on image tasks, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum part is responsible. This paper proposes QCA-DenseNet, a static American Sign Language (ASL) recognition pipeline in which an eight-qubit variational circuit acts as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 features. The quantum channel attention (QCA) gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51 times fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. The pipeline is tested on 1,815 MU HandImages images by holding out one of five signers at a time, and a frozen-backbone ablation uses small parts of the Kaggle ASL Alphabet data. On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy, above SE (93.72%) and within 0.28 points of the best model. A matched classical MLP and a model without attention perform about the same, and no difference is significant. QCA gives a much smaller attention gate without a detectable loss in accuracy, but no quantum advantage.

title: What extraction cannot slim, and whether function injection can: a pre-registered study of 580 Java repositories
abstract: A method of 26 code lines or more reads as a Long Method, and Extract Method is the usual fix. Some long methods have no single-exit fix: a return cannot leave an extracted piece, a piece hands back one value, and some methods are knotted so that every cut is blocked. Function injection, as the OfficeFloor framework does it, cuts differently: each piece becomes a function the framework injects and sequences, an early return ends a function, and a function hands on several values. The framework's author pre-registered a test of whether it takes apart what extraction cannot. A stratified random sample of 580 open-source Java repositories, each pinned before AI coding assistants were in general use, was scanned by released tools whose cost models were fixed before the sample was drawn: 3,026,902 methods, 168,466 of them long. Single-exit extraction cannot slim 22.8% of the long methods. The registered hypothesis, that at least a quarter of those stuck methods are ones only function injection takes apart, is refuted: 22.2% (95% CI 20.3 to 24.3). Nearly half of the stuck methods are early-return methods the plan counts as conventionally fixable, and the split takes three in four of those apart as they stand. Where extraction would do, the split chooses injection and costs less for 29.0% against extraction wrapped as one function and 17.2% against plain extraction, almost always as a straight sequence of functions. An exploratory reading of the quarter of the stuck methods that neither takes apart finds a third of it tables and literals, long for their data rather than their logic, and most of the rest blocked by a jump inside a loop, by a nested statement too large to cut, or by values too many for any cut. Three registered studies are proposed: the classes as rules in the tools, a refinement per class, and the same measures on code written with AI assistants.

title: Pinching an elastic potato chip
abstract: Thin shells deform by transmitting stress across their surface, yet how a shell of general shape carries a localized load remains unclear. Combining experiments, simulations, and theory on pinched saddle-shaped elastic shells, we show that the asymptotic lines, curves of zero normal curvature, dictate both deformation and stiffness. Isometry turns the shell mid-surface into a medium obeying a wave equation in space. Material points lit by the pinch are lifted, while those in its shadow sink. Finite thickness blurs the lit--shadow boundary, and the same rule maps where a clamped shell is rigid. Our findings indicate that light and shadow offer a unified framework for understanding mechanical stress propagation along shell structures.

title: HSGNav: Hypothesis Scene Graphs for Multi-Scale Lifelong Navigation under Object Relocation
abstract: In real homes, assistive robots must repeatedly locate targets from large furniture to tiny tabletop items, as people move objects between household surfaces. Uniformly instantiating detections at different scales as 3D objects can be brittle for small on-surface items; without explicit object-state validation, stale entries may persist after scene changes. Our key insight is to separate persistent 3D furniture entities from revisable surface-object hypotheses, retaining their visual evidence without requiring independent object geometry. We formalize this design as the Hypothesis Scene Graph (HSG), which preserves small-object evidence and supports local revision without rebuilding the stable entity topology. Building on HSG, HSGNav uses this separation for multi-scale lifelong navigation: retrieval selects entity or hypothesis evidence according to target scale, exploration acquires additional surface observations, and verification confirms target presence or invalidates contradicted hypothesis records. Because existing lifelong benchmarks such as GOAT-Bench rarely require mid-episode memory invalidation or multi-scale search, we introduce FAROS-Bench (Find And Re-find Objects across Scales) for mid-episode relocation of surface objects and multi-scale find goals. Experiments show that HSGNav performs competitively on GOAT-Bench while substantially outperforming prior methods on FAROS-Bench.

title: The hierarchical structure of the Milky Way I. A model-agnostic clustering of 1 billion stars in 5D
abstract: The Milky Way exhibits a hierarchical structure shaped by mergers, accretion, and internal dynamics. Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) enables a global view of this structure, but requires scalable, model-agnostic methods to extract multi-scale clustering patterns. We aim to characterise the hierarchical clustering structure of the Milky Way in a model-agnostic way and to assess how the resulting structures relate to existing catalogues. We apply the hierarchical density-based clustering algorithm AstroLink to a locally magnitude-complete subsample of over one billion Gaia DR3 stars with five-dimensional astrometric information. The data are corrected for selection effects and transformed using a distance contraction and feature scaling. We compare the resulting cluster hierarchy to catalogues of open clusters, globular clusters, dwarf galaxies, and stellar streams using custom availability-aware metrics and a bi-directional best-match framework. At a significance threshold of $S = 3.8σ$, AstroLink identifies 7410 statistically significant clusters spanning a wide range of morphologies. Compact systems are often recovered as reciprocal matches with many also exhibiting internal substructure, while extended structures are typically fragmented or partially recovered. A substantial fraction of clusters have no counterpart in the comparison catalogues, these may be new structures but additional physical checks are needed to verify this. A model-agnostic, hierarchical clustering approach can recover the multi-scale structure of the Milky Way at Gaia DR3 scale and provides a unified framework for comparing heterogeneous catalogues and identifying candidate structures.

title: On the domain of attraction of source--type solutions of the porous medium equations
abstract: We study the rate of convergence to Barenblatt profiles of the solutions to porous medium equations in $\R^n, n \ge 1$, by means of a certain class of Energy distances, a class of discrepancies between probability measures which have been recently widely used in problems related to AI, in particular for tasks related to machine learning. If $n \ge 3$, it is shown both that the rate of decay in Energy distance is improved with respect to known results which are based on the decay of relative entropy, and that, with respect to this distance, any initial value of bounded mass belongs to the domain of attraction of the source--type solution. Similar results are shown to hold for the fast diffusion case.

title: Dual-Granularity Learning for Regression with Continuous Noisy Labels
abstract: Learning with noisy labels has been extensively studied for classification, yet its regression counterpart remains relatively underexplored. Unlike classification, regression involves continuous-valued targets where label noise exhibits heterogeneous magnitudes across instances, which poses conflicting requirements on the model: correcting small-to-moderate deviations requires sensitivity to label values for instance-level refinement, whereas large deviations caused by corrupted or outlying annotations render exact label values unreliable, necessitating reduced reliance on exact labels and instead leveraging ordinal structure among samples. These requirements call for methods that capture both global structure and sample-specific deviations in a unified manner. To this end, we propose GRAIN, a dual-granularity framework for robust noisy regression. At the fine-grained level, we derive an explicit residual learning mechanism from a robust loss formulation, introducing instance-specific auxiliary variables to decouple label noise from predictive signals. At the coarse-grained level, we introduce a binning-based contrastive regularization that enforces an order-preserving feature structure aligned with label proximity, addressing noise beyond the capacity of local residual refinement. The two levels are coupled via a histogram-based bridging mechanism that enables bidirectional information flow: coarse-grained structural guidance establishes a well-ordered feature space that anchors residual learning, while fine-grained residual refinement corrects instance-level deviations that structural regularization alone cannot resolve. Experimental results show that GRAIN consistently improves robustness and generalization under diverse noise conditions.

title: Removing the floor from Hoeffding and Bernstein inequalities for finite-population U-statistics
abstract: Let $C$ be a uniformly sampled $n$-element subset of a finite population $D$ of size $N$, and let $U_C$ be the complete U-statistic of order $k$ built from a bounded kernel on the $k$-subsets of $D$. We prove a product inequality for the uniform distribution on $\binom{D}{n}$ and deduce from it the comparison $ \log \mathbb{E}\left[e^{θ(U_C-\mathbb{E}U_C)}\right] \le \frac{n}{k}\log \mathbb{E}\left[e^{\frac{kθ}{n}(Y-\mathbb{E}Y)}\right]$, where $Y$ is a single kernel value taken at a uniformly sampled $k$-subset of $D$. This yields Hoeffding, Bennett and Bernstein inequalities for $U_C$ with effective sample size $n/k$ in place of the $\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ available so far. The gain is negligible when $n$ is much larger than $k$, but it approaches a factor of two in the exponent when $k$ is close to $n$.

title: Seeing Isn't Enough: Unlocking Visual Reasoning by Bridging the Reasoning-Access Gap with TIGER
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) inherit strong textual reasoning capabilities from their language backbones and text pretraining, but often fail to apply the same level of competency to visual inputs. We show that this degradation cannot be attributed to only perception failures, by evaluating models on semantically-equivalent text and rendered-text image inputs: models can accurately read text in the images and recover near-text performance when provided their own transcriptions, but just cannot reason well on the images directly. We characterize this discrepancy as a modality reasoning-access gap, where models fail to route perceived visual content into existing reasoning machinery accessible with text. To bridge this, we propose TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning), which first mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails when provided the corresponding rendered image, and post-trains the model on the image input via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. Importantly, although trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, TIGER results in model performance improvements across diverse real-world visual benchmarks including geometric diagrams (MathVerse), multi-disciplinary sciences (EMMA, MMMU), complex charts (ChartQAPro), and embodied spatial reasoning (RoboSpatial-Home). TIGER also complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods, yielding further performance gains. Analysis involving reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching provide support indicating that TIGER helps to align visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/minhngh/Tiger.

title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) trains agents to adapt to novel tasks from test-time experience, but requires diverse training environments and reward functions. While environments are becoming cheaper to generate, it remains difficult to anticipate every objective an agent may be asked to pursue at test time. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) learn policies from reward-free data and support zero-shot RL (ZSRL): adaptation to new objectives at test time using a large reward-labeled dataset. Recent work has shown that BFM task inference can instead be performed online without prior task-specific data. We note that this capability positions BFMs and meta-RL as alternative approaches for online adaptation to new reward functions in a fixed environment. We then ask whether we can extend BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly, including in novel environments, and identify four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision. We study each individually, then propose MetaBFM, a hybrid method that addresses all four. During training, it combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning; at test time, it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference. We demonstrate that MetaBFM can recover the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set. Our work suggests that BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions whose combined strengths allow adaptive agents to learn more diverse behaviors from a fixed set of supervised objectives.

title: Balancing Confidentiality and Attack Detectability in Networked Control Systems over Lossy Wireless Channels
abstract: We study the joint protection of a networked control system (NCS) against eavesdropping and data integrity attacks over a lossy wireless channel. The eavesdropper intercepts the transmitted sensor measurements and control inputs to reconstruct the system state. In contrast, the integrity attacker in this study replaces the sensor measurements with fabricated data to drive the system to undesired operating conditions. Although these two threats are typically studied separately, a wireless NCS should be protected against both simultaneously, and a defence against one affects the other. We employ an observation-encoding scheme that renders the eavesdropper's state-estimation error covariance unbounded under packet drops, and show that transmission energy governs how long this error remains bounded. In particular, lower transmission energy improves confidentiality. For integrity protection, we combine stochastic physical watermarking with a CUSUM-based sequential change detector. The proposed attack detection scheme accounts for intermittent communication and encoded measurements. The detection delay is governed by the Kullback--Leibler divergence (KLD) between the pre- and post-attack distributions of the test signal, and we show that a higher transmission energy increases the KLD and thereby reduces the detection delay. Furthermore, we derive analytical expressions for the eavesdropper's estimation error and the worst-case expected KLD, providing guidelines for selecting transmission energy to balance confidentiality and integrity protection and characterising the privacy--security trade-off. Finally, we run numerical simulations to validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate the privacy--security trade-off in practical scenarios.

title: YRC-Bench: Benchmarking Culturally Aware Machine Translation for Historical Heritage via Tri-Level Semantic Bridging
abstract: Translating historical cultural heritage poses profound challenges for machine translation systems due to the acute semantic asymmetry across eras and cultures, where terse classical syntax frequently obscures domain-specific cultural knowledge. While Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable prowess in generic translation benchmarks, they struggle to negotiate Culturally-Specific Items and diachronic shifts in domain-rich historical texts, such as Yellow River cultural records. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce YRC-Bench, the first human-curated, multi-parallel benchmark dedicated to historical heritage translation across Classical Chinese, Modern Chinese, and nine target foreign languages. YRC-Bench establishes a tri-level parallel corpus incorporating modern explanatory glosses as explicit semantic bridges and operationalizes translation strategies through paired conserved versus substituted CSI variants categorized by cultural translatability. Systematic evaluations of nine leading LLMs across bidirectional translation directions reveal that leveraging modern Chinese glosses - especially human-curated ones - dramatically elevates both lexical fidelity and semantic adequacy. Furthermore, multidimensional human preference audits by native experts unveil distinct cross-cultural preferences between Sinographic-tradition and non-Sinographic language groups.

title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

title: The cofinite regularity spectrum of $F$-irregular graphs
abstract: For a connected graph $F$, a graph $G$ is $F$-irregular if the numbers of copies of $F$ containing its vertices are pairwise distinct. We characterize which connected patterns admit regular $F$-irregular hosts of every sufficiently large degree. Stars admit no regular $F$-irregular host; for every other $F$, every sufficiently large integer $r$ is realized by a connected $r$-regular $F$-irregular graph of diameter two and order $r+o(r)$, optimal to first order. For triangles, and equivalently four-vertex paths in regular graphs, we construct such hosts of order less than $r+73r^{\log29/\log58}$ above an explicit threshold, with the constant reduced to $44$ for even $r$. Lexicographic words encode distinct rooted subgraph counts, while layered connections allow the common degree to be prescribed. Rooted-homomorphism expansions and spectral amplification establish separation for general patterns; an exact uniform-increment identity gives the quantitative triangle construction. The finite seed graphs are explicitly constructed, and their required rooted-count distinctions are verified by exact-arithmetic certificates.

title: A Cooperative Game Theoretic Model for Sustainable, Smallholder Carbon Farming
abstract: Carbon farming offers a promising path to improve farmer livelihoods, mitigate climate change, and make farming sustainable. However, smallholder farmers, who dominate agriculture in developing economies, face structural barriers to participating in carbon farming due to high certification costs, limited landholdings, and limited budgets available to them. In this paper, we develop a cooperative game-theoretic framework to study how coalition formation can enable viable and profitable participation of smallholder farmers in carbon farming.
