Here, an alternative and elementary derivation for the spin conductivity expression is presented. This is done within the context of perturbation theory. It indicates that our derived expression for the $\mathcal{T}$-even ($\mathcal{T}$ for time reversal) spin conductivity agrees exactly with those derived from the Kubo linear response theory and quantum kinetic theory. In addition, the expression for the $\mathcal{T}$-odd spin conductivity in the clean limit is exactly consistent with those presented previously. We show that the $\mathcal{T}$-odd ($\mathcal{T}$-even) spin conductivity arises from the contribution of zeroth-order (first-order) wave function correction. Our work provides some physical insight into the spin conductivity from the perturbation theory and shines more light on the charge-to-spin conversion mechanism in magnetic materials.

title: Studying the Fullerene Nest: JWST Observations of the Planetary Nebula Tc 1. III. Tracing Fullerene-Linked Dust Variation
abstract: We have observed the fullerene-rich planetary nebula Tc 1 with the MIRI/MRS on JWST. The mid-infrared spectra of this spatially resolved source reveal that the dust emission is not co-spatial with the fullerene emission. Three broad features can be distinguished: a 6$\unicode{x2013}$9 $μ$m plateau, a 9$\unicode{x2013}$13 $μ$m plateau and the 30 $μ$m feature. The 6$\unicode{x2013}$9 $μ$m plateau does not change shape spectrally across the entire field of view, indicating it is produced by stochastically heated material. Spectral variations of the 9$\unicode{x2013}$13 $μ$m plateau reveal at least three distinct components, peaking at 9.5 $μ$m, 11 $μ$m and 12 $μ$m respectively. SiC produces most likely at least the 11 $μ$m component and we find evidence that the 12 $μ$m component might be produced by SiC grains too. The variation in relative strength of these components across the field of view hints at dust processing taking place in Tc 1. The 9.5 $μ$m component of the 9$\unicode{x2013}$13 $μ$m plateau has a strong correlation with the SiC component(s) and is thus likely produced by similar material.

title: When Calibration Data Matter in Sub-4-Bit Language Model Quantization
abstract: Low-bit post-training quantization reduces language-model memory but can sharply degrade downstream task accuracy. Calibration usually relies on generic text, but when task-informed data recover accuracy and which quantizers benefit remain poorly understood. We introduce FragCal-DC, which supplements generic text with training documents from task families with low retention of full-precision accuracy in a two-bit scan. We use a two- to four-bit sweep to locate functional regimes and four-seed calibration comparisons to evaluate six data-dependent methods across six dense models (1.7B-8B) and ten tasks. At their lowest tested functional bit widths, iterative SignRound V2 and OmniQuant improve at two bits, whereas single-pass GPTQ and AWQ show small mean responses at three bits. At two bits, SignRound V2 gains 1.83 percentage points in mean ten-task accuracy over generic-text calibration across six models. At 70 billion parameters, GPTQ and SignRound V2 both improve at two bits, with functional generic-calibration baselines. For two-bit SignRound V2, task-level controls show that recovery concentrates on families included in calibration, while incorrect answer designations retain about 90% of the mean accuracy gain. Changes in reconstruction error do not consistently track accuracy gains. These findings support task-informed calibration as a design principle for preserving downstream accuracy in low-bit quantization.

title: Two barriers for minimal time firing squads, with applications to four and five states
abstract: A minimal-time solution of the firing squad synchronization problem synchronizes every line of n cells at time 2n minus 2. Six states suffice; whether five do has been open since 1987. Every line agrees with the half line until its right ends echo returns. For minimal time solutions with any number of states, we prove that cells at distance j behind the half lines front become time-periodic only after time (1.5 minus epsilon)j, for every epsilon greater than 0 and infinitely many j, and that the half line is never periodic in time and space on a wedge at its left border, hence not eventually regular in our sense. With certified satisfiability checks, we exclude four states using the lines of lengths 2 to 5 and parts of the next five, and show that every five state minimal time solution uses at least 15 non quiescent neighbourhoods on its half lines first 78 anti-diagonals. We give five state rules synchronizing exactly the lengths 2 to 14.

title: A Hierarchical Tokenization Framework for Voxel-Level fMRI Representation Learning
abstract: We introduce HBAR (Hierarchical Brain Activity Representation), a hierarchical tokenization framework for learning compact, multi-scale representations of neuroimaging data. HBAR organizes voxel-level resting-state fMRI into a hierarchy spanning sub-parcel voxel groups, parcels, and large-scale functional networks, enabling up to 415x compression while preserving fine-grained spatial information beyond conventional parcellation. The framework supports fixed atlas-based, fully learned, and softly prior-guided hierarchies, allowing us to systematically study the role of structured priors in brain representation learning. On HCP-YA, at approximately 415x compression, HBAR achieves higher parcel and network correlations than rate-matched flat tokenizers, while at a lower 52x compression rate, shuffling the anatomical grouping reduces parcel correlation from 0.920 to 0.886. Demographic readouts with autoregressive training also reveal potential gains from the hierarchical structure. By combining sub-parcel inputs, compact discrete tokens, and multiscale brain structure, HBAR offers a practical framework for representation learning in high-dimensional neuroimaging data.

title: A seven-element interval of power-semiring varieties
abstract: We determine the interval between the varieties generated by the nonempty and full power semirings of a semigroup satisfying \(xy\approx x^2\). It has two elements for a one-element semigroup, three for a nontrivial left-zero or null semigroup, and seven otherwise, without any finiteness assumption. In the seven-element case the interval is \([\Rvar,\Rvar^0]\), where \(\Rvar=\Mod_{\rm ai}\{xy\approx xz\}\) and \(\Rvar^0\) is its zero-adjunction variety. Every word absorption valid in \(\Rvar\) but not in \(\Rvar^0\) is equivalent over \(\Rvar^0\) to one of six relative identities. We give exact absorption criteria and finite bases for all seven varieties. Three have basis rank two and four have basis rank three; their two-generated free algebras have orders \(15\), \(24\), or \(35\). We also count the finite-rank free algebras of both endpoints.

title: Who Benefits from Wikipedia's Growth Mentorship? The Role of Newcomer Information Needs
abstract: Evaluations of Wikipedia's programs for new editors usually ask whether a program works on average; we ask which newcomers benefit when their question to a mentor gets a reply. English Wikipedia's Growth mentorship system assigns every new account a volunteer mentor, and about a quarter of the questions newcomers send never get a reply. Using the first questions of 34,073 newcomers (2021 to 2026), we compare newcomers who received a reply with similar newcomers who did not, matched on 164 characteristics recorded before the question (propensity score stratification). (1) Does a reply help newcomers keep editing? Yes, in the short term: in the 14 days after the reply, newcomers who received one were 1.8 percentage points (pp) more likely to edit an article (22% vs. an estimated 20% without a reply) and 1.8pp more likely to edit on two or more days. Later in the first year, the only difference that remains significant after correction for multiple testing is in the share who edit an article at least once between six months and one year after the reply (+1.5pp). (2) Does the effect depend on what the newcomer asked? Yes. We sort questions by Morrison's (1993) information-seeking types, which earlier studies measured mostly through self-reports, using a language model checked against human labels. A reply has significant effects for questions about rules and norms (+3.4pp), questions that show the newcomer's earlier editing (+3.4pp) and specific how-to questions (+2.4pp). For newcomers who do not know what to work on, a reply has no detectable effect, and the effect is 4.2pp smaller than for newcomers with other questions. (3) Which replies are followed by more editing? Among newcomers who received a reply, those whose reply came sooner or stayed closer to the topic of their question edited more.

title: Towards large-scale ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Efficient Sampling-based Quantum Computing Algorithms
abstract: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) requires the calculation of highly accurate electronic-structure energies and nuclear forces at every time step, which can quickly become computationally expensive. Sample-based quantum diagonalization offers a route to such calculations on quantum hardware, but its use in AIMD simulations has so far been limited to active spaces of about 20 qubits. In these spaces, exact diagonalization is tractable, and the quantum circuits are typically built from standard coupled-cluster amplitudes. Here, we introduce SqDRIFT-AIMD, which combines randomized sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SqDRIFT) with analytical nuclear gradients. With SqDRIFT-AIMD, we obtain more accurate ground-state energies than the conventional coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) driven AIMD simulation for the $40$-qubit active space. We apply SqDRIFT-AIMD to study the dynamics of proton transfer in the Zundel cation, using circuits executed on IBM Heron r3 quantum processors. SqDRIFT energies fall below CCSD across the $40$-qubit double-well PES and stay within a few m$E_\text{h}$ of CCSD at 52 qubits. The $40$-qubit SqDRIFT-AIMD trajectory tracks the SHCI-driven proton transfer to within $1.33$ mÅ and exhibits excellent total energy conservation, with a standard deviation of only $0.245$ m$E_\text{h}$. These results extend quantum-centric AIMD to active spaces beyond the reach of exact diagonalization.

title: ObjectWorld: Scaling Object-Centric World Models with A Large-Scale 3D Full-Object Flow Dataset
abstract: Generative world modeling from large-scale visual data offers a promising path toward scalable robot manipulation. This calls for an intermediate representation that can be supervised at scale and remains actionable for downstream control. We propose 3D full-object flow, an object-centric motion representation that assigns dense 3D trajectories to points across the complete surface of a target object, including its occluded regions. By extending visible-surface object flow to the full object geometry, this representation makes complete object motion explicit and applies uniformly to both rigid and deformable objects. To realize the potential of this representation at scale, we introduce a 1210-hour full-object flow dataset that addresses the scarcity of large-scale supervision for complete 3D object motion. The dataset integrates diverse real-world videos and physical simulations, with a scalable annotation pipeline for recovering full-object motion from real-world observations and quality metrics for systematically assessing annotation quality. We then train a world model that takes an image and a task description as input and predicts dense full-object flow over the reconstructed object geometry. Experiments show reliable annotation quality, data-scalable flow prediction, and effective downstream manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments. Project website with additional results and videos: https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/ObjectWorld/.

title: A reachability criterion for spectrally factorable SPDC in coupled waveguides without periodic poling
abstract: Producing spectrally pure photon pairs by spontaneous parametric down-conversion without periodic poling would broaden the choice of nonlinear materials. It requires optical modes that provide both phase matching and suitable group velocities. We derive a joint reachability criterion for a constant-cross-section coupler with a nonlinear main guide and a linear auxiliary. In a two-mode description, phase closure fixes the hybridization parameter that also determines the main-guide participation and the attainable group-delay ratio. This relation screens material and mode pairs and specifies detuning and participation targets for full-vector refinement. A first-order purity map connects the reachable delay ratio and bandwidth--length product to the photon-pair spectrum. A full-vector AlN/TiO$_2$ feasibility example satisfies direct phase matching with a ratio of pump--idler to pump--signal group-delay mismatches of $-0.899$ and yields a calculated unfiltered Schmidt purity of 0.789 over 5 mm. The criterion links phase closure, dispersion control, and nonlinear participation when assessing coupled-waveguide sources beyond periodically poled materials.

title: SoftPAT3D: Physics-Augmented Text-to-3D Scene Generation with Deformables
abstract: We present SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented framework for text-to-3D scene generation in which deformable objects, such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes, are generated as physically valid, simulation-ready bodies and placed in intersection-free contact with the furniture that supports them, with one another and with themselves. Existing physics-augmented pipelines simulate rigid bodies only and cannot accommodate a generated deformable object, which text-to-3D generation returns as a geometrically invalid mesh, sometimes self-intersecting, that has no rest shape, no material model and no admissible initial state. These are the inputs a deformable simulation requires, and we construct each from information already in the pipeline. The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured rather than from the generated physically inconsistent deformed configuration, and a material library assigns each deformable object its initial elastic parameters, which can then be optimized. The occluded support is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, each object is released from an optimizable placement above the supporting part that the prompt specifies, and the complete scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with completion verified by geometric checks and a vision-language model. When a scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, and the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same contact energy reaches the targets the grid does not, places several bodies jointly and recovers and optimizes material parameters. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, and the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone. On all sixty-five prompts, SoftPAT3D produces no undesired interpenetration of any kind, whereas every other system does, and its scenes directly support scene editing and robotic manipulation.

title: Dual Model Predictive Control through Sampling-Based Belief Propagation
abstract: We propose a sampling-based dual model predictive control (MPC) approach that combines belief propagation with parameterized feedback policy optimization. By sampling uncertain dynamics and process noise, we approximate the evolution of the hyperstate over the prediction horizon, allowing future control decisions to adapt to anticipated observations and belief updates. This enables the controller to account for the future value of information without explicit exploration incentives. We establish almost-sure uniform convergence of the sample-average objective to the finite-horizon expected objective over a compact policy class. The approach is specialized to Bayesian linear regression and evaluated on stochastic systems with constant and time-varying uncertain dynamics. We compare our approach to certainty equivalent control, and an MPC that optimizes over open-loop control sequences rather than feedback policies, demonstrating the benefits of our method in terms of both control performance and information gain.

title: Control-Aware Command Generation for Asynchronous Control and Action Inference with Vision-Based Policies towards Fast Execution
abstract: Vision-based control policies, including vision-language-action models, have enabled robots to perform increasingly complex tasks. However, their execution speed is often limited by the high computational cost of action inference. In this work, we investigate what can be achieved at the control level without modifying the underlying policy learning process. We introduce an asynchronous inference and control framework that enables fast task execution while maintaining smooth and stable robot motions. By formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous model predictions as a tracking control problem, our method makes asynchronous inference practical for real robots. We further accelerate execution through adaptive action skipping based on the variance of predicted positions. Experiments with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot demonstrate substantial speedups while preserving high task success rates.

title: Large-Scale Hierarchical Decision-Making in Robot Control via ADMM
abstract: Sparse hierarchical nonlinear programming (SH-NLP) based on the $\ell_0$-norm provides a powerful framework for integrated, efficient hierarchical decision-making in robot kinematic control, for example in the presence of a large set of possible end-effector candidate locations. While Sequential Sparse Hierarchical Quadratic Programming (S-SHQP) with interior-point method based SHQP sub-problem solvers exploit the hierarchical, sparse structure of such problems, they are less amenable to effective warm-starting between subsequent, coherent control steps. In this work, we formulate an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to efficiently solve related SHQP sub-problems. We introduce efficient substitutions for auxiliary variables representing $\ell_0$-norm surrogates. The solver efficiently handles separable decision functions by evaluating linear algebra expressions in the appropriate order. Results in large-scale kinematic and dynamic control show reduced computation times of up to 23.5% compared with a structure-exploiting interior-point method in low- to moderate-accuracy regimes. Furthermore, hierarchical decision-making is extended to whole-body dynamic control for humanoid walking, where the need for high-accuracy solutions is highlighted.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Reward Labeling for Reinforcement Learning under Limited Feedback
abstract: In reinforcement learning from limited feedback (RLLF), only a small fraction of an offline dataset can be labeled with rewards, and the central question is which samples should be labeled to learn a high-performing policy from the resulting partially labeled dataset. Prior work formalized this as a reward-selection problem by focusing on the selection stage while treating downstream policy learning as a black box, in a regime where queried rewards are not retained for reward-model training. We instead study the retained-label setting, where queried rewards can be stored and used to fit a reward model before policy learning. We bound the suboptimality of the learned policy in terms of two sources of error: one arising from offline RL on a fixed, offline dataset, and the other from uncertainty in the reward model. Since reward selection cannot change the offline dataset, the limited labeling budget must be used to strategically reduce reward uncertainty. Motivated by RLLF's observation that useful rewards tend to keep the agent on high-return trajectories, we introduce Successor-Guided Uncertainty REduction (SURE), a novel method that uses successor features to select rewards that are both uncertain and associated with states from which high-valued states are reachable. We formally derive SURE from a bound-induced design objective and characterize its exact one-step marginal gain. Empirically, SURE reaches near full-feedback performance with few reward labels across a variety of domains and offline-RL backbones, yielding an effective method for feedback-efficient reinforcement learning.

title: Twisted pencils of quartics, braid monodromy factorizations, and non-Hopfian Hurwitz curves
abstract: We study which groups arise as fundamental groups of complements of affine Hurwitz curves. In every such group the product of the meridians is central and maps to the vector of component degrees in homology; this rules out, for instance, the Baumslag-Solitar groups $\operatorname{BS}(p,q)$ with $\lvert p\rvert\neq\lvert q\rvert$, and the groups of links with at least two components and vanishing linking numbers. O. V. Kulikova circumvented this obstruction for $\operatorname{BS}(2,3)$ by passing to the non-Hopfian group $\operatorname{BS}(2,3)\times\mathbb{Z}$, which Vik. S. Kulikov's doubling algorithm realizes in degree $768$. We give an explicit braid monodromy factorization of degree 12 with this group. The corresponding curve is not isotopic to an algebraic curve, yet it is obtained from a union of three quartics in a pencil by a single twist along a circle. More generally, for every closed braid $\hatβ$ we realize $π_1(S^3\setminus\hatβ)\times\mathbb{Z}$ by an explicit Hurwitz curve, again a twist of a union of quartics in a pencil. In the other direction, a Hurwitz curve with group $\operatorname{BS}(k,k+1)\times\mathbb{Z}$ has degree at least $4$, as every Hurwitz curve consisting of a conic and a line is H-isotopic to an algebraic one, after separation of its critical points. Finally, we show that certain semiholomorphic germs, among them those realizing the generalized Borromean rings, are braided surfaces but not Hurwitz curve germs.

title: Does Pose Encoding Matter? Analyzing Geometric Representations for Discrete Motion Vocabulary Learning
abstract: Compressing continuous human motion into a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens is now the first stage of many motion understanding and generation pipelines. Vector quantization partitions a latent space into Voronoi cells around a finite codebook, but the geometry of that latent space is inherited from the input pose encoding, and it is unclear which encoding admits an efficient discretization. We study four encodings that place skeletal motion in different geometric spaces: Gaussian joint heatmaps on the pixel lattice, which we show to be a morphological dilation of the joint point set by a quadratic structuring function; root-relative joint positions in Euclidean space; local joint rotations on $\SO$ through a continuous 6D embedding; and a redundant full kinematic encoding. For each, we train VQ-VAE tokenizers whose codebooks lie on the unit hypersphere, varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension. Beyond reconstruction, we measure codebook utilization and the effective vocabulary size, i.e., the number of equiprobable spherical Voronoi cells with the same entropy as the observed token distribution. Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty. The smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings, and the effect of temporal stride depends on the encoding. Encodings of the same pose family can thus yield effective vocabularies differing by an order of magnitude, a difference that reconstruction loss alone does not reveal, which points to input geometry as a first-order design choice in motion tokenization.

title: Is Dark Energy Inhomogeneous?
abstract: The discovery of dark matter deficient galaxies motivates a fundamental question: Could sufficiently large regions of the Universe be deficient in dark energy as well? We investigate this possibility by developing a phenomenological framework that distinguishes genuine dark energy deficiencies from ordinary matter voids through nonlinear expansion, coherent peculiar velocities and density-momentum correlations. We show that a $10\%$ dark energy deficiency can suppress the expansion of a representative nonlinear void by approximately $2.7\%$, generating peculiar velocity residuals of order $60$-$100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ across scales of $30$-$50\, Mpc$. Intriguingly, we find that deficiencies of order $20\%$ extending over several hundred megaparsecs could also influence the locally inferred Hubble constant, potentially contributing to the $H_0$ tension, subject to stringent isotropy and dynamical consistency constraints. We identify observational strategies involving DESI, Rubin, peculiar velocity surveys, and cosmic void catalogues, opening a new avenue for testing whether the dark energy driving cosmic acceleration is truly homogeneous.

title: Study of the weak radiative decay $B_c^+\to B_u^{\ast+}γ$
abstract: We investigate the rare radiative decay $B_c \to B_u^\astγ$ within the Standard Model by using the instantaneous Bethe-Salpeter (BS) approach. The short distance (SD) $c \to uγ$ penguin, weak annihilation, and long distance (LD) vector meson dominance (VMD) contributions are all included. In the calculation of LD contribution, we use two scenarios, namely the decay width of $ρ$ being set to zero or kept as the experimental value, which gives $\mathrm{Br}_{\rm LD}=5.0\times10^{-9}$ and $7.3\times10^{-8}$, respectively, indicating an important role of $Γ_ρ$ in the calculation. The SD contribution is comparable in magnitude to the LD contributions, but one order larger than the annihilation contribution. This shows the $B_c \to B_u^\astγ$ channel can provide an important way to study the flavor changing neutral current processes of charm quark.

title: The Role of Small-Scale Flux Emergence in Pre-eruptive Magnetic Destabilization
abstract: Recent high-resolution observations have reported the emergence of small-scale magnetic flux shortly before the onset of solar flares; however, their role in solar eruption processes remains unclear. In this study, we perform three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to examine the effect of small-scale emerging flux on the eruption process. We construct a bipolar active region by extrapolating a potential magnetic field from a pair of sunspots and drive the system with sustained rotational motions to build up strong shear along the polarity inversion line. A small-scale emerging flux, amounting to approximately 0.6%-3.0% of the total magnetic flux and having a polarity opposite to that of the main sunspot, is then introduced at the center of the bipole. As a result, although no significant differences are found in the pre-existing magnetic field during the early phase with or without the emerging flux, the current sheet formed in the sheared field lines collapses more rapidly, and the reconnection-driven eruption is initiated earlier in the case with small-scale emerging flux. This result suggests that small-scale emerging flux accelerates the destabilization of the pre-eruptive magnetic configuration through enhanced current-sheet thinning and magnetic reconnection, leading to an earlier eruption onset. Furthermore, we find that the involvement of highly twisted field lines during the pre-eruption phase plays a crucial role in determining the eruption onset time.

title: QoS-Aware Energy-Efficient Sub-THz Near-Field Multiuser Hybrid MIMO Systems Employing Circular Arrays
abstract: Near-field communications have emerged as a promising technology for future sixth-generation (6G) networks. However, designing energy-efficient hybrid beamfocusing schemes for multiuser (MU) systems remains challenging due to the non-convex quality-of-service (QoS) constraints and hardware limitations of hybrid architectures. In this paper, we investigate a hybrid massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) architecture for a near-field sub-THz MU downlink system employing a large uniform circular array (UCA) at the base station. A QoS-aware transmit power minimization problem is formulated for energy-efficient beamfocusing and addressed through a two-stage penalty-driven joint optimization (PDJO) framework, where auxiliary variables are introduced to reformulate the QoS constraints into second-order cone (SOC) constraints. Furthermore, a near-field polar-domain codebook is developed via joint angle- and distance-domain sampling. We establish that the fully digital (FD) beamfocuser lies within the column space of the proposed codebook, enabling hybrid precoder design to be formulated as a multiple measurement vector (MMV)-based sparse approximation problem. The formulated problem is then solved using a low-complexity simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm under hardware and transmit power constraints. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves spectral- and energy-efficiency performance close to the ideal FD beamfocusing scheme while providing a favorable trade-off between hardware complexity and system performance.

title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

title: Covariant Hamiltonian Gravity in Spherical Symmetry
abstract: Building upon the covariant Hamiltonian gravity in spherical symmetry, we construct the effective Einstein equation governing gravitational dynamics. For any prescribed one-parameter family of static, spherically symmetric metrics, this equation can be constructed such that the prescribed family constitutes their vacuum solutions. As an application, we construct generalized Vaidya solutions to the effective Einstein equation and show that the corresponding energy-momentum tensor takes precisely the standard Vaidya form. The results demonstrate that standard null dust sources can serve as matter source for dynamical black-hole geometries beyond general relativity, including regular black holes. Furthermore, this work suggests that quantum gravity corrections alone may not account for Hawking-like evaporation, as mass loss in the ingoing Vaidya solution necessarily requires a violation of the null energy condition within our effective framework.

title: Application-Defined Abstractions to Separate Numerical Intent from Computation Orchestration
abstract: In High-performance Computing the holy grail has been to translate numerical algorithms expressed in mathematical notation into code that performs well across a range of platforms. A variety of portability frameworks have abstracted data layout, parallelization and orchestration from application's view, however, the resulting format is still code that conforms to the idioms of the framework. Additionally, substantial refactoring is typically needed to achieve performance goals. Increasing sophistication of Large Language Models (LLMs) naturally raises the question whether they can be used to make application codes and/or solvers both portable and performant. The obstacle is the lack of correctness guarantee in LLM produced code. In this paper we pose the question differently -- can we start with expressing numerical intent of the code into an immutable core arithmetic component isolated from the surrounding code such that the surrounding code can be safely generated by the LLMs? We answer this question by using Spark, a mature compressible hydrodynamics solver in Flash-X, a multiphysics software system. We use LLM assistance in devising the abstractions and embedding them in the solver. Once properly verified, the resulting solver is lowered to concrete realization deterministically with tools also built with LLM assistance. The driver of the numerics and the code for interfacing with the application are generated by the LLMs. The resulting solver is exercised within Flash-X and with a separate environment we built for this experiment. Our results show that this is a viable approach for producing correct and performance portable code.

title: Feasibility-Aware Learning for Network-Constrained Unit Commitment
abstract: Learning-based approaches to network-constrained unit commitment (NCUC) usually still rely on an optimization solver to repair or complete their predictions, which limits the speedup they can deliver. This paper proposes FALCON-UC, a feasibility-aware graph learning framework that predicts commitment and dispatch jointly and produces final schedules without solving a mixed-integer program at inference time. It combines an LSTM--GraphSAGE predictor over a fully connected generator graph, a differentiable correction that embeds commitment-dependent dispatch bounds, power balance, and PTDF-based branch flows in training, and deterministic commitment, dispatch, and ramp-coupled reserve repairs at inference. On the 2383-bus system, FALCON-UC achieves $99.09\%$ commitment accuracy and a $0.4350\%$ mean absolute cost gap with all evaluated constraints within tolerance at $0.0562$ s per instance, a $2.27\times10^{3}$ speedup over the solver. MTLR R-SCUC-FL is slightly more accurate but still needs an optimization solver to complete each schedule, which takes $262.2$ s per instance, $4.67\times10^{3}$ times the FALCON-UC runtime. A label-only baseline without repair violates the balance and branch limits on every 2383-bus test instance, and FALCON-UC also meets all evaluated constraint tolerances on a 1354-bus system.

title: Task presentation and execution paths shape LLM mathematical performance
abstract: Mathematical performance depends on how a language model receives information, uses generated text and submits an answer. We study these dependencies through paired comparisons that separate submission requirements, draft reuse and candidate availability. On 65 development problems, an instruction permitting continued derivation produced no valid final answers in 390 short-output calls; a single-line submission instruction produced 390 format-valid outputs, including 389 parseable answers. Under the fixed submission protocol, 198 problems with failed initial submissions were answered correctly in 9.09p of cases with the question alone, 33.84p with its draft, 46.46p with candidates, and 59.60p with both. Drafts added 13.13 percentage points with candidates fixed, and candidates added 25.76 points with drafts fixed; both effects were significant after Holm correction and were subadditive on the accuracy scale. Retaining a trailing excerpt outperformed retaining a leading excerpt of similar average length by 10.10 points Holm-adjusted p 0.027. A second completion model showed the same directions of input effects on the fixed materials. In a cohort with parseable initial submissions, candidates added no correct answers when the previous draft was supplied, but added 27 points when it was absent. These results establish a conditional value of generated text: a failed submission can leave useful material, whose contribution depends on what else is supplied and what is retained.

title: An In-Ear Sleep Modulation SoC Featuring a CNN-LSTM Accelerator with Long-Kernel Memory Reuse and Runtime Dynamic Quantization
abstract: This work presents a 65 nm SoC for closed-loop in-ear sleep modulation. The SoC performs low-noise in-ear EEG sensing, CNN-LSTM-based sleep stage classification, and phase-specific auditory stimulation under 1 mW. A dedicated accelerator is developed, featuring a memory reuse technique to efficiently process long kernels required for low-frequency EEG feature extraction. A runtime dynamic quantization is incorporated, reducing model size by 3.88 times with only a 0.28% loss in accuracy. A sensitivity of 98.3% is achieved for deep sleep detection, enabling effective sleep modulation.

title: Tracing MCP Security Vulnerabilities: Constructing and Analyzing an MCP Security Vulnerability Dataset
abstract: As a core protocol for integrating large language models (LLMs) with external data sources and tools, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has quickly become a key interface in emerging AI agent systems. As the MCP ecosystem expands, reported vulnerabilities have also increased, creating a growing software-security attack surface. However, MCP vulnerability information remains scattered, noisy, and difficult to study systematically. This paper addresses that gap by constructing a curated MCP vulnerability dataset from CVE disclosures. Starting from 119 MCP-related records retrieved through February 2026, we filter unrelated cases out and obtain a validated snapshot of 24 MCP vulnerabilities. Our filtering methodology explicitly addresses acronym ambiguity and achieves 96.7% inter-rater agreement on a sampled exclusion audit while retaining all known high-severity MCP cases identified in public advisories. Using this initial dataset snapshot, we find that 87.5% of validated vulnerabilities are Critical or High severity, and that injection and path traversal vulnerabilities account for 66.7% of cases. We further identify recurring issues involving insufficient input validation, inadequate access control, and protocol-level security gaps. Through six representative case studies, we illustrate common exploitation patterns and map them to practical defenses. We release the dataset, reproducibility tooling, and a sustainable maintenance workflow as a foundation for future MCP security measurement, benchmarking, and defense research.

title: Local exact boundary controllability for the full compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations
abstract: In this paper, we are concerned with the local exact boundary controllability for the full compressible magnetohydrodynamic equations in a bounded domain in two and three space dimensions. We establish the local exact controllability around a constant equilibrium state. Our proof relies on the observability and controllability analysis of a suitably reformulated linearized system, together with a fixed point argument in weighted Sobolev spaces. The main novelty of this paper is to overcome the structural difficulties arising from the divergence free constraint and the strong coupling between the fluid and magnetic variables. To accommodate the solenoidal constraint, we introduce a magnetic potential formulation and develop a mixed coordinate approach.

title: Jointly Optimizing Memory, Computing and Offloading for Energy-Efficient DNN Inference
abstract: In edge intelligence systems, computation offloading and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) are widely used to improve energy efficiency. However, as applications like deep neural network (DNN) inference evolve in complexity, their demands for memory resources have progressively increased, establishing memory as a critical bottleneck that impacts both latency and energy consumption. In this paper, we propose a joint optimization scheme integrating memory, computing and offloading for energy-efficient DNN inference. We formulate the energy minimization problem under deadline constraints as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, where the main challenge arises from the coupling between offloading and resource optimization. To address this issue, we decompose the original problem into two subproblems under a fixed offloading policy. The local subproblem is transformed into an equivalent geometric programming (GP) problem to derive the optimal memory frequency and computing frequency, while the edge subproblem is solved via convex optimization. An efficient coordinate descent (CD) algorithm is further developed to jointly optimize all variables. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with the gap from the optimal policy being at most 9.3%, and reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 16.1% compared with benchmarks without memory frequency optimization.

title: Probing faint radio activity from cores to filaments in two $z=2.24$ protoclusters with uGMRT
abstract: We present deep 1.26 GHz radio continuum observations of the two $z=2.24$ protoclusters BOSS1244 and BOSS1542 with the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT) to investigate their members' radio emission and its possible environmental dependence. Among 187 and 105 H$α$ emitter (HAE) members in BOSS1244 and BOSS1542, we identify ten and two robust radio counterparts, respectively, together with five potential counterparts from forced photometry. Two HAEs and the massive quiescent galaxy QG1 in BOSS1244 show strong radio excesses relative to their H$α$-based star formation rates (SFRs) and are identified as strong radio-excess AGN candidates. Median stacking of the remaining 173 and 102 radio-undetected HAE members yields positive signals at $2.8σ$ and $3.2σ$ in BOSS1244 and BOSS1542, respectively. The stacked radio luminosities are consistent with those expected from the median H$α$-based SFRs, indicating that star formation can account for the average faint radio emission. After excluding the robust radio counterparts, we divided the HAE members by the projected distance from QG1 in BOSS1244 and from the filament spine in BOSS1542. The largest stacked radio luminosities are found toward the denser regions in both systems, but the differences are not statistically significant, and stellar mass shows no significant dependence on environmental distance. These results identify strong radio-excess AGN candidates among the individually detected members, while the faint HAE population is on average consistent with radio emission from star formation. The similar environmental ordering is suggestive but remains tentative. Deeper radio observations at multiple frequencies and higher angular resolution are required to determine whether this apparent trend reflects weak AGN activity or variations in radio emission associated with star formation.

title: Evaluating generative samplers for lattice field theory by scale
abstract: Generative samplers for lattice field theory are commonly evaluated by their effective sample size (ESS). We show that a small global ESS need not imply inaccurate long-distance observables: errors spread over many short-distance modes can dominate this diagnostic. We introduce a scale-resolved diagnostic based on the overlap between coarse-grained model and target distributions. At the lattice cutoff, this overlap determines the asymptotic ESS fraction; lower cutoffs isolate long-wavelength errors. In the exactly solvable free theory, two samplers with comparable ESS yield a $32\%$ bias and no bias in the susceptibility, respectively. In two-dimensional $ϕ^4$ theory near criticality, trained diffusion samplers show the same separation of scales: their path-weight ESS fraction falls rapidly over the volumes studied, while low moments of the magnetization remain close to their target values. Varying the reference parameters substantially changes infrared observables, with little effect on the log-weight variance. Given the target magnetization distribution, a marginal Metropolis test maintains an acceptance rate of order one in our tests. Combined with exact local updates, it reduces the remaining mismatch, although residual bias remains at finite relaxation length. In the free field, uniformly bounded relative errors in the proposal mode variances give a volume-independent bound on the number of updates needed for a prescribed accuracy of the chain's stationary mode variances at fixed correlation length. The target marginal must be supplied or computed separately; estimating it from the samplers' own weights can inherit the poor global overlap.

title: On Size-Biased Distributions and the Chainability of Positive Infinitely Divisible Distributions
abstract: Bar-Lev and Letac (2025) introduced the concept of chainability of infinitely divisible distributions on $\mathbb R$. In this note, we show that a simpler notion of chainability can be used for infinitely divisible distributions on $[0,\infty)$. We derive some properties and give a probabilistic interpretation in terms of so-called size-biased distributions. As an application, we discuss simulation from size-biased distributions associated with an important class of tempered stable distributions.

title: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
abstract: Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops Statopia Prover, an independent agent specialized for formalizing and proving results in statistics and machine learning, and Statlib, a Lean~4 library built with the prover and organized for automated use. The prover controls its own execution without relying on external coding agents. It is built for formal proof discovery and checking existing proofs. A natural-language proof, when available, guides its search but is not required: from a statement alone, the prover develops the argument itself and constructs a Lean proof. Its workflow integrates source preparation, statement review, library supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable proof development. Statlib's shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and its coverage of statistics keeps expanding. Verified results and usage feedback from the prover inform reviewed library updates, so that proof development drives this expansion. A cross-platform application provides an interactive workspace for uploading source files and running tasks locally or in the cloud.

title: Beyond Hard Labels: LLM Probabilities Improve Human-Assisted Regression
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text annotation, but their outputs are often reduced to a single categorical label before downstream analysis. This hardening step discards the model's relative support across categories, which may contain useful information when category boundaries are ambiguous. We study whether retaining the full probability vector improves downstream regression when LLM annotations are combined with a limited amount of human annotation. Using matched soft and hard representations from three LLMs across three social-science text datasets, we compare direct regression and human-assisted correction. Soft inputs are not uniformly better when used directly as outcomes, but after human correction, using the probability vector consistently improves regression efficiency across models and datasets. Analyses of repeated human judgments and controlled simulations further show that these gains arise when probability variation beyond the hard category carries useful information about the human-coded outcome. Our results identify output representation as an important design choice in LLM-assisted measurement and support preserving probability outputs for downstream statistical analysis. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/soft-label-LLM-D201/

title: The Effect of the U.S. Federal Production Tax Credit on Negative Energy Prices
abstract: Negative prices frequently arise in electricity markets and production subsidies are commonly cited as a leading cause. Using data from the U.S. Eastern Interconnection wholesale electricity markets for the period 2000-2023, we document that at least 18 percent of the total hours with negative energy prices cannot solely be attributed to the federal production tax credit (PTC), a large, persistent production subsidy during the period of study. Next, we provide the first causal evidence that the PTC leads to negative energy prices. On average, increasing PTC-eligible wind generation by 1 percent increases the probability of a negative energy price by 3.4 percentage points. However, significant heterogeneity exists across electricity markets, and some markets show an effect that is an order of magnitude larger. Furthermore, the PTC explains only 10 percent of the observed negative prices that could potentially be attributable to it. Finally, we use the causal estimate to calculate a plausible value for the environmental benefits accrued from the PTC subsidy when energy prices are negative.

title: PCG-RAG: Progressive Compositional Grounding for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Complex Web Question Answering
abstract: Complex Web question answering requires retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems to identify target entities from multi-clue descriptions and connect evidence scattered across long Web pages. Individual pages often support only some of the required semantic constraints, while clues discovered on one page guide subsequent searches on others. However, premature reliance on partially supported entity hypotheses can divert retrieval from the original information need. RAG systems must therefore use partial evidence to guide further searches while seeking the evidence needed to establish the intended entities. We propose PCG-RAG, a novel RAG framework based on Progressive Compositional Grounding (PCG). Progressive Evidence Acquisition directs subsequent searches toward missing evidence for candidate attributes and relations. Compositional Reasoning separates candidate-guided retrieval from evidence-based answering along a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subquestions. Provisional names make dependent searches specific, while answering tasks use accepted results and unresolved identifying conditions, assessed against the original question. New passages connect the identifying clues to the requested relations, supporting evidence-based downstream answers. Evidence Grounding combines identifying and relational source passages with supported intermediate answers, connecting evidence across Web pages to the original conditions during final generation. On BrowseComp-Plus and WebWalkerQA, PCG-RAG improves accuracy over the leading compared baselines by 5.43 and 5.15 percentage points, respectively.

title: Compositional Conformal Risk Control for Multi-Stage LLM Cascades
abstract: Multi-stage large language model (LLM) cascades balance accuracy and inference cost, but reliable deployment also requires controlling error risk and identifying its sources across stages. We propose Compositional Conformal Risk Control (CompCRC), a risk-control framework for pre-specified multi-stage LLM cascades. We decompose the risk of accepting incorrect answers into additive stage-wise contributions over the full query population, linking local risk budgets to a system-level guarantee. CompCRC constructs and freezes candidate budget allocations and acceptance thresholds, selects one candidate on independent data, and certifies its stage-wise risk contributions on separate held-out data. Under conditional exchangeability, we establish a finite-sample guarantee: the marginal expected accepted-error risk of the complete deployment procedure does not exceed the global risk budget. At the reported comparison budget of $α=0.45$, all three stages of CompCRC pass their local checks on MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag. Compared with Global-CRC, which passes system-level risk certification at the same budget, CompCRC reduces observed accepted-error risk by 1.33--2.00 percentage points, improves final accuracy by 0.67--2.00 percentage points, and reduces weighted inference cost by 30.37\% on HellaSwag. The selected cost-based budget allocation also improves accuracy per unit cost by 10.6\%--46.7\% over uniform allocation. Further experiments show that stage-wise statistics identify stages that fail local certification checks, providing diagnostic information alongside system-level risk control.

title: MySign: A High-Fidelity Motion-Capture Dataset for 3D Sign Generation in Bahasa Isyarat Malaysia
abstract: Progress in 3D sign generation is constrained by the scarcity of high-fidelity 3D sign language datasets, a limitation that is particularly severe for under-resourced languages. We introduce MySign, the first motion-capture dataset for isolated signs in Bahasa Isyarat Malaysia (BIM). Its 5,000 samples cover 1,000 lexical items (glosses) and were produced by five Deaf native signers. Prior datasets that rely on SMPL-X parameters regressed from video provide pseudo-labels, which are often affected by depth ambiguity, inaccurate finger poses, and temporal jitter. MySign instead provides ground-truth SMPL-X sequences retargeted from recordings made with a motion-capture setup tailored for sign language; these sequences offer higher-fidelity motion, particularly in fine-grained hand and finger articulation. A controlled comparison on the same glosses and signers indicates that training on these sequences improves generation over training on such pseudo-labels. We establish MySign as a challenging benchmark for gloss-conditioned 3D sign generation: state-of-the-art models produce visually plausible outputs but fall short of the ground truth, most notably in fine-grained articulation, revealing persistent gaps in modeling articulated sign motion. In contrast, recognition baselines consistently achieve high lexical accuracy, indicating that the dataset reliably supports supervised learning. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/mysigner/MySign

title: Query-Only Prompt-Agnostic Attacks on Visual In-Context Learning
abstract: Visual In-Context Learning (VICL) enables promptable segmentation by conditioning RGB predictions on visual demonstrations, making it attractive for auto-labeling, but its robustness under query-only access and unknown deployment prompts remains underexplored. We study query-only, prompt-agnostic targeted attacks where the attacker observes only returned RGB outputs, without access to model internals or deployment prompts. Treating prompt-conditioned RGB rendering as a distinct attack surface, we introduce two appearance-space attacks: Color Hijack (CH) drives foreground colors toward the background to suppress visibility, while Task Hijack (TH) collapses instance-distinguishing colors toward a shared color assignment. To transfer across unseen prompts, we propose a Self-Prompt Surrogate (SPS) constructed from the clean query and its output. In a paired, matched-budget SegGPT comparison, SPS outperforms the Random-Prompt Surrogate (RPS), reducing CH instance foreground retention from 0.918 to 0.155 and TH palette-aware tolerance distance from 0.345 to 0.225. Across four VICL models on COCO and HierText, CH suppresses foregrounds across semantic-, instance-, and text-style outputs, while TH collapses instance colors under held-out deployment prompts. After palette-based decoding, TH also reduces the decoded instance count and mask retention while increasing instance merges. Finally, at 30% corruption, CH-corrupted annotations from a publicly accessible VICL-based auto-labeling pipeline reduce downstream YOLO-seg mAP50 from 0.761 to 0.281.

title: Keel: A Verified In-Kernel Proof Checker for Proof Carrying BPF
abstract: Recent systems such as the eBPF Certificate Framework (BCF) and Proof-Carrying BPF address the imprecision in the Linux eBPF verifier with proof-carrying code. When the verifier's abstract domains cannot prove a safety condition, an in-kernel proof checker checks an untrusted user-space refutation proof. A single bug in this checker can compromise the security of the entire kernel. While formalizing BCF's in-kernel checker, we discovered 13 bugs such as unsound rewrite rules, silently unchecked proof steps, and memory safety errors. We demonstrate that forged certificates can trick the kernel to accept arbitrary unsafe eBPF programs. To address this problem, we propose Keel, a formally verified in-kernel proof checker for the Linux eBPF verifier. First, we specify the checker as a pure functional program in Lean and prove its soundness against bit-vector semantics. We decouple the steps of the proof certificate checker from the mathematical rewrite rules, which enables us to extend the rewrite rules without the need to change the checker. Second, we implement the checker in EmbC, a deeply embedded C fragment, and prove that our C implementation refines the functional specification without undefined behavior or memory leaks. Third, using an amortized potential argument, we prove linear time and memory bounds for the C checker. Keel is correct-by-construction while also being faster than the BCF checker inside the kernel, 1.3X in total and 2.0X on the slowest 1.4% of certificates.

title: When gene summaries reveal the answers: Gene Ontology circularity in gene embedding benchmarks
abstract: A gene summary can contain the very annotations used to evaluate an embedding of its text. The Alliance of Genome Resources converts Gene Ontology (GO) annotations into sentences, which NCBI Gene displays and GenePT includes in its input. These summaries covered 6,172 of 19,256 human protein-coding genes (32.1%), including 58% of genes with one to ten linked publications. We embedded the same corpus with and without the generated summaries and refitted a function-prediction probe on each version. Among genes with one to ten publications, removal reduced the reported per-gene area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) by 0.078 with a linear probe (95% bootstrap interval 0.072-0.084) and by 0.033 with a multilayer perceptron. These estimates use a historical GO scorer that mishandled ties. The original predictions are unavailable for rescoring. A simple TF-IDF encoder also benefited from the summaries, as did models evaluated only on experimental annotations. Replacing generated summaries with UniProt function descriptions recovered much of the lost performance despite little verbatim overlap. UniProt also curates many of the evaluation labels. In mouse and yeast, we found a similar dependence on the source of the description. We introduce GeneProv to compare encoders on matched text and to examine how representation rankings change across GO recovery, non-GO endpoints and co-essentiality.

title: Scalable Neural Safety Certification via Monotonicity
abstract: Learning-based safety certification offers a promising route for verifying complex dynamical systems when explicit models are unavailable, but existing data-driven methods often scale poorly: they treat the system as a black box, rely on dense discretizations or Lipschitz bounds, and consequently suffer from sample complexity that grows exponentially with dimension. This paper shows that a common structural property of dynamical systems--monotonicity--can be used to break this curse of dimensionality. We develop a data-driven framework for robust safety verification and safe controller synthesis for unknown monotone systems using only simulator queries. Our main theoretical result proves that, for monotone systems with upper-closed unsafe sets, safety is completely characterized by the existence of monotone inductive barrier certificates. This structure reduces certificate verification over continuous state spaces to localized boundary checks over finitely many cells. To learn such certificates, we introduce Max-Monotone Networks, a monotone neural architecture with universal approximation guarantees for monotone functions. We then propose a training and refinement algorithm that, upon successful termination, returns formally valid neural barrier certificates and, under mild partition assumptions, requires only $O(n)$ simulator queries. Across high-dimensional benchmarks, including oscillator networks with up to $13{,}659$ states and traffic networks with $1{,}000$ states, our method certifies safety in regimes where prior approaches either do not converge or exceed memory limits. These results demonstrate that exploiting order structure can make neural safety certification both scalable and formally sound.

title: The Escobar Constant for Two-dimensional Disks
abstract: Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth compact Riemannian surface homeomorphic to a closed disk, with boundary length $L$. We establish sharp upper bounds for its Escobar constant under upper bounds on the Gaussian curvature. If $K_g\leq 0$, then $I(M,g)\leq 2/π$, with equality if and only if $(M,g)$ is isometric to a Euclidean disk. If $K_g\leqκ$ for some $κ>0$, $L<2π/\sqrtκ$, and $\operatorname{Area}_g(M)<2π/κ$, then $I(M,g)\leq\frac{4}{\sqrtκL}\arcsin(\frac{\sqrtκL}{2π})$, with equality if and only if $(M,g)$ is isometric to the geodesic disk of the same perimeter contained in an open hemisphere of the sphere of constant curvature $κ$. We also discuss the higher order Escobar constant for planar domains. In particular, we construct counterexamples to Hassannezhad and Siffert's conjecture.

title: Phase-Constrained Self-Supervised Reconstruction and Denoising for Ultra-High-Resolution MRI
abstract: Ultra-high-field gradient-echo (GRE) MRI reveals fine anatomy with strong susceptibility contrast, but small voxels reduce signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), while susceptibility-induced phase variation and wrapping complicate reconstruction. These challenges are especially consequential for quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM), which requires denoising GRE phase without blurring anatomy or distorting phase. We propose a measurement-domain self-supervised learning (SSL) framework for joint reconstruction and denoising of complex-valued images from a single noisy acquisition. By splitting acquired k-space samples into input and held-out subsets, the method trains without clean or fully sampled references. An explicit phase-modulation operator, estimated from low-resolution phase and embedded in the unrolled network's encoding model, simplifies phase patterns encountered by the learned regularizer while preserving consistency with acquired complex k-space measurements. We evaluated ex vivo mouse brain MRI at 15, 18, and 72 um isotropic resolution; in vivo mouse brain MRI at 30 um isotropic resolution; and in vivo human brain MRI at 0.3x0.3x0.4mm3 resolution. Across controlled noise levels, SSL improved image-quality metrics in most conditions, preserved fine anatomy, and reduced error propagation into T2* maps and QSM. Ablation studies showed that phase regularization suppressed localized artifacts from rapid phase variation, while in vivo experiments demonstrated denoising with structural preservation. These findings support phase-constrained, measurement-domain SSL for high-resolution anatomical and quantitative MRI when clean references are unavailable.

title: What You Show Is Not What You Get: Rethinking Demonstration Following in Visual In-Context Segmentation
abstract: Visual in-context segmentation uses visual demonstrations to guide predictions for a new image. In SegGPT, we identify background color mapping deviation, where non-target regions sharing a background label receive different output colors, and part-to-parent expansion, where predictions extend beyond the requested part into its parent object. These deviations can occur even when the relevant regions remain distinguishable in internal features. Controlled changes to demonstration colors and requested targets support an account in which demonstrations guide role and color assignments over familiar semantic regions, influenced by learned semantic and color preferences. Building on these findings, we introduce Semantic Contrast Prompt Selection (SCPS). Its semantic contrast encoding assigns separate colors to the requested part and the rest of its object while keeping the remaining scene black. SCPS combines existing retrieval scores with quality estimates from labeled development images to select demonstrations and their binary or semantic contrast encodings. Averaged across seven retrieval methods on three benchmarks, SCPS improves target IoU by 0.054 and reduces leakage into the rest of the object by 22.7% relative to the original binary selectors. Our findings offer a new perspective on understanding and improving demonstration following in visual in-context segmentation.

title: HARP-Bench: Benchmarking Robot Manipulation Around Active Humans
abstract: Recent robot manipulation benchmarks have enabled systematic evaluation of general-purpose robot policies across diverse objects, scenes, instructions, and embodiments. However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on HARP-Bench. Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/harp.

title: Optimal Polynomial-Query Approximation for Consistent Submodular Maximization with Short Lookahead
abstract: Elements arrive one at a time, and after each arrival an algorithm holds a set of at most $k$ arrived elements. Its goal is a held set whose value under a monotone submodular function is close to the best value that $k$ arrived elements can achieve. The recourse of an update is the number of elements inserted into or removed from the held set, and we require it to be bounded independently of $k$ and of the number $n$ of arrivals. With evaluations only on sets of arrived elements and polynomially many of them, the best ratio a randomized algorithm can achieve is $2-\sqrt{2}\approx0.5858$. We show that seeing future arrivals raises the best ratio for polynomially many evaluations to $1-1/e\approx0.6321$, for deterministic and for randomized algorithms; no algorithm with polynomially many evaluations exceeds $1-1/e$, even when all elements are available at once. For every $\varepsilon>0$, a deterministic algorithm that sees the next $\lceil\varepsilon k/3\rceil$ arrivals keeps a set of value at least $1-1/e-\varepsilon$ times the optimum at every time, changes $O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ elements per arrival and makes $(n+1)^{O(\varepsilon^{-2})}$ evaluations. With the whole arrival sequence known in advance, a deterministic algorithm attains the same ratio with $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ changes per arrival. A randomized algorithm with the same short lookahead makes $O(n^2k)$ evaluations, changes $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ elements per arrival, and attains the same ratio in expectation at each fixed time. The main tool is a greedy algorithm with an explicit guarantee for each of its partial solutions combined with each initial segment of the known future arrivals. A second tool moves between two such solutions one element at a time while keeping the value high, and the deterministic algorithm times each move using upper bounds on the optimum from failed searches.

title: LongCap: Hour-Scale Timestamped Audio Captioning via Chunk-wise Processing
abstract: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.

title: Lower bound on the size of splitting systems
abstract: For even $t$ and an $n$-set $X$, an $(n,t)$-splitting system is a family ${\mathbb{B}} \subseteq 2^X$ with the property that for each subset $Y \in {X \choose t}$, there exists $B \in \mathbb{B}$ such that $|B \cap Y| = t/2$. The problem of interest is to determine the minimum size of such splitting systems. We show that any $(n,t)$-splitting system has size at least of order $t$, improving the previous lower bound of $\sqrt t$ while the best known upper bound is of order $t^{3/2}$.

title: From Festival Video to the Stage: A Sim-to-Real Ladder for Long-Horizon Expressive Whole-Body Dance on a Commercial Humanoid
abstract: We present a pipeline for transferring Awa Odori, a traditional Japanese festival dance, from monocular video to a commercial Unitree G1 EDU humanoid. The pipeline combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, reinforcement learning for motion tracking in simulation, and onboard deployment via ONNX. Training ran on a single RTX 5070 GPU. An eleven-version deployment ladder evaluated on hardware examines three interventions. We detect and repair silent corruption of deployment artifacts, model state-estimator drift during training, and edit the reference motion to support stable execution and a controlled ending. The final policies achieved three consecutive rope-free completions of a 43-second routine, a 46-second performance with automatic handoff, and a continuous 9.7-minute rope-free performance composed from the captured motion. In a live handover, a single remote request let the robot start from and return to the manufacturer's walking controller on stage, with a measured torque-free window of 45-140 ms. We report the training dynamics and hardware outcomes and discuss failure boundaries involving compliant flooring and occlusion in monocular capture.

title: Triangle-overlap cores and density bounds for Tuza's conjecture
abstract: For a finite simple graph $G$, let $ν(G)$ be the maximum number of edge-disjoint triangles and let $τ(G)$ be the minimum number of edges meeting every triangle. We prove $τ(G)\le2ν(G)$ when each edge belongs to at most four triangles, the edges belonging to four triangles form components with at most two edges, and the maximum average degree is at most $25/2$. No upper bound on maximum vertex degree is imposed. We also localize the density condition. Let $K$ be the Hifumi core, defined as the vertex set of the 4-core of the spanning subgraph formed by edges belonging to at least three triangles. It suffices to impose the density condition on $G[K]$, including all original edges between vertices of $K$. More generally, when the four-triangle edges have maximum degree at most two, reductions produce a subgraph $R\subseteq G[K]$ with $τ(G)-2ν(G)\leτ(R)-2ν(R)$. Consequently an empty core gives a density-free sufficient condition. For the first graph class, a quantitative surplus argument strengthens both the global and localized density conditions to the strict bound $25/2+2/56775$. The proof combines edge reductions, discharging, finite certificates and a weak König--Egerváry lemma for links of arbitrary order. The general conjecture and the removal of the density condition from the first graph class remain unresolved here.

title: On-the-Fly Reduced Bases Through the Lens of Augmented Krylov Methods
abstract: On-the-fly reduced order models (ROMs) are widely used in applications where multiple queries of large-scale models are required in an iterative method, like PDE-constrained optimization or fluid-structure interaction. When compared to classical offline--online ROMs, they have the advantage of being agnostic to any precomputed training data, mesh or geometry, which makes them more general linear/nonlinear solver accelerators. The main goal of this work is to study the effect of using a reduced basis constructed on-the-fly to accelerate a restarted Krylov algorithm, and to formally bridge this category of data-driven methods with classical augmented Krylov methods. The guiding principles of on-the-fly reduced basis will be translated into the framework of Krylov subspace methods, for a Petrov-Galerkin projection method. Previous corrections generated by the algorithm are stored in a snapshot matrix, and a singular value decomposition (SVD) is used to determine a reduced subspace containing the most significant directions. It will be shown that this approach can be embedded in the framework of Krylov methods with augmented or deflated restart, but with a different, data-driven recycling strategy. An analytical study will be presented to determine the consequences of augmentation by ROM-based vectors. Numerical experiments on a convection-diffusion problem with various degrees of convection will show that the proposed methodology yields results comparable to classical iterative linear solvers in some regimes, especially for nearly symmetric or skew-symmetric operators. At equal sizes of the augmentation basis, the convergence was sometimes faster with the proposed framework than with deflation methods.

title: Virtual-Flow: Virtual Microphone-based Speech Enhancement via Semi-supervised Flow Matching
abstract: Neural network-based virtual microphone estimation (neural-VME) synthesizes microphone signals at unobserved spatial locations from a limited set of real microphone (RM) physical recordings. This enables high-resolution arrays that improve spatial processing for downstream tasks such as speech enhancement. However, existing methods rely on supervised training with ground-truth signals captured at virtual locations, requiring datasets that scale with the number of virtual microphones (VM) and leaving open the question of how to design optimal large-array configurations. We propose Virtual-Flow, a flow-matching framework that implicitly generates VM signals conditioned on real recordings, without requiring ground-truth VM signals. We introduce a semi-supervised training strategy based on pseudo-VM targets constructed from time-delayed superpositions of real recordings. Virtual-Flow shows improved magnitude estimation in high-frequency bands, yielding richer spatial cues for beamforming. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed Virtual-Flow, combined with reflow distillation, outperforms existing neural-VME baselines in VM-based beamforming and achieves competitive end-to-end speech enhancement performance with low computational cost.

title: CrossLiDAR: Controllable Multi-Sensor LiDAR Sequence Generation
abstract: High-fidelity LiDAR simulation remains a bottleneck for scalable development and validation of autonomous systems. Existing generators can synthesize realistic scans, but they are typically constrained to a single sensor configuration, offer limited control over structure and geometry, and drift in long-horizon 4D generation. We present CrossLiDAR, a unified transformer-based framework capable of generating controllable and spatio-temporally consistent multi-sensor LiDAR sequences. Our approach leverages a rectified flow objective with a Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT) backbone, within a compact latent space of range images. To support multiple LiDAR sensors, an Inter-sensor Module enables interaction across sensors, while a ControlNet-style branch provides structural conditioning (e.g., BEV priors or 3D bounding boxes). For modeling the temporal consistency, CrossLiDAR generates short $N$-frame sequences and extends them autoregressively to improve long-horizon coherence. Our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 29.56\% in JSD and 15.36\% in MMD evaluated on nuScenes and the Waymo Dataset. CrossLiDAR bridges the gap to modern autonomous-driving simulation by enabling calibration-consistent multi-sensor LiDAR rollouts over long horizons for controllable, scenario-based testing.

title: Confidence-driven adaptive semantic transmission for task-oriented communication
abstract: Image-based remote monitoring over wireless networks faces a trade-off between communication cost and classification reliability. Transmitting complete images is communication-intensive, whereas relying solely on lightweight edge classifiers may compromise accuracy.
