The areas of these bodies are seen to be well-defined and their expression is explicitly computed. To this end, a result concerning the continuity of the Lebesgue measure with respect to the Hausdorff metric for compact sets is given. Furthermore, the Hausdorff dimension $w$ of these fractal curves is shown to coincide with the Hausdorff dimension of the graph of a Weierstrass function associated to the corresponding fractal projective hedgehog. The fractal Zindler curves are proved to have halving chords of constant length that split both the area and the $w$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of the curve into exact halves.

title: sdos: spectral densities of large sparse Hermitian and generalized eigenproblems
abstract: sdos is an open Python package that computes the density of states (DOS) and related spectral quantities of very large sparse Hermitian matrices A, and of generalized problems A psi = lambda B psi, from Chebyshev moments estimated with random vectors. The density is reconstructed by the kernel polynomial method (KPM, the default) or by maximum entropy (Maxent); the same interface gives band energies, Fermi levels, local and projected densities, harmonic thermodynamics, exact HOMO-LUMO gaps and eigenpairs in a spectral window. Interfaces cover electronic (empirical tight-binding, DFTB, SIESTA) and vibrational (matrix-free LAMMPS Hessians) problems. I checked most ingredients against dense diagonalization or an independent code; the exceptions are listed in Sec. V. On a workstation (4 threads, 19 GB) the DOS of an 884,736-atom amorphous silicon model (a 6^3 tiling of a 4096-atom cell; 3.5 million orbitals; the orthogonal empirical tight-binding model of Kwon et al.) takes 71 s (M=100, R=2, no exact moments; 383 s with the default exact moments), and a matrix-free 2,097,152-atom crystal 10 min in 1.8 GB. A 17^3 replica of a 216-atom amorphous cell (1,061,208 atoms) agrees with exact Bloch spectra: electronic DOS in 229 s, matrix-free ACE vibrational DOS in 2.2 h on one GPU. Shift-invert, incomplete-Cholesky setup, exact moments of high order and Maxent at high moment counts do not scale. The underlying methods are due to Silver, Roder, Kress, Voter, Drabold, Sankey and collaborators; the Introduction states what is added.

title: Causal discernment and the direction of clinical research
abstract: A clinical trial can establish an intervention's effects while leaving their causal pathways unresolved. We call causal discernment the practice of identifying explanations that fit the evidence but imply different decisions or research directions, and seeking studies that distinguish them. METHOD: We combine causal graphs and prose around four questions: delivery of the intended target change, routes of benefit and harm, stability of causal relations across regimes, and whether unresolved pathways could change the decision. With quantitative assumptions, graphs support plausible reasoning by showing which findings could distinguish explanations even when effects are not identified. Prose specifies clinical meaning, effect size and timing, and supporting evidence. We use conceptual analysis, hypothetical calculations, CAST and lipid-lowering therapy. SUBSTANTIVE RESULTS: Concordant coronary associations for HMGCR and PCSK9 perturbations support LDL mediation over target-specific explanations predicting unequal effects per unit of LDL reduction, but leave a shared receptor pathway possible. Diabetes associations leave LDL lowering, receptor-mediated uptake and weight gain as possible explanations. An illustrative causal record specifies a genetic comparison and assumptions under which it could distinguish them. CONCLUSION: The causal record formalises the reasoning behind the choice of the next study by making competing explanations, evidence and assumptions explicit and stating what each design could resolve. Prepared before a design or recommendation is adopted, it enables scrutiny of that reasoning and interpretation of results in relation to the stated explanations. Its added value over ordinary rationale review remains to be assessed.

title: A Discrete de Rham method for linear and nonlinear fourth-order plate models
abstract: We develop and analyze a Discrete de Rham (DDR) method for the Kirchhoff--Love plate problem on general polygonal meshes and demonstrate its extension to geometrically nonlinear plates. The construction uses local degrees of freedom and polynomial reconstructions, avoiding the implementation difficulties associated with globally $C^1$-conforming approximation spaces. A new deflection reconstruction obtained from the discrete Hessian permits a uniform treatment of the load term at all polynomial degrees. The use of this reconstruction improves the convergence rates of previous DDR methods and enables the formulation of a lowest-order scheme with only vertex unknowns. We provide a stability and convergence analysis of the method and validate the theoretical results through a comprehensive set of numerical tests. The method is then extended to the coupled von Kármán equations, for which we demonstrate convergence numerically. We also study the flat-branch spectrum of a compressed perforated plate and its small-amplitude forced nonlinear response near the first critical load.

title: Shape-Adaptive Subspace-Constrained Quadratic Matrix Factorization
abstract: Quadratic manifold fitting provides a flexible framework for modeling nonlinear low-dimensional structures embedded in high-dimensional spaces. However, existing methods typically employ prescribed noise models or fixed loss functions, limiting their adaptability to varying noise characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose an alternating maximum likelihood estimation method for subspace-constrained quadratic matrix factorization, termed AMLE-SQMF, which jointly estimates the quadratic manifold and the underlying noise distribution. Specifically, we model the residuals using a generalized Gaussian distribution (GGD), whose shape parameter controls the tail behavior and determines the associated fitting loss. By exploiting the closed-form maximum likelihood estimator of the scale parameter, we eliminate the scale variable and derive a profile negative log-likelihood. Based on this formulation, we develop an alternating optimization algorithm that iteratively updates the manifold parameters and estimates the noise shape parameter. This enables adaptive loss selection within a unified likelihood-based framework, without requiring prior specification of the noise characteristics. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of AMLE-SQMF in quadratic manifold fitting and its robustness to diverse noise distributions.

title: Ricci pseudo symmetric Anisotropic Fluid Spacetime admitting Hyperbolic solitons with Ricci vector field
abstract: This work focuses on an anisotropic fluid spacetime with these unique forms of the stress-energy tensor associated with radial pressure and a transverse pressure p. In an anisotropic fluid spacetime , we mani- fest curvatures symmetry such as Ricci pseudo-symmetric and prove that Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime is generalized quasi- Einstein spacetime. We deduce the Einstein gravitational field equation of Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime. In the framework of pseudo-Riemannian geometry, specifically, we study the quasi-conformal Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime, which exhibit the dark matter era. Moreover, we discuss the hyperbolic Ricci soliton and Hyperbolic Yamabe soliton on Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime with a time-like Ricci vector field. Finally, we turn up the char- acteristics of hyperbolic Ricci soliton and hyperbolic Yamabe soliton on Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime with a time-like Ricci vector field.

title: Flash evaporation Riemann Problem: Thermodynamic Relaxation and Oscillation-Free Real Fluid Finite Volume Method
abstract: The Flash evaporation Riemann problem (FeRP) formulated the wave structures of flash evaporation in the vapor-liquid homogeneous equilibrium limit. However, physical flash evaporation involves finite-rate interphase heat and mass transfer, inducing the wave structure to deviate from the equilibrium state. To solve such a non-equilibrium Riemann problem, this paper first derives the governing equation of mechanical equilibrium evolution in a relaxation system, based on which an oscillation-free Homogeneous Relaxation Real Fluid (HRRF) finite volume method is developed. In addition to the Euler equations with mass relaxation, the HRRF method evolves advection equations for the internal energy--pressure affine parameters and the vapor volume fraction, in order to eliminate numerical pressure oscillations inherent in conservative methods while preserving phase-transition-induced pressure changes, and consistently degenerate into a completely pressure-equilibrium method in supercritical flows. The HRRF method is then employed to comprehensively evaluate how thermodynamic relaxation affects the FeRP solution. Results indicate that the non-classical expansion shock of the FeRP loses its traveling-wave characteristics with increasing relaxation time, continuously degenerating into a self-similar rarefaction wave. Compared with the equilibrium limit, an increased mass transfer relaxation time smooths the expansion branch of the RP solution, lowers the intermediate pressure and velocity, and induces a pseudo-splitting of the rarefaction wave as well as a pseudo-advance of the phase transition onset. Meanwhile, the heat transfer relaxation time primarily dictates the temperature difference in the vapor-liquid mixture, thereby modulating the liquid superheat and in turn influencing the mass transfer rate.

title: ReGKG-2025: A GKG-Compatible Reconstruction of the GDELT Global Knowledge Graph for the Missing Period of 14 June to 2 July 2025
abstract: The June 2025 outage in the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) collection pipeline left a gap in the Global Knowledge Graph (GKG), interrupting article-level news metadata used in downstream research. ReGKG-2025 is an archive-derived sample of 281,620 reconstructed article records covering all 1,665 missing 15-minute batches. Articles were recovered from Common Crawl and the Wayback Machine using source quotas estimated from surrounding native GKG data. Text was screened and normalized, non-English bodies were translated, and flagged records were manually reviewed. Eligible articles were converted to the 27-column GKG 2.1 layout. The versioned package includes record-level provenance, archive replay and WARC locators, source summaries, source-by-day calibration weights, and the complete manual decision journal. The sample reaches about 14% of modeled native volume and represents sources accounting for 84% of selected reference record mass. In an intact-week test, 41% of recovered articles matched native GKG records; field agreement on matched pairs is close to the processor baseline (tone MAE 1.69). The dataset supports retrospective content analysis and source-level aggregates; its tone and theme distributions differ from native GKG, and it does not support exhaustive counts. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23964265.

title: Understanding Spike Encoding across IoT Sensing Modalities: An Empirical Study
abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a path to energy-efficient sensing on Internet of Things (IoT) devices. The input encoder shapes that opportunity by changing the cues available for recognition and the work required to process them. We study these choices across wireless, inertial, surface electromyographic, and tactile sensing. For wireless activity recognition, interleaving reduces estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers, latency from the prepared input window to returned scores, and energy on the graphics processing unit and system-on-chip (GPU/SoC) rail, compared with repeating the full window on Jetson AGX Orin. With the same input size at each SNN time step, repeating a compact input can yield higher mean development accuracy than interleaving. The inertial experiments show that higher accuracy can come at higher device cost. Direct input can also be faster and more accurate than an event encoder while using less energy on the measured rail, even when its estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers is higher. Level crossings improve grasp recognition on a later day for previously observed users. In tactile slip detection, level crossings shift the balance between missed slips and false alarms, and checkpoint selection can reverse which input offers higher slip recall. We use these findings to outline how edge sensing systems can profile encoders against the signal structure, the errors that matter to the task, and the cost of the full inference pipeline.

title: PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling
abstract: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.

title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference
abstract: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(ε, δ)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.

title: Beyond Similarity Entropy: A Rank-Guided Data-Free Quantization Framework for Vision Transformers
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, yet their computational and memory demands pose significant challenges for deployment on mobile devices. Data-free quantization (DFQ) enables the compression of ViTs without access to their original training data. Existing DFQ methods often synthesize calibration samples by maximizing the entropy of patch similarity. However, similarity entropy describes the dispersion of similarity values without ensuring that the generated samples cover diverse feature directions, potentially limiting their effectiveness for quantization calibration. To address this limitation, we propose RankQ-ViT, a rank-guided DFQ framework for ViTs. We first observe that patch similarity matrices derived from Gaussian noise tend to have lower ranks than those derived from real images. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a block-aware self-contrastive objective that promotes feature diversity during synthetic data generation without explicitly computing matrix rank at each optimization step. We then select calibration samples based on their rank and semantic consistency and use them for block-wise reconstruction of the quantized model. Experiments on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet demonstrate the effectiveness of RankQ-ViT across multiple architectures and tasks, particularly under low-bit quantization. The code is available at https://github.com/Runqing-forMost/rankq-vit.git

title: Monk and Pieri rules for forest polynomials
abstract: This article gives Pieri rules for forest polynomials and Monk rule for double forest polynomials. We construct binary relations $\lessdot_i$ and $\prec_i$ based on the local Tamari moves on indexed forests. These relations are explicit and constructive. For ordinary forest polynomials, the $h$- and $e$-Pieri rules are given by all chains of a fixed length along the cover relations, with certain restriction on the left or right endpoints. For double forest polynomials, our Monk rule shows every off-diagonal degree-one structure coefficient is always a single positive root, whose weight is also controlled by Tamari moves. Additionally, we introduce an insertion algorithm on positive injective words that yields a Monk rule for the corresponding slide polynomials. Regrouping this rule along Sylvester classes gives an independent Monk rule for ordinary forest polynomials.

title: Capability-Guided Iterative Online Optimization of Cascaded Spoken-Dialogue Modules
abstract: Cascaded spoken dialogue systems comprise perception-and-comprehension, decision-making, and response-generation modules. We study iterative optimization of the first and last modules. Their reciprocal speech-content interfaces enable one-sided data to provide cross-module supervision: acoustic observations, such as waveforms or feature sequences, can be pseudo-labeled to train generation, whereas content-only samples can be rendered into speech to train comprehension. Because the reliable teacher-student direction varies across domains, we propose a two-stage, capability-guided pipeline for iterative online optimization. Stage 1 compares both modules through a shared intelligibility probe and obtains a domain-wise capability prior. Stage 2 activates the compatible one-sided-data route, constructs and filters supervision with the current teacher, updates the selected student, and refreshes the relevant checkpoints across cycles. We instantiate comprehension with Whisper large-v3 and generation with CosyVoice2. After only 200 steps for Whisper and 600 for CosyVoice2 of our iterative online optimization, we observe that, on the Chinese MAGICDATA-RAMC dataset, Whisper reduces CER from 14.18% to 10.77%, while CosyVoice2 reduces it from 4.78% to 4.04%. On the Japanese Common Voice dataset, Whisper reduces CER from 15.23% to 15.10%, while CosyVoice2 reduces it from 14.85% to 11.18%. These results demonstrate the feasibility of capability-guided iterative optimization of complementary spoken-dialogue modules.

title: Stanley Deser 19th March 1931 - 21st April 2023
abstract: Stanley Deser was Ancell Professor Emeritus at Brandeis University and Visiting Professor at the California Institute of Technology. He was a world-renowned theoretical physicist whose accomplishments include the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) formulation of general relativity, supergravity with Zumino, the dynamics of flat space with Jackiw and 't Hooft and many other contributions to the quantum theory of gravity. In the 1980s he was instrumental in securing National Science Foundation approval of the LIGO gravitational wave experiment against much opposition. He was awarded the Einstein Medal in 2015 for important contributions to general relativity, in particular the development of the ADM formalism. Other awards include: The Dannie Heineman Prize 1994; Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences 1994; Honorary Member of the Torino Academy of Sciences 2001; Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences 1979, Fellow of the American Institute of Physics.

title: When Sensors Fail: Coverage Auditing with Incomplete Sensor Records
abstract: Sensor outages can conceal prediction-interval coverage deficits behind acceptable marginal performance, while unavailable future readings leave some issued forecasts unscorable. We present a measurement-record audit that links issue-time outage duration, original target availability, and time-uniform statistical evidence. The audit retains complete forecast keys, batches all sensors and overlapping horizons at each measurement tick, and projects simultaneous covered-count and scored-count bounds onto a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio. This target is distinguished from empirical coverage and outage-conditional population coverage. Selected traffic and air-quality results illustrate the gap between pooled and long-outage coverage; in METR-LA, only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets. Of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support. This concise presentation gives the core construction and selected aggregate evidence without the full experimental supplement.

title: Linking Event-sequence Data Claims to Analytic Provenance in Chatbots: Technique and Evaluation
abstract: Chatbots are increasingly used to analyze temporal event sequences of which website clickstreams are among the most common. Explanations are essential for understanding claims about event-sequence data. However, existing systems often require programming expertise to interpret these explanations and fail to explain the data processes underlying the data claims. We introduce a technique for linking a data claim to its analytic provenance (i.e., the analytic steps and results that produced it). It has two components: a reference table that records analytic steps and results in addressable cells, and a citation format that binds each claim to one or more cells. To operationalize this technique for clickstream analysis, we curated a set of analytic operations for clickstream analysis, organized them through a pivot-table abstraction, and developed tools that an AI agent can invoke to create a reference table and assemble a natural language response with cited data claims. To evaluate how citations affect users' assessment of data claims, we conducted two crowdsourced experiments with 90 participants each. The experiments showed that participants perceived correct data claims to be more accurate with citations when compared with no explanations, and that they perceived incorrect data claims to be less accurate with citations when compared with code and no explanations.

title: Conditional Diffusion-Based Proxy Representation Recovery for BCVA Prediction with Missing SLO Modality
abstract: Preoperative prediction of postoperative best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) can support prognosis assessment and individualized decision-making in cataract surgery. Multimodal learning can integrate preoperative optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO) images, and clinical text to characterize patient status. However, SLO images are often missing in real-world clinical data due to acquisition or data-management issues, resulting in incomplete multimodal inputs. To address this problem, this paper proposes a conditional diffusion-based method for SLO proxy representation recovery and fusion prediction. Instead of reconstructing raw SLO images, the proposed method formulates SLO missingness as proxy representation recovery in the latent feature space. Specifically, OCT image features and clinical text features are first fused to construct an OCT-text conditional representation, which guides the reverse denoising process of the diffusion model to estimate sample-specific SLO proxy representations. The recovered SLO proxy representation is then used as a substitute for the unavailable SLO modality and incorporated into the downstream multimodal fusion prediction network for postoperative BCVA prediction. Experiments were conducted on 2,141 preoperative multimodal cataract samples, with an SLO missing rate of 58.80%. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 0.9714 under the criterion of an absolute prediction error within 0.1 LogMAR and a mean absolute error of 0.0423, outperforming representative postoperative visual acuity prediction and missing-modality learning methods. These results indicate that representation-level proxy recovery can alleviate the impact of SLO modality missingness on postoperative BCVA prediction.

title: DIY Customized Speech Recognition for a Person with Speech Disabilities
abstract: General-purpose state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems fail systematically for speakers with moderate to severe speech disabilities. This paper describes the design, implementation, and evaluation of a customized ASR system built for the first author, a researcher with cerebral palsy and dysarthria. We fine-tuned OpenAI's Whisper medium and large-v3 models using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on audio samples recorded from the first author's own speech on consumer-grade hardware. On a held-out test set of 100 previously unseen utterances, the corresponding transcriptions resulted in a Word Error Rate drop from 49% to 17% for medium and from 30% to 12% for large-v3, while the Character Error Rate fell from 26% to 7% for medium and from 16% to 5% for large-v3, indicating that the residual errors are minor phonemic substitutions. Based on these models, the first author developed AVoz, a mobile application that acts as a real-time interpreter, converting his speech into synthesized voice for the listener. All processing is performed locally, ensuring that no audio data leaves the user's machine. We argue that the methodology is replicable. Moreover, we publish the full LoRA configuration, the implementation, and a step-by-step recording and training protocol, so that other people with speech disabilities, or their family members and caregivers, can build their own systems with a few hours of labeled audio data and a couple of days of GPU time.

title: Observation of a strange $J^P=1^{-}$ resonance $K^{*}_1(1870)$ in $χ_{c1}\to K^+K^-η^{\prime}$ decays
abstract: A partial wave analysis of the process $ψ(2S)\to γχ_{c1}$, $χ_{c1}\to K^{+}K^{-}η^{\prime}$, with the $η^{\prime}$ meson reconstructed in the $π^+π^-γ$ and $π^+π^-η$ decay modes, is performed using a sample of $(2712.4 \pm 14.3)\times10^{6}$ $ψ(2S)$ events collected with the BESIII detector. In the $Kη^{\prime}$ system, a resonant contribution with quantum numbers $J^{P}=1^{-}$ is observed for the first time and is denoted as the $K_1^*(1870)$ meson. Its statistical significance is $11.0σ$, and its mass and width are measured to be $M=(1869.0 \pm 14.6\pm 18.6$) MeV/$c^{2}$ and $Γ=(167.3 \pm 34.0\pm 24.2$) MeV, respectively. The branching fraction of the $χ_{c1}\to K^{\mp}K_1^*(1870)^{\pm}\to K^{+}K^{-}η^{\prime}$ decay chain is determined to be $(1.48 \pm 0.30\pm 0.33)\times10^{-5}$. The branching fraction of the $χ_{c1}\to K^{+}K^{-}η^{\prime}$ decay is measured to be $(7.90 \pm 0.48)\times10^{-4}$. Several intermediate scalar, vector, and tensor states are required to provide a good description of the data. These results provide new input for understanding strange-meson spectroscopy and investigating possible hybrid-state candidates.

title: Approximation by subsequences of matrix transform means of Vilenkin--Fourier series
abstract: In this paper we study the rate of approximation by matrix transform means of a special subsequence of partial sums of Vilenkin--Fourier series in the spaces $L_p(G_m)$ $(1\le p<\infty)$ and $C(G_m)$.

title: When Credit Turns Against Tools: Transition-Aware Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. We trace this degradation to three coupled mechanisms: (1) tool-token imbalance produces negative overall tool credit when incorrect trajectories contain more tool tokens per turn than correct ones; (2) aggregation amplification can further strengthen this negative signal as token-mean aggregation gives longer incorrect trajectories greater weight in policy updates; and (3) failure-driven retries prolong trajectories as models tend to call tools again after execution errors, extending potential negative credit to recovery attempts. To counter this suppression, we propose Transition-Aware Credit Assignment (TACA), which targets the transition from reasoning to tool use through supervision of both call initiation and generation. Specifically, TACA uses Advantage Projection to enforce a nonnegative mean advantage on tool-call tokens within each prompt group through a minimal uniform shift. Additionally, TACA guides tool-use decisions with Decision Contrast, comparing rewards for tool-assisted and direct answers to the same prompt. Through Supervised Replay, it reinforces tool-call generation using calls from previously sampled correct trajectories. Across models and tasks, TACA improves performance and sustains more reliable tool interaction during training, raising mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks by 4.61 percentage points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 for Qwen2.5-3B. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/TACA.

title: Harmonic functions and comparsion geometry for noncompact 3-manifolds with nonnegative scalar curvature
abstract: In this paper, we establish several sharp comparsion results for noncompact 3-manifolds with nonnegative scalar curvature and with a compact, connected boundary under a boundary mean curvature condition. Then we apply these gradient estimates to establish a Cohn-Vossen type bound for the average of the scalar curvature. This generalizes the work of Colding-Minicozzi \cite{Cold4} and Oronzio \cite{Oro2}.

title: CVaR Deep Optimal Stopping
abstract: Risk-sensitive optimal stopping is useful when poor stopping outcomes carry substantial costs, as in option exercise, sequential medical treatment, and safety-critical control. A natural objective is Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the stopped reward. We develop a theoretical framework and algorithm for CVaR deep optimal stopping. The framework and algorithm address four difficulties in applying risk-sensitive reinforcement learning to optimal stopping: state augmentation, score-function pathology, blindness to success, and dependence on auxiliary networks. We isolate three structural properties of optimal stopping: single-point reward, action-independent dynamics, and sum-zero gradient. We exploit these properties to establish Markov optimality without state augmentation and derive a pathwise gradient estimator. Under bounded policy derivatives, the pathwise estimator has bounded second moments near deterministic policies, avoiding the divergence that can occur with score-function estimators. Building on this framework, we propose DIOS (Distribution-Informed Optimal Stopping) to address the remaining two difficulties. A per-time-step soft penalty combined with tail-level annealing mitigates blindness to success. Estimating the reward quantile directly from each batch removes the need for an auxiliary critic. For a fixed tail level, we establish a finite-time stationarity guarantee under regularity assumptions along the training iterates. Across the 24 main Bermudan max-call configurations, DIOS achieves the highest mean CVaR and the shortest recorded training time among the tested CVaR baselines.

title: Unbounded advantage of adaptivity in entanglement-assisted communication
abstract: Shared entanglement can reduce the amount of classical communication needed to perform distributed computation. This can be achieved either by first measuring the entanglement and then communicating classically, or by adapting the quantum measurement to the received message. Here, we introduce tasks that adaptive protocols can solve using just three entanglement-assisted messages, while the communication cost grows without bound when the quantum receiver is not adaptive. Consequently, no bounded amount of classical communication can reproduce all correlations generated by an entanglement-assisted ternary classical channel. We establish two complementary limitations on the relation between adaptive and non-adaptive quantum protocols. First, every adaptive protocol using a finite entanglement dimension admits a non-adaptive simulation at finite communication cost. Second, every adaptive protocol sending $d$ messages can be simulated to within error $\varepsilon$ using $O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))$ non-adaptive messages. Our results reveal the fundamentally unbounded advantage of adaptivity in quantum communication, but also that observing very large advantages requires both high-dimensional entanglement and very precise observations.

title: MoT3DVG: A Benchmark for Outdoor 3D Visual Grounding with Motion-Aware Descriptions and Temporal Cues
abstract: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.

title: Directional asymmetry of atmospheric pole-to-pole teleconnection
abstract: Paleoclimate proxies show that abrupt Greenland changes were followed by Antarctic responses within decades, suggesting a fast atmospheric pole-to-pole teleconnection involving shifts in the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and reorganization of extratropical jets. Here, we examine how the mean ITCZ position modulates this interhemispheric teleconnection. Using an aquaplanet slab-ocean model, we apply northern high-latitude forcing in climatologies with different mean ITCZ positions. The southern high-latitude response is about twice as large when the mean ITCZ is in the Southern Hemisphere. The teleconnection is therefore directionally asymmetric. The asymmetry arises in the subtropical jet response per degree of ITCZ shift, because, even with a comparable Hadley cell response, the angular momentum carried into the upper branch depends on the distance of the ITCZ from the equator, so that an ITCZ shift toward or away from the equator reinforces or offsets the jet response. Our results suggest that the southward-displaced glacial ITCZ made Arctic-to-Antarctic transmission more efficient than today, whereas the present-day ITCZ favors the reverse.

title: Where Should a Gate Look? Input vs. State Gating in Diagonal State Space Models
abstract: Modern state-space models owe much of their computational efficiency to their linear, often diagonal, dynamics. Classical recurrent neural networks instead allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions, which can be beneficial when memory updates need to depend on the past context. In this paper, we ask whether state feedback through a simple gate regulating memory updates can enhance the expressivity of diagonal state-space models. To investigate this question, we compare gates that depend on the current input, the recurrent state, or both. We establish a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, whereas input gating fails on a finite instance under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix. Experiments show that state gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying tasks. Together, our results show that even a simple, diagonal form of state-feedback gating can unlock capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, while input and state gating offer complementary strengths and achieve the strongest overall performance when combined.

title: OPSRL-SSP: Optimistic Posterior Sampling for Stochastic Shortest Path with Minimax-Optimal Regret
abstract: We study online reinforcement learning for the stochastic shortest path (SSP) problem with unknown transition dynamics. Although existing posterior-sampling methods perform well empirically on SSPs, their regret guarantees do not achieve the minimax-optimal order. We address this limitation by proposing OPSRL-SSP, an optimistic posterior-sampling algorithm for the SSP setting. The algorithm operates in epochs and uses a logarithmic, time-dependent schedule for the number of posterior samples. To induce optimism, we augment the transition model with a pseudo-state assigned an optimistic boundary value. We establish a high-probability regret bound of $\tilde{O}(B_\star \sqrt{SAK} + B_\star S^2 A)$, where $B_\star$ is an upper bound on the expected cost of the optimal policy, $S$ and $A$ are the numbers of states and actions, respectively, and $K$ is the number of episodes. In addition, we extend the analysis to general zero-cost SSPs using a universal cost-perturbation argument. The leading term matches the minimax lower bound $Ω(B_\star \sqrt{SAK})$, thereby addressing the open problem raised by Jafarnia-Jahromi et al. [19] for posterior sampling in the SSP setting.

title: Gamma classes, central connection matrices, and tt* geometry
abstract: We review the gamma class of complex projective space, but from the point of view of topological-antitopological fusion. We deconstruct the central connection matrix which appears in the work of Dubrovin, Galkin-Golyshev-Iritani, and Cotti-Dubrovin-Guzzetti.

title: Visualizing d-wave pairing symmetry at the atomic scale in a cuprate high-Tc superconductor by Josephson tunneling
abstract: Superconducting pairing symmetry provides crucial insight into the microscopic mechanisms of Cooper pairing. However, probing the local manifestations of sign-changing superconducting order parameters remains experimentally challenging. Here, we investigate the superconducting condensate in optimally doped (OPT) Bi2Sr2Ca2Cu3O10+δ (Bi-2223) using scanning Josephson tunneling microscopy (SJTM), equipped with an s-wave superconducting tip. Measurements at ultra-low temperatures reveal a pronounced modulation of the Josephson tunneling signal at different locations inside the crystallographic unit cell. A distinct Josephson tunneling signal is detected above O sites in the underlying CuO2 plane, whereas the signal nearly vanishes above the Cu-plaquette diagonals, including Cu sites and plaquette centers. This unique intra-unit-cell spatial pattern agrees with the theoretical prediction for the symmetry-dependent cancellation of Josephson tunneling between an s-wave superconducting tip and a d-wave superconducting sample. Our findings provide atomic-scale, real-space evidence for d-wave pairing symmetry in OPT high-Tc Bi-2223 and establish SJTM as a powerful approach for investigating the pairing symmetry of unconventional superconductors.

title: Agentic Attribution of Cloud Resource Ownership
abstract: Security tools raise findings across cloud environments, and AI agents now investigate and prioritize them. A finding is still resolved by people: it has to reach the people responsible for fixing it and accountable for the resource it concerns. Ownership is the organizational context that decides who that is. Where recorded, it is declared by hand in configuration management databases or owner tags and goes stale unless kept current; accounts are shared, and automation creates much of the infrastructure. The knowledge sits in work records, code history, audit logs and identity directories, encoded in each organization's own conventions. Recovering it poses four challenges: the signal is scattered across sources, none of them authoritative; the conventions that carry it differ between organizations; reaching an owner takes multi-hop links; and those related to a resource differ in the strength of their relation. We define ownership as a set of entities, people or teams, each related to the resource by one of five patterns ordered by strength. We present a reference architecture for agentic ownership attribution that derives ownership from these records instead of declaring it: it profiles an organization offline into tested signal procedures and an ownership playbook, then attributes each resource with a coordinator agent and parallel investigators, with confidence computed by rules. On 100 resources of 50 Amazon Web Services (AWS) resource types in one organization, we pool the architecture's candidates with those of an unprimed general-purpose agent and verify every evidence piece against the records. The architecture reaches 92.1% weighted recall and 86.6% weighted precision, against 54.8% and 77.4%, at 0.55 times the agent's cost per unit of coverage. The difference lies in people who build and change resources without an explicit owner, found through work records and code history.

title: On quantitative aspects of ideal membership certificate and GCD inequality for polynomials evaluated at almost units
abstract: In this paper, we obtain an effective bounds for the ideal membership certificate in polynomial rings over almost all rings of S-integers, thereby generalizing results of Aschenbrenner and Evertse and Gyory. We also establish an effective refinement of a result of Xiao, building on earlier work of Levin and Corvaja and Zannier. In particular, we provide explicit bounds for both the number and the total degrees of the exceptional hypersurfaces arising in an inequality that bounds the greatest common divisor of multivariable polynomials evaluated at almost S-units under consideration. As an application of our results, we obtain an effective refinement of a theorem of Corvaja and Zannier: Let $(F_n)_n$ and $(G_n)_n$ be two linear recurrence sequences and $\mathcal{N}$ be the set of positive integers $n$ such that $F_n/G_n$ is an integer. Hadamard quotient theorem, conjectured by Pisot and proven by Van der Poorten states that if the set $\mathcal{N}$ coincides with $\mathbb{N}$ then $\left(F_n/G_n\right)_n$ is itself linear recurrence sequence. Corvaja-Zannier proved that if $\mathcal{N}$ is infinite set, then there exists a nonzero polynomial $P(X)$ such that $\left( P(n)F_n/G_n\right)_n$ agrees with a linear recurrence sequence for all $n$ in a suitable arithmetic progression. We give an explicit bound $C$, depending explicitly on the parameters of the recurrence sequences such that, the conclusion holds if $\mathcal{N}$ contains at least $C$ elements.

title: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
abstract: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

title: Ergotropy as distance from equilibrium
abstract: We show that the ergotropy (a.k.a available energy) of a thermally isolated system is the $1$-Wasserstein distance between two energy probability density functions. Specifically, between the energy profile of the system state, and the energy profile of its associated passive state. We prove this for both classical and quantum systems, and illustrate it with examples. Our result formalises the intuition that ergotropy is a quantifier of distance from equilibrium

title: Spatial Harness: Grounding Spatial Reasoning in Executable World States with Physics Engines
abstract: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness

title: Extremal graphs for Alon's graph coupon-collector conjecture
abstract: Let \(G\) be a finite simple graph without isolated vertices. Starting with every vertex uncovered, at each step sample a vertex uniformly and independently and cover one of its uncovered neighbors, chosen uniformly, if any. Let \(\cc(G)\) denote the expected number of steps required to cover all vertices. Alon conjectured that disjoint unions of \(K_{d+1}\) maximize \(\cc(G)\) among \(d\)-regular graphs of a prescribed order whenever such unions exist. In this paper, we disprove this conjecture for every fixed \(d\ge2\) and give a complete characterization of the extremal graphs for \(d=2\) at every order \(n\ge3\). In particular, all but at most six vertices of any such extremal graph lie in four-cycle components.

title: IntentLens: Grounding Underspecified Multimodal Queries for Recommendation via Tool-Augmented Reasoning
abstract: As intelligent personal assistants are increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios, recommendation paradigms are shifting from passive preference matching to inferring user intent from underspecified multimodal inputs. In practical interactions, users typically issue a reference image paired with a vague natural language query, keeping key visual attributes, personalized preferences, and item-side constraints implicit. Existing recommendation methods either leverage historical user interactions augmented with multimodal item features or assume fully articulated textual queries; both paradigms struggle to resolve underspecified multimodal queries for accurate item matching. To address this limitation, we propose IntentLens, a tool-augmented recommendation framework that grounds ambiguous multimodal queries into query-relevant evidence prior to user-item matching. IntentLens follows a ground-then-rank pipeline: a shared multimodal LLM leverages visual tools, user memory modules, and item attribute retrieval tools to (i) infer latent user intent from image-text inputs and (ii) augment each candidate item with fine-grained, query-conditioned evidence. Subsequently, a lightweight ranker scores candidates based on the grounded representations. To facilitate research in this novel setting, we construct two benchmarks with underspecified multimodal queries, namely \textsc{GoogleReview-MMTool} and \textsc{Yelp-MMTool}. Extensive experiments on these benchmarks demonstrate that IntentLens outperforms competitive MLLM and retrieval baselines, and exhibits strong generalization to unseen categories and datasets.

title: Elliptic flow of $ϕ$ and $Ω$ via quark recombination mechanism in relativistic heavy-ion collisions
abstract: Multi-strange hadrons, such as the $ϕ$ meson and $Ω$ baryon, serve as unique probes for the properties of the quark-gluon plasma in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Using a quark recombination model with the quark phase-space information parameterized in a viscous blastwave, we show that the elliptic flow $v_2$ of $ϕ$ and $Ω$ can be describled by quark recombination in a wide energy range from $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 7.7 GeV to 5.02 TeV. We check the scaling properties of $v_2$ of $ϕ$ and $Ω$ and find the number-of-constituent-quark (NCQ) scaled $v_2$ of $ϕ$ and $Ω$ are approximately equal. We further present the $v_2$ of strange quarks at hadronization extracted from $ϕ$ and $Ω$ data. We find the $v_2$ of strange quarks is close to the NCQ-scaled $v_2$ of $ϕ$ and $Ω$ at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 7.7-200 GeV, but significant larger than the latter at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 2.76-5.02 TeV, suggesting that the $v_2$ of strange quarks cannot be simply equated to the NCQ-scaled $v_2$ of $ϕ$ and $Ω$. Our results demonstrate that the quark recombination mechanism is valid for $ϕ$ and $Ω$ production in heavy-ion collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 7.7 GeV to 5.02 TeV, indicating the existence of constituent quark degree of freedom at these energies.

title: Separation of Skilling Context for Standard Operating Procedure-based Agents
abstract: Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) are kept concise for human readability, so LLM agents that generate executable skills from them lack the tacit knowledge and implementation details needed for automation. Human intervention fills these gaps, but must be repeated as SOPs evolve---a problem we call \textit{SOP-skill drift}. We propose managing SOPs and Contextual Knowledge (CK) separately, together with a \textit{contract-aware} evaluation that distinguishes genuine violations from CK-resolved differences. On eight Indeed-derived workflows (single LLM), it raises the functional-equivalence rate from 12\% to 58\%. Under three SOP-revision perturbations, previously extracted CK already covers 79.5\% of newly introduced automation gaps.

title: AOP-Smart-Finder: A High-Throughput Human-AI Hybrid Framework for AOP Discovery and Evidence Mapping from Large-Scale Literature
abstract: The rapid growth of scientific literature and the high heterogeneity of biological terminology and mechanistic descriptions make it difficult for researchers to integrate scattered research evidence, identify connections among biological events, and construct mechanistic networks. Here, we developed a high-throughput human-AI hybrid framework, AOP-Smart-Finder, for biological event discovery, relationship mining, and Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) construction and evidence mapping from large-scale literature. This framework integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), AOP-Smart retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) technology, and Python-based automation, supporting two analysis modes: one based on a single compound and the other based on a predefined set of biological events. In the di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) case, the system processed 12,983 articles within 30 min and included 1,093 of them, from which it extracted 1,589 biological events (including 458 official key events [KEs] and 1,131 candidate KEs) and 2,519 key event relationships (KERs). In the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) case, the system identified 55 stressors from 437 articles and extracted 278 biological events and 548 event relationships. Following manual curation and Weight of Evidence (WoE) evaluation, a mechanistic network comprising 16 KEs and 23 KERs was ultimately constructed. This framework can either use existing AOPs as knowledge guidance for mechanistic expansion and evidence supplementation, or discover novel event connections and construct mechanistic networks around user-specified research topics. It provides a high-throughput, traceable, human-AI hybrid methodology for complex biological mechanism elucidation and AOP discovery driven by large-scale literature.

title: Financial Connectedness: Heavy Tails andResponse Attribution
abstract: A financial market can appear mainly dependent on its own shocks under a variance account and mainly dependent on external shocks under a cumulative-response account. We establish how these opposite diagnoses arise from the same propagation system. For a given cumulative magnitude, squaring gives greater weight to responses concentrated across sources and time. Source priorities can therefore reverse even in stable Gaussian systems with known parameters. Heavy tails raise a separate question: whether the reported shares have a fixed population basis. One innovation with an infinite second moment removes the full network's finite covariance input. We characterize when normalized shares nevertheless stabilize and construct rank-amplitude connectedness, a cumulative-deviation target without finite first or second moments. It can be consistently estimated under local dependence and identification conditions. With fitted dynamics and rank scatter fixed, changing attribution replaces 3.14 names in the daily Top 10 of forty stocks, selecting recipients with greater external persistence relative to their own adjustment. In five futures contracts, mean external share rises from 28.0% to 55.9%, and 70.9% of recipient-dates switch from own to external dominance.

title: The Fate of Collisional Neutrino Flavor Conversion: Fixed Points, Period Doubling, and Chaos
abstract: Core-collapse supernovae and neutron star mergers are among the most energetic astrophysical events and promising sources of multimessenger signals. Their dynamics and nucleosynthesis depend sensitively on neutrino transport, yet the impact of neutrino flavor evolution in these dense environments remains poorly understood. Predicting the outcome of collisional flavor instability (CFI) remains a challenge, despite progress in local-relaxation methods for fast flavor conversion. Here we construct homogeneous collective-precession states with stationary flavor populations in two-flavor quantum kinetics with collisional relaxation. The method applies to arbitrary energy spectra and energy-dependent collision rates. Our numerical examples exhibit persistent oscillations and a period-doubling route to chaos. Even in these regimes, the stationary populations estimate the time-averaged flavor populations to within $10\%$ in our tests. These fixed points provide a physically motivated input for incorporating CFI into astrophysical simulations, with implications for neutrino heating and ejecta nucleosynthesis.

title: Zero forcing is not unimodal
abstract: The zero forcing polynomial of a graph counts the number of distinct zero forcing sets of every possible size. In 2018, Boyer et al. asked whether the zero forcing polynomial is always unimodal, and provided some evidence that it is. We answer this question by constructing an infinite family of graphs whose zero forcing polynomials are not unimodal. Our construction also shows that the graph polynomials associated with connected forcing and total forcing are also not unimodal in general.

title: Crystal and magnetic structures of MnSi in zero magnetic field: Neutron diffraction and symmetry analysis
abstract: Combining high-resolution wide-angle neutron powder diffraction with magnetic-superspace symmetry analysis, we refine the crystal structure and present, to our knowledge, the first systematic refinement of cubic $P2_13$ MnSi's zero-field magnetic structure across multiple magnetic satellite families. We compare single-arm rhombohedral 3+1D and cubic four-arm 3+4D magnetic superspace-group (MSSG) descriptions with propagation vectors along $\langle111\rangle$. Simultaneous extinction of the two satellite groups around $\{100\}$ dictates a transverse circular-helix model. This suppression and refinements of 18 separately varied satellite-group intensities support this ideal limit with only one adjustable magnetic amplitude. In the ideal single-arm model with MSSG $R3.1'(0,0,g)ts$, the moment has constant magnitude 0.535(3) $μ_B$ per Mn. An explicit four-arm 3+4D cubic superspace construction presented here combines four interpenetrating helices and, for the illustrated phase choice, has moments ranging from zero to 0.874(5) $μ_B$ per Mn, with the same root-mean-square moment as the 3+1D structure. Their identical powder profiles prevent the present measurements from distinguishing them. The average crystal structure remains cubic within experimental resolution, providing structural motivation for the cubic magnetic model. The mean lattice parameter, determined with formal relative precision $σ_a/a \lesssim 10^{-5}$, exhibits nonmonotonic temperature dependence below the Néel temperature.

title: An Adaptive Short-Step Variant of BroxGD with Linear Convergence under Quadratic Growth
abstract: Broximal Gradient Descent (BroxGD), recently analyzed by Richtárik et al. (arXiv:2605.08850v1), is a projection-free sister method to Projected Gradient Descent (ProjGD) for solving $\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)$, where $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ and $\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ is nonempty, closed and convex. The method performs local linear minimization over the feasible set intersected with a Euclidean ball and carefully prescribed radius. Like ProjGD, BroxGD enjoys linear convergence in the smooth strongly convex setting, with the same condition-number dependence. However, the known radius rule leading to linear convergence requires unavailable information and is therefore impractical. We develop an adaptive short-step variant of BroxGD which converges linearly for smooth convex functions under quadratic growth (generalizing strong convexity), without requiring unavailable information. We use $$z_k\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal X\cap\mathbb B(x_k,t_k)}\langle\nabla f(x_k),z\rangle,\quad x_{k+1}=\mathrm{Proj}_{S_k}(x_k-\nabla f(x_k)/L),$$ where $L$ is the smoothness constant of $f$, $\mathbb B(x,t)$ is the Euclidean ball centered at $x$ of radius $t$, and $S_k$ is the line segment connecting $x_k$ and $z_k$. The radius is updated by $t_{k+1}=\max\{\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|,t_k/2\}$. Projection onto $S_k$ requires only scalar clipping. Assuming an exact local linear minimization oracle, each update uses one oracle call. For any positive initial radius, we bound all oracle calls to reach objective error at most $\varepsilon$ and obtain $O((L/α)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ for fixed initialization, where $α=\min\{α_0,L\}$ and $α_0>0$ is the quadratic-growth constant.

title: Attacking Slide Puzzle CAPTCHAs Based on Time and Space Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: CAPTCHAs can protect websites from malicious attacks. As a typical representative of behavior CAPTCHAs, slide puzzle CAPTCHAs have become increasingly popular in recent years due to their user-friendliness and high security. Previous attack methods on slide puzzle CAPTCHA mainly face challenges in the following four aspects. (1) The defense mechanisms of previous slide puzzle CAPTCHAs were relatively simple. The current slide puzzle CAPTCHAs have added complex interferences, detected slide trajectory features in the two-dimensional space, and added other defense mechanisms. (2) The previous notch detection methods were difficult to accurately locate the notch positions. (3) Previous attack trajectories were limited to the horizontal dimension, making them impossible to pass the existing detection. (4) The previous attack trajectories were generated by fitting functions, which were relatively simple and could not well simulate the slide characteristics of human users. In response to the above challenges, firstly, we systematically analyze the defense strategies of six most popular slide puzzle CAPTCHAs: Capy, Dingxiang, Geetest, Kyger, Shumei and Tencent. Secondly, for each type of CAPTCHA, we construct a notch detection dataset and a slide trajectory dataset separately. Thirdly, we use advanced YOLOv11 to detect the notch positions and train generative adversarial networks (GAN) to generate attack trajectories. As far as we know, we are the first to generate attack trajectories by directly learning human slide trajectory characteristic. According to the experimental results, this method cracked six most popular slide puzzle CAPTCHAs with success rates of over 90\%, and the attack time is only about 5 seconds, indicating that the security of existing slide puzzle CAPTCHAs is facing challenge. At the same time, we propose various methods to enhance the security of slide puzzle CAPTCHAs.

title: What an Observer Reads off a Holographic Screen
abstract: What does an observer read off a holographic screen that is an array of qubits rather than a surface? In the generalized holographic principle the interaction between two separable systems acts on such a screen as a weighted sum, up to an overall prefactor, of commuting observables with values plus and minus one. When the weights are nonnegative and the prefactor is one and the joint eigenspaces are lines, everything a probe reads off the spectrum depends only on the list of weights, which we call the profile. On the screen with equal weights summing to one the running dimension read by a diffusion probe falls short of two at unit time by at most twice the reciprocal of the number of qubits; a geometric profile gives instead, through its level count, a plateau of any positive height. An observer correlates sets of qubits; its readout carries a profile at a given weighting when the levels it reads, counted with multiplicity, are those of a screen with one weight per set. We prove that a readout carries a profile at every weighting exactly when the distinct nonzero traces of its qubits are linearly independent over the field with two elements, the trace of a qubit being the list of sets that contain it; such a readout is a partition of the qubits it covers up to an invertible recoding, and a dependent one carries a profile only on finitely many proper linear subspaces of weightings. Refining a grouping without end builds a tower whose boundary is a profinite set and hence a condensed set, on which a strictly positive compatible profile separates the locally constant functions by a distance. Applications certify probabilistic and strong contextuality and give the leading shortfall of the distance between the poles of the fuzzy sphere; in a model of monogamous entanglement the pairs that weight-one threads representing operational ER=EPR can occupy at once are exactly the partial matchings.

title: A divisorial domain with non-Prüfer normalization
abstract: We answer a 1968 question of Heinzer by constructing a two-dimensional local divisorial domain whose normalization is not Prüfer.

title: Persistence landscape velocity: Closed formulas and a topological probe of quantum criticality
abstract: We introduce the landscape velocity $ξ$, a scalar measure of variation of a parameter-dependent persistence landscape. For families of finite barcodes whose bars are all born at the fixed filtration value $0$, we show that $ξ$ is the $L^2$ speed of the landscape curve where the sorted death times are differentiable and derive an exact closed formula that requires no persistence landscape at all: the death times of the barcodes, as functions of the parameter, suffice. For the velocity of the empirical mean of several landscapes we also prove a closed formula which, again, strikingly requires neither the empirical mean landscape nor any of the individual landscapes, only the individual barcodes. As an application, we revisit Olsthoorn's persistent homology analysis of the transverse-field Ising chain. Whereas his approach uses different homology degrees and summaries depending on the boundary conditions, ours uses $H_0$ only and a single rule: the position of the maximum of $ξ$. This rule locates the quantum critical point for both periodic and open boundary conditions, and for both mutual-information and correlator-based dissimilarities. The position of the maximum converges to the critical point faster than all the estimators we can extract from Olsthoorn's work. In the 4 scenarios considered (different boundary conditions and different dissimilarity matrices), the peak of the normalized velocity becomes increasingly pronounced with system size, with observed logarithmic growth. This logarithmic growth is proved for periodic boundaries with correlator dissimilarity under stated hypotheses, identifying landscape velocity as a singular topological response to quantum criticality.

title: NuJEV: Structured Visual Judgments for Consistent Nuclei Quantification
abstract: Nuclear quantification requires locating and typing nuclei, beyond generating a count. Inspired by Jev's structured decisions in place of free-form generation, we introduce NuJEV for nuclear perception in Qwen3-VL-2B. We jointly train visual LoRA and a parallel head to predict nuclear presence, centers, and types. One image encoding feeds both the nuclear head and original language decoder. The decoder interprets region and type requests, with counts computed from the predicted nuclei. On 2,732 PanNuke test images, NuJEV achieves a five-query mean absolute error ($\mathrm{MAE}_5$) of 1.844 overall and 5.268 on dense images, with localization/typed F1 of 0.816/0.682. A matched encoder ablation shows 41.0\% lower dense error with visual adaptation. For language requests, NuJEV reduces request MAE by 76.2\% relative to direct generation. Our code will be released as open source.

title: Uniqueness of Axisymmetric Vortices in the Magnetic Ginzburg-Landau Equations
abstract: We study vortex solutions of the magnetic Ginzburg-Landau model (or the Abelian-Higgs model). We establish uniqueness of axisymmetric vortex solutions for every winding number $n\geq1$ and coupling constant $λ>0$. Our proof uses a lattice inequality and constrained minimization to construct a positive radial solution lying above any two given radial solutions. A comparison argument based on the virial identity then establishes uniqueness. We further prove that the unique radial solution depends real analytically on $λ$ and that both radial profiles are strictly increasing with respect to $λ$.

title: Uncertainty principle on $\mathbb{T}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$
abstract: This paper establishes an uncertainty principle on the mixed space $\mathbb{T}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$ for $n \ge 2$. Leveraging the paraboloid restriction theorem on $\mathbb{Z}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$ derived from Barron's global-in-time Strichartz estimates for the semi-periodic Schrodinger equation, we construct measurable sets $S \subset \mathbb{T}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$ and $A(R,δ) \subset \mathbb{Z}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n$ that form a strong $L^2$ annihilating pair, satisfying the uniform inequality $\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb{T}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n)} \le 3(\|f\|_{L^2((\mathbb{T}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n)\setminus S)} + \|\widehat{f}\|_{L^2((\mathbb{Z}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n)\setminus A(R,δ))})$ for all $f \in L^2(\mathbb{T}^m \times \mathbb{R}^n)$, where the measures of $S$ and $A(R,δ)$ can be made arbitrarily large while the constant 3 remains unchanged. As an application, we derive a two-time observability inequality for the semi-periodic Schrodinger equation under a support condition on the phase-modified solution at the first observation time.

title: Fundamental Groups of Permutation Complexes
abstract: We present an elementary argument showing that fundamental groups of permutation complexes are free. Hence, $\mathbb{R} P^2$ cannot be realized by a permutation complex, answering a question of Chachólski, Levi and Meshulam.

title: Sections of the Kottwitz homomorphism and affine pinnings
abstract: Let $G$ be a connected reductive group split over $\mathbb{Z}$. The Kottwitz homomorphism identifies the group of connected components of the loop group of $G$ with the group $Ω$ of length zero elements of the extended affine Weyl group. We show that this homomorphism always has a homomorphic section, and that the section can be chosen inside the normalizer of $T$ in $G(\mathbb{Z}[t,t^{-1}])$. We then ask whether the section can be chosen to preserve an affine pinning. This is possible if no simple factor of $G$ is of type $B_{2m}$ or $C_{2m}$. It is impossible for $(SL_2\times Sp_{2n})/μ_2$ and $(SL_2\times Spin_{2n+1})/μ_2$ when $n$ is even. We show that the obstructions for $G$ and for its Langlands dual group are dual to each other, and we compute them by a lattice computation with a Coxeter element. As an application, we show that the component group of the centralizer of any semisimple element lifts to the centralizer. Under the same condition on the simple factors, the lift can be chosen to preserve a pinning of the neutral component.

title: OOM: Offload-Optimized Full-Parameter MoE Training via Memory-Execution Co-Design
abstract: Offloading model state to host memory and streaming layer weights let a single multi-GPU node train large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. GPU memory then becomes a performance budget, shared by resident expert state, retained activations, and execution worksets. The best allocation depends on the expert execution path, batch size, and sequence length. We present OOM (Offload-Optimized MoE), a full-parameter MoE training system that co-designs expert execution and memory allocation. For expert-parallel execution, OOM updates resident experts on their owning GPUs and jointly plans state residency and MoE activation retention according to pipeline dependencies. For local execution, OOM bounds GPU worksets through dependency-aware partitioning; in hybrid models, it also retains attention results on the host to avoid costly recomputation and selectively regenerates layer boundaries through cheaper layers to make room. Calibrated cost models guide joint configuration within GPU and host budgets to minimize step time; OOM selects among the configured paths through short executions. On four H100s, OOM trains with 1M-token contexts, whereas FSDP2, ZeRO-Offload, and MegaTrain exhaust GPU memory at 512K. It also trains a 122B-parameter MoE model, on which all three exhaust host memory. On four 24 GB RTX 4090s, it trains 512K-token contexts and 1,024 1K-token sequences per step without gradient accumulation. Across matched-global-batch comparisons, OOM delivers 1.58x and 4.08x geometric-mean (up to 2.14x and 7.77x) throughput over CPU-offloaded FSDP2 on the two platforms while using the least host memory among the evaluated systems -- as little as 1/3.0 of FSDP2's.

title: MG-Cache: Multi-Granularity Caching for Accelerating Diffusion Transformer Inference
abstract: Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models, while having become a powerful backbone for generative synthesis, suffer from high inference cost on generating high-resolution images. Diffusion caching has emerged as a promising acceleration technique to reduce inference cost. However, existing caching strategies fail to accurately identify the varying importance of different computational modules and rarely coordinate cache reusing across the timestep and layer granularities, making it difficult to control error accumulation. To address these limitations, we propose multi-granularity caching (MG-Cache) for DiTs, a novel and fully training-free approach to exploit computational redundancy both on timesteps and Transformer layers. Our core innovation contains a two-stage caching strategy: an offline timestep profiling analysis that identifies redundant timesteps for cache reuse, followed by an adaptive layer-wise caching strategy that combines input stability with importance of each Transformer layer to selectively cache stable Attention and MLP submodules. Extensive experiments on mainstream open-source DiT models validate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant acceleration while maintaining high fidelity to the uncached output, with up to a 4.18x acceleration on HunyuanVideo.

title: Exceptional Points in Scalar Quasinormal Modes of Rastall String-Fluid Black Holes
abstract: In this paper, we study exceptional points (EPs) in scalar quasinormal modes(QNMs) of Rastall string-fluid black holes by adding a localized Pöschl--Teller perturbation to the scalar potential, with the bump position $a$ and amplitude $\eb$ serving as independent controls. We solve the hyperboloidal problem with two-domain Chebyshev collocation and arbitrary-precision linear algebra, and use the complex discriminant, eigenvector coalescence, Jordan-chain residuals, square-root splitting and closed-loop mode exchange as complementary tests of defectiveness. For the regular $A=1$, $\eR=-1$ branch, the two-parameter search locates a resolution-stable second-order EP from $N=24$ to $N=60$, while constrained semidiscrete evolution gives the Jordan response $(C+Dt)e^{\iiω_{\rm EP}t}$. For the logarithmic $A=2$ branch, defective points occur in each finite truncation but their coordinates do not converge, so we make no continuum claim for this branch.

title: Probing Exotic Electron-Electron Interactions via Adiabatic Spin Inversion in MRFM
abstract: Light bosons beyond the Standard Model can mediate exotic spin-dependent interactions between electrons, motivating sensitive searches at short distances. We propose a magnetic resonance force microscopy (MRFM) scheme that exploits oscillating-cantilever-driven adiabatic reversals (OSCAR) of electron spins to convert these interactions into measurable mechanical signals. The ferromagnetic tip serves as both a dense polarized-spin source and a source of magnetic-field gradients, enabling force detection without magnetic shielding between the source and sensor. Within a linearized treatment of the coupled spin-mechanical dynamics, we derive resonance-frequency shifts associated with the $V_2$ and $V_3$ interactions and a second-harmonic force signal arising from the velocity-dependent $V_8$ interaction. We further investigate interrupted-OSCAR differential detection and distance-dependent measurements to discriminate exotic signals from conventional magnetic backgrounds. Using representative parameters from ensemble and single-spin MRFM experiments, we estimate the projected sensitivity under specified noise and statistical assumptions. The results suggest that the proposed scheme could provide complementary sensitivity to short-range spin-dependent interactions, with the potential to improve existing constraints on $V_2$ over selected submicrometer interaction ranges. Our study establishes adiabatic spin-inversion MRFM as a promising approach to probing exotic electron-electron forces.

title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.

title: Tiling of Hyperbolic Surface by Maximal Number of Tiles
