abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can write the weights of small neural networks directly, without gradient descent. This weight-space programming creates policies for sequential decision-making from a task description alone, but nothing guarantees that a written policy behaves as intended. We combine weight-space programming with probabilistic model checking. Given an environment modeled as a Markov decision process and a requirement in probabilistic computation tree logic (PCTL), an LLM writes all weights of a policy network, optionally repairs them on a dataset of optimal actions, and receives model-checking feedback until the requirement holds or a round limit is reached. The model checker Storm computes, rather than estimates from simulations, the probability that the policy satisfies the requirement, so every returned policy is verified. With two LLMs on three environments, the created policy of each of the 18 runs attains the optimal probability, before any dataset or model-checking feedback. Four of six policies programmed for two transporter jobs also complete three jobs with probability 1, so they generalize to a task that the LLM never saw. The pipeline also programs a policy that satisfies a complex safety requirement expressed with the PCTL until operator in all six runs. In one of them, dataset repair raised the accuracy to 98.4\% but broke the requirement, and one round of model-checking feedback restored it.

title: ScanDreamer: A Map-Grounded World Model for Quadrotor Navigation
abstract: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.

title: A Poisson-gas approach to medium-induced gluon radiation
abstract: The precision era of jet-quenching phenomenology requires a quantitative control of medium-induced gluon radiation. We consider the BDMPS-Z spectrum in the soft-gluon limit for a Yukawa (Gyulassy-Wang) potential. Writing the Yukawa dipole cross section as a Laplace superposition of Gaussians, we express the fully resummed spectrum as an average over Poisson-distributed configurations of Gaussian scattering centers, each of which is solved in closed form. This yields a master formula for the spectrum both differential in the transverse momentum $k_\perp$ and integrated with a cut on $k_\perp$, valid for static and expanding media with arbitrary profiles. Its evaluation by Monte Carlo sampling of the configurations is efficient and trivially parallelizable. The method reproduces the first order in opacity and published results without kinematic cuts, while with a cut we find sizeable relative deviations from previous results. We argue that the same construction extends to the more complex building blocks of an in-medium parton cascade, such as finite energy fraction and emissions off color antennas, and provides a natural starting point for analytical approximations. The code is publicly available.

title: Rethinking Geometric Depth in Monocular 3D Object Detection: A Projection-Consistent Reformulation
abstract: Monocular 3D detection (Mono3D) hinges on recovering depth from a single image, for which the geometric formulation $z \approx f \cdot H / h_{2D}$ is widely adopted due to its simplicity and direct grounding in projective geometry. We show that this formulation harbors a systematic, projection-induced bias: substituting the 2D bounding-box height $h_{2D}$ recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation that persists even under ground-truth inputs. We address this front-surface bias with MonoPCA, a unified framework built on a projection-consistent reformulation. At its core, PCDepth retains the measurable $h_{2D}$ and closes the gap to center depth through an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, eliminating the bias without introducing ill-posed regression targets. Because PCDepth couples depth to predicted object size and orientation, attribute perception becomes essential. We therefore introduce GeoAlign, a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student, strengthening attribute perception at no inference cost. Across four challenging benchmarks, MonoPCA achieves SoTA performance, including a +1.44% AP$_{3D}$ gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D$_{OUT}$. Code is available at https://github.com/alanzhangcs/MonoPCA.

title: The Canonical Family of Reduced Row Pivot Echelon Forms and the Induced Lexicographic Canonical Algorithm for Linear Programming
abstract: A complete canonical family of uniquely normalized, row-equivalent representatives of an $m\times n$ matrix is introduced and termed the family of Reduced Row Pivot Echelon Forms (RRPEFs). All RRPEFs represent the same row space, with the standard reduced row echelon form, renamed the Upper RREF (URREF), and the Lower RREF (LRREF) as its extreme members. A reformulation of Noether's Complementary Subspace Basis Theorem yields normalized bases of the row space that coincide with the nonzero rows of the corresponding RRPEFs. Constructively, each RRPEF is obtained by multi-index Gauss--Jordan reduction of a nonsingular transition submatrix. Factoring the admissible pivot-index sets by equality of their associated RRPEFs yields a quotient set in canonical bijection with the set of distinct RRPEFs. This bijection transfers the strict lexicographic order to the distinct RRPEFs and induces a finite chain from the URREF to the LRREF. The resulting structure gives rise to the Induced Lexicographic Canonical Algorithm (ILCA). Lexicographic confinement and singular-transition skipping restrict the candidate domain, whereas RRPEF reuse and scalar-equivalent transition bypassing avoid redundant Gauss--Jordan reductions while retaining the corresponding basic-solution tableaux. Strict lexicographic progression prevents cycling, while the traversal proceeds independently of objective improvement under degeneracy-induced stalling. ILCA terminates when a feasible tableau satisfies the standard optimality conditions and otherwise completes the finite traversal, including for Tucker- and Cunningham-type totally degenerate configurations.

title: Building heterogeneous multistep workflows in automated microscopy: reward design and knowledge transfer for autonomous structure property discovery
abstract: Autonomous microscopy can turn fast acquisition into scientific progress when it decides not only where to measure, but also what information to acquire, at what scan rate, and when to recalibrate the instrument. We develop a budget constrained framework for such multistep structure-property workflows. It combines explicit scientific rewards, action costs, instrument observation models, transfer of pre experiment knowledge into the online campaign, and evaluation kept independent of the controller. The transferred knowledge includes predictor accuracy and computational cost, empirical learner maturity functions that weight model-derived rewards, and drift characteristics established before controller training. Using a real electron energy-loss spectroscopy dataset, we run two complementary campaigns. In the first, the controller chooses between imaging and spectroscopy, image size, and scan speed. In the second, the instrument drifts and the controller also decides when to recalibrate. The campaigns show that response discovery and structure-property learning favor different surrogate models and acquisition strategies. They also show that simple acquisition rules form strong, practical baselines. Independent error analysis reveals where model uncertainty is and is not a reliable learning signal. In the drift campaign, explicit registration greatly improves positional accuracy, and the framework measures what this costs in spectroscopy throughput. Together, these results provide a reproducible way to design, compare, and audit autonomous experiments, and they define what microscopes must provide for deployment: independently executable actions, characterized scan and detector responses, timestamped registration telemetry, and complete action records.

title: Estimating Permeability of Carbonate Rocks from NMR T2 Distribution and Formation Factor Using a Physics-Based Model
abstract: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) logging provides a nondestructive method for characterizing pore structure and fluid distribution in reservoir rocks. Conventional permeability models, such as the Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) and Timur-Coates (TC) equations, have been widely used to estimate permeability from NMR T2 relaxation time distributions. However, these empirical models require calibration against core-measured permeability, and their fitted coefficients often vary substantially across lithologies and pore systems. In this study, we formulate and evaluate an NMR-informed implementation of a physics-based permeability relationship derived from critical path analysis (CPA) by linking the characteristic pore length scale to the dominant NMR relaxation time. We estimate permeability (k) using NMR T2 distributions and electrical formation factor (F) for 14 carbonate rock samples collected from the Morro do Chaves Formation in the Sergipe-Alagoas Basin, Brazil. We compare the predictive performance of this formulation with that of calibrated SDR and TC models. The proposed CPA-NMR formulation achieves a root mean squared logarithmic error (RMSLE) of 0.56 without calibration against measured permeability from the investigated formation. These findings indicate the potential of combining NMR relaxation measurements with electrical formation factor for physics-based permeability estimation. Further evaluation using independent datasets is needed to assess applicability across formations and lithologies.

title: Lift Height and the Structure of Classification Failure
abstract: We introduce a framework for measuring the depth of classification failure relative to a chosen invariant. A \emph{shadow map} records visible structure while suppressing finer information; lift packages recover this information in successive layers, and lift height measures the depth through which classification ambiguity persists. Canonical reduction removes redundant stages and yields an essential notion of lift height. For nilpotent groups, the lower central series provides a natural commutator lift tower, with lift height controlled by nilpotency class and decreasing under refinement of the shadow. The associated graded structure gives a Lie-theoretic interpretation of the successive commutator layers. The main examples show that classification depth is genuinely unbounded. Over any field of characteristic different from two, and for every positive integer, there exist nilpotent Lie algebras with the same fixed four-dimensional abelianisation whose commutator lift packages agree through the prescribed number of layers but differ at the next layer. Moreover, such separation can occur at arbitrarily large degree even when the complete underlying lower-central graded vector space is fixed. Thus neither a fixed shadow nor the dimensions, or even the underlying vector-space structure, of the lower-central graded object impose a uniform bound on the depth at which new commutator information may appear.

title: The $ϕ$-$η$ Puzzle and the Five-Layer Effective-Temperature Hierarchy in $pp$ Collisions at 2.76 and 7 TeV
abstract: Sequential kinetic freeze-out in high-energy collisions probes the dynamics governing the final stages of strongly interacting matter. Inspired by the recently established quadruple freeze-out scenario, we present a thermodynamic analysis of transverse momentum spectra for a set of identified particles produced in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 2.76$ and $7$ TeV. Using a modified Tsallis-Pareto function, we extract the effective temperature and the non-extensivity parameter for each species. We observe a robust five-layer hierarchy in the effective temperature. At both energies, the layers are: non-strange hadrons, singly-strange hadrons, multi-strange hadrons, light nuclei, and the $ϕ(1020)$ meson. At $7$~TeV, the $η$ meson joins the $ϕ(1020)$ meson in the highest-temperature layer. At both energies, each pair of neighboring layers is separated by more than $ 3σ$, and the separation at the top exceeds $7σ$. The grouping persists at both energies, while the temperatures shift upward at 7 TeV. The observed pattern shows that the decoupling sequence is driven by an interplay of strangeness, cross-sections, and the OZI rule rather than by particle mass alone. Notably, the $ϕ(1020)$ meson has a mass close to the proton, but a significantly higher temperature due to its OZI-suppressed coupling to the hadronic medium. The unexpected coincidence of $η$ and $ϕ(1020)$ at 7 TeV presents a puzzle that may point to a common early production mechanism or in-medium effects, which are not yet understood. The five-layer hierarchy provides new constraints on theoretical models of hadronization. It suggests that the sequential decoupling of particles from the evolving medium is even more sensitive to their internal structure and interaction than previously assumed, with implications for the QGP-like matter formation in small systems.

title: Daily Emergency Call Volume Forecasting using Univariate and Multivariate TimeGPT
abstract: This study investigates the potential of TimeGPT, a pretrained foundation model for timeseries, for forecasting daily emergency call volumes. Real-world emergency call data, comprising 2,101 daily observations, are used to evaluate both univariate and multivariate forecasting settings under one-step-ahead and seven-day multi-step-ahead scenarios. The multivariate forecasting incorporates temporal, meteorological, demographic, and socioeconomic variables. A chronological training, validation, and test split is adopted to prevent information leakage, while hyperparameters are selected using the validation set through grid search and early stopping when applicable. Forecasting performance is evaluated using multiple error metrics. Its forecasting performance is compared with several established forecasting approaches, including Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Regressors (SARIMAX), Poisson regression (PR), Negative Binomial regression (NBR), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). The results show that SARIMAX achieves the best overall performance in the univariate setting. In the multivariate setting, NBR and PR provide best performance. These findings indicate that the large-scale pretraining of TimeGPT do not necessarily translate into superior forecasting accuracy for emergency call volumes. Frugal methods trained solely on the available data remain better for this application.

title: Pluriclosed flow on Kähler manifolds
abstract: We prove the maximal existence conjecture for pluriclosed flow on Kähler backgrounds. This leads to a priori generalizations of the Aubin-Yau and Calabi-Yau theorems, and resolves the question of connectedness of generalized Kähler structures on Calabi-Yau backgrounds.

title: A Talenti-type result for the Pompeiu-Schiffer Conjecture
abstract: Schiffer's conjecture asserts that the ball is the only bounded simply connected domain carrying a Neumann eigenfunction of the Laplacian that is constant on the boundary; it is equivalent to the Pompeiu problem. In August 2026 it was disproved in the plane by computer-assisted constructions. We revisit the shape-optimization approach of~\cite{Se24} in the light of these counterexamples. We first show that the vanishing of the material derivative on the boundary, assumed in~\cite{Se24}, never holds, and we compute the correct optimality condition, involving an adjoint state, for the associated functional $J_2$. We prove that every planar Schiffer domain satisfies $\max|u| > \sqrt{2}|c|.$ Our main result is a Talenti-type theorem: if $u < c$ in $Ω$ , then $kR^* \geq j_{1,1},$ where $R^*$ is the radius of the disc of equal area, and equality holds only for the disc. Finally, using Siegel's transcendence theorem, we prove the infinitesimal rigidity of the disc for the Berenstein problem.

title: Coherent Control of High-Order Lightwave Currents in Gate-Tunable Bilayer Graphene
abstract: The sub-cycle acceleration of charge carriers in an electronic circuit by tailored terahertz (THz) electric-field waveforms, rather than conventional pulsed bias voltages, opens a transformative frontier for lightwave electronics operating far beyond the scaling limits of gigahertz electronic technologies. Yet gate-tunable coherent control of multi-order and non-perturbative currents has remained elusive. Here, we demonstrate lightwave control over the amplitude, phase flips, and zero-crossings of THz field-driven high-order currents by utilizing phase-locked pairs of single-cycle THz fields in a dual-gated bilayer graphene (BLG) device. By leveraging the in-situ tuning of both bandgap and charge doping, we reveal extreme THz photocurrent rectification and sub-THz-cycle current generation that are governed by a strong field-driven crossover from interband multi-photon coherence to intraband lightwave acceleration, whose competition provides an exceptional sensitivity to the THz-pulse pair drive. Our interferometric nonlinear THz photocurrent spectroscopy of sub-cycle electronic excitations accesses and controls non-perturbative, multi-quantum photocurrents, which manifest as an extreme-order THz frequency comb. Quantum-kinetic simulations map these lightwave-controlled electron trajectories, revealing that sub-THz-cycle ballistic transport underpins gate- and THz-field-driven functionality enabled by electrostatic doping and bandgap tuning within the atomically thin device architecture. The demonstrated on-demand coherent control of nonperturbative photocurrent transport regimes can be extended to a broad range of atomically thin device architectures, opening new avenues for gate- and field-programmable logic, memory, and quantum simulators in which electronic pathways are steered on sub-cycle, petahertz timescales and atomic length scales.

title: Unveiling a Concentration of Hard X-Ray Point Sources in the Nuclear Stellar Disk with XMM-Newton
abstract: The Galactic Center is home to the largest known concentration of X-ray sources ever detected in our Galaxy, including a sizable population of accreting compact objects. Utilizing data from the XMM-Newton Galactic Plane Heritage Survey of the central $20^{\circ}\times2^{\circ}$ of the Milky Way, we investigate the varying source populations in the inner regions of the Galaxy. We identify for the first time a concentration of extremely hard X-ray sources within $|l|<1.3^{\circ}$ and $|b|<0.3^{\circ}$, a region that overlaps the nuclear stellar disk (NSD). We determine that this hardness is intrinsic to the sources and not a manifestation of high line-of-sight column density ($N_{\rm H}$). Unlike the "soft" X-ray sources, this population does not trace the stellar mass distribution, indicating an overabundance compared to the underlying stellar population. We simulate spectra for a variety of source types to model their X-ray hardness and compare their distributions to those we observed in our survey data. We find that a significant subset of the Galactic Center X-ray population may comprise intermediate polars (IPs) with massive white dwarfs, possibly formed through dynamical processes. Our study provides novel observational insights into the distribution of stellar remnants and other X-ray sources in the vicinity of our supermassive black hole, Sgr A*.

title: Delegating Computation with Approximate Arithmetic: Interactive Proofs for Wizards
abstract: We study interactive proofs for arithmetic circuits over the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ in which both the prover and the verifier compute approximately (unlike muggles, wizards can use magic, i.e., floating-point numbers). The goal is to prove that a claimed output $y$ is close to the exact output $C(x)$: for thresholds $0<Δ_0<Δ$, the honest prover is accepted whenever $|y-C(x)|\leΔ_0$, and every prover is rejected with high probability whenever $|y-C(x)|>Δ$. Existing proof systems for real-valued data verify rounded finite-field computations. Bitan et al.~[EUROCRYPT~2026] gave an approximate sum-check protocol. We extend the protocol of Goldwasser, Kalai, and Rothblum (GKR) [STOC~2008] to public-coin interactive proofs for logspace-uniform layered circuits over $\mathbb{C}$ of size $S$, depth $L$, and $n$ inputs, under public bounds on gate values and wiring coefficients. At constant soundness error, the verifier runs in time $(n+1)\mathrm{poly}(L,\log S,b)$, the communication is $\mathrm{poly}(L,\log S,b)$, and the prover runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(S,b)$, where $b$ is the bit precision. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first doubly efficient interactive proofs in which both parties compute approximately. GKR reduces two claims about a layer to one on a random line, which leaves the unit circle, where our error bounds hold. We instead label gates by complex roots of unity and combine the two claims with a random root of unity as coefficient. We choose the error thresholds backward from the input layer, so that a large output error survives the verifier's rounding at every step. The honest prover needs only $O(S \log S)$ complex operations. We also obtain zero-knowledge proofs from one-way functions, one-round arguments from private information retrieval, and interactive PCPs whose proof length is polynomial in the witness length.

title: Division ring extensions and the realization of Coxeter diagrams $I_2(n)$
abstract: For each integer $n\ge5$, we construct a hereditary artinian ring of finite representation type with Coxeter diagram $I_2(n)$. Both of its diagonal division rings are two-generated over the field $\mathbb{Q}(ζ)$, where $ζ$ is a primitive root of unity of order $n-2$. The construction is based on a chain of quantized Weyl relations and a shift automorphism. We give one-sided bases for the corresponding division ring extensions and compute the right dimension sequence of the bimodule. The resulting ring has exactly $n$ isomorphism classes of indecomposable finitely generated right modules.

title: A Talenti-type rigidity theorem and P-function constraints for the Pompeiu--Schiffer problem in every dimension
abstract: Schiffer's conjecture asserts that the ball is the only bounded domain, with boundary homeomorphic to a sphere, carrying a nonconstant Neumann eigenfunction of the Laplacian that is constant on the boundary; for such domains it is equivalent to the Pompeiu problem. In 2026 it was disproved in the plane and in many higher dimensions by computer-assisted and analytic constructions. We study what survives. Our main result is a Talenti-type theorem valid in every dimension $N\ge2$: if the eigenfunction $u$ stays strictly below its boundary value $c>0$, then $kR^*\ge j_{N/2,1}$, where $k^2$ is the eigenvalue, $R^*$ the radius of the ball of equal volume and $j_{N/2,1}$ the first positive zero of $J_{N/2}$; equality holds only for the ball. We compare this threshold with the unconditional bound $kR^*\ge 2^{1/N}j_{N/2-1,1}$ given by the Krahn--Szegő inequality. Using Payne's P-function $P=|\nabla u|^2+λu^2$ we prove that every Schiffer domain satisfies $\max|u|>\sqrt N\,|c|$, together with pointwise and distance bounds. We correct the shape-optimization approach of an earlier work by computing the optimality condition of the associated boundary functional with an adjoint state. Using the transcendence of the zeros of Bessel functions of integer and half-integer order, we prove the infinitesimal rigidity of the ball, in every dimension, both for the Schiffer problem and for the Berenstein problem. Finally, we reconstruct numerically the convex four-dimensional counterexample of Guo and check the above statements on it.

title: ODSA: Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation
abstract: Test-time scaling improves the accuracy of a language model's answers by spending more computation at inference time. Established methods do so either sequentially, revising a single solution over several passes, or in parallel, generating several independent solutions and selecting among them. We present ODSA (Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation), an LLM-directed scaling framework in which an orchestrator LLM is given existing test-time scaling methods as actions --- discovery of a new independent solution, comparison of existing solutions to build a better one, and acceptance of a proposed answer, which triggers its verification --- and directs stateless workers to carry them out. The orchestrator does not solve the problem itself: it allocates computation, feeds the results of earlier actions into later ones, and takes every action from a single context, so that each decision is informed by everything tried before. On Humanity's Last Exam, ODSA improves accuracy by 4.7 to 18.0 points across three models over a single direct call to the model with no test-time scaling. On LiveCodeBench, where a single direct call already solves most problems, it improves accuracy by 0.6 to 14.0 points.

title: GenISys: Integrated Ship Systems Design Using Subsystem-Conditional Tabular Diffussion
abstract: Ship design requires coordinating coupled subsystems to satisfy engineering constraints and balance competing performance and cost objectives. Generative artificial intelligence has supported component design, but integrated ship generation must also account for interactions among hull geometry, structure, propulsion, and operation. This paper presents GenISys, a framework for generating integrated systems, demonstrated through early-stage bulk-carrier design. Its dataset contains 217,999 proposed designs, including 16,247 that satisfy the formulated engineering constraints. The proposed simultaneous conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (SCDDPM) generates subsystems together, allowing each subsystem model to respond to changes elsewhere during generation. Experiments compare this approach with monolithic whole-ship generation and sequential subsystem generation across five independent training runs per architecture. In a study targeting lower cost per tonne of cargo transported, designs were generated for a required voyage range of 5,000 nautical miles. SCDDPM produced designs satisfying the formulated engineering constraints and meeting a common low-cost target in 55.70% of generation requests, compared with 51.10% for the monolithic model and 47.54% for the sequential model. These correspond to 9.0% and 17.2% more qualifying designs, respectively, while maintaining similar estimated transport costs. These results show how generative artificial intelligence can coordinate subsystems to generate feasible, high-performing integrated systems.

title: When Strategies Do Not Determine Play: Infinite Hat-Guessing Games on Subsets of the Reals
abstract: We study infinite hat-guessing games indexed by linearly ordered sets $S\subseteq\mathbb R$, where players guess sequentially using information determined by the order. While well-ordered standing sets admit the naive, recursive definition of play, we found a surprising example showing that this approach fails for non-well-ordered ones, where local decision rules do not determine a unique global outcome. By requiring uniqueness of play, we aim to provide a natural framework for hat-guessing games on arbitrary standing sets. For the classical visibility model, it was previously known due to Glivický that at most one incorrect guess can be guaranteed when $S$ is well-ordered. We prove the same result for backwards well-ordered sets, even in the case when $S$ has no first element. In the full-visibility version of the game, Glivický proved that at most one incorrect guess can be guaranteed if the standing set has a first element. We extend this result to arbitrary nonempty standing sets.

title: Karhunen-Loève Transforms of Autoregressive Windows Based on Matched Symmetry Groups
abstract: The Karhunen-Loève transform of a window of a stationary autoregressive process of any order $p$ is described through its poles, extending the Algebraic Diversity framework, which selects a transform by the matched group. For simple roots every basis vector is a sum of at most $p$ sinusoids, at the frequencies where the spectrum equals the eigenvalue, plus modes decaying from the ends. The window covariance differs from a member of the class diagonalized by the type-II discrete cosine transform by a closed-form matrix of rank $2p$, exactly when no pole is zero, so the eigenvalues interlace spectrum samples on the cosine grid, and the coding-gain loss of the cosine transform is an exact function of that matrix with computable bounds: for the $8\times8$ Markov block of image coding at pole $0.95$ it is below 1.2 percent. By Kronecker's theorem the rank is at most $2\max(p,q)$ for rational spectra; a moving-average window departs in its Hankel corners, and an integrated (ARIMA) window departs by low rank from the type-VII sine class, exact for the random walk. The exact symmetry is generically the reflection and contains a wreath product for interleaved windows; the dihedral group of the even extension is matched approximately, the dominant pole's sign choosing cosine or sine. The two groups give the transform a fast form: a parity fold, half-length cosine cores and a cascade of at most $p$ first-order Cauchy stages, exactly $p$ for a minimal AR($p$) model. The first-order case recovers results obtained by other means.

title: Sparse Fault Detection in Linear Systems: Equivalence of GLR Tests and $\ell_1$-regularized Least Squares
abstract: This paper studies the detection of an impulsive fault of unknown time and input channel in a linear system with unknown initial state and Gaussian measurement noise. First, we show that the generalized likelihood ratio test, after the initial state is eliminated by projection onto the parity space, is the zero-solution test of a weighted lasso with an unpenalized nuisance block; the regularization parameter is the test threshold, and for unknown noise variance the same holds for the square-root lasso. Second, we show that the null distribution depends on the system only through a Gram matrix, so that the threshold is computed exactly and offline, and we compare it with closed-form bounds. Third, we characterize the fraction of a fault that survives the projection: we give it in closed form through observability Gramians, we show that it converges to a geometrically decaying profile for strictly stable systems, and that, for systems with unit-modulus modes, it grows linearly with the fault time as a fraction of the record length. Numerical studies, including a two-input, two-output example, illustrate the results.

title: Proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture: An Exposition
abstract: We give an exposition of a recent proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which states that every degree-$d$ polynomial $p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0,1]$ has a variable of influence at least $\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d)$. This implies that quantum query algorithms for decision problems can be efficiently simulated classically on most inputs. It also yields a near-equivalence between the status of the $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$ problem in the random oracle and unrelativized worlds. We organize the proof around four main steps and discuss how each connects to the literature on the analysis of boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. To bring out the key ideas, we do not optimize parameters, and our presentation yields weaker exponents than the original. $\textbf{Authors' note.}$ The proof was discovered by David Turturean using a research system developed at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), in combination with a non-public Anthropic model. The proof was then shared with the authors, who worked to understand it and prepare this exposition. Anthropic's public models were used in this process. The authors did not receive financial compensation from Anthropic or PSI. This article is not intended for publication at a conference or in a journal.

title: Attack Injection to Vehicle Reactions: Extensible Closed-Loop Adversarial Evaluation Framework
abstract: Autonomous vehicles can use information exchanged with other vehicles and roadside infrastructure to support driving decisions. However, applications that rely on this information can make unsafe decisions when it is falsified. Studying the resulting traffic effects requires following received information through application decisions, vehicle reactions, and subsequent interactions. We present an extensible closed-loop adversarial evaluation framework built on VaN3Twin, a platform for traffic and wireless network simulation, with a diverse attack library and a labelled dataset covering benign and attack conditions. A key advantage of the framework is that it can be extended with additional attacks, message paths, receiving applications, and logging fields. The added library contains 76 configurable attack profiles adapted to message formats defined by the European Telecommunications Standards Institute. These profiles are organized into nine groups of related attacks, referred to as suites. The framework connects live attack injection and simulated network delivery to receiving applications, whose selected commands update vehicle movement. The resulting state feeds subsequent message generation, closing the loop. The dataset links physical vehicle states and message exchanges to attack labels, application decisions, selected commands, and traffic outcomes. Evaluation with individual and combined attack suites confirmed execution of all profiles, and every suite produced requests linked to attacked messages. A recorded sequence also showed a vehicle reacting to an attacked message and subsequently influencing another vehicle through an unmodified message describing its updated movement. These findings demonstrate how live injection and vehicle feedback support the study of direct and indirect effects as traffic evolves.

title: Combinatorial Invariants for Metacyclic Groups
abstract: We study product-one invariants of finite metacyclic groups, with particular attention to metacyclic $p$-groups. For semidirect products $C_n\rtimes C_m$ such that $\operatorname{ord}_n(\ell)=m$ and $\operatorname{ord}_q(\ell)=m$ for every prime divisor $q$ of $n$, we give a short proof of the known formula for the small Davenport constant and determine the exact value of the $η$-constant. When $n=p$ is prime, we use Vosper's theorem to obtain a growth result for products of non-trivial conjugacy classes contained in $C_p$, from which we derive a block-saturation principle for product-one sequences. For split metacyclic $p$-groups, we determine the small Davenport constant in terms of the order and the exponent, and obtain bounds for the $η$-constant and the Erdős--Ginzburg--Ziv constant. The Davenport bound is also extended to finite nilpotent split metacyclic groups. Our approach relies in part on a general quotient-lifting principle for the three invariants $\mathsf d$, $η$, and $\mathsf s$. For non-cyclic metacyclic $p$-groups, this principle applies through the Frattini quotient, which is isomorphic to $C_p^2$. We further establish upper and lower bounds for the Erdős--Ginzburg--Ziv constant of arbitrary metacyclic $p$-groups, and show that both bounds are best possible within this class. The lifting method also provides a short proof of a known theorem of Han and Zhang for groups $C_m\ltimes C_n$ with $m\mid n$. Finally, we determine the Olson constant of the dihedral group $D_{2p}$, for every prime $p>3$, in terms of the Olson constant of $C_p$.

title: Practical Deep Learning-Based Block Demapping for mmWave MIMO Systems
abstract: Deep learning is expected to play a central role in 6G systems, by enabling data-driven physical layer designs that can adapt to practical wireless impairments. This is particularly important for millimetre-wave (mmWave) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which are strongly affected by residual channel distortions, interference, and hardware non-idealities that are difficult to capture with analytical models. In this paper, we propose a deep learning-based soft demapper that performs block-wise processing of received symbols instead of conventional symbol-wise detection. The demapper employs a one-dimensional convolutional neural network to learn temporal structure induced by practical propagation and hardware effects, while producing soft bit outputs compatible with soft-decision decoding stages. The proposed approach is trained and evaluated for a 4$\times$4 wideband mmWave MIMO system at 60~GHz, using an over-the-air dataset collected across multiple days and settings. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over a conventional soft-decision demapper, including up to a 2.6$\times$ reduction in bit error rate for 16QAM and up to a 17.6$\times$ reduction for 64QAM under real over-the-air mmWave MIMO conditions. The proposed demapper is further implemented on a Zynq RFSoC platform using a reconfigurable convolution engine and fixed-point arithmetic, achieving an approximately 34.3$\times$ speedup compared to a processor-based implementation, and demonstrating that learning-based demapping can be deployed efficiently on resource-constrained edge hardware.

title: Geometric Endpoints, Global Trajectories, and Teichmüller Projection for the Möbius-Invariant Willmore Flow
abstract: We study endpoints and conformal projection of the Möbius-invariant Willmore flow in the round three-sphere. Under uniform nonumbilicity or an integrable weighted condition, image-measure transport yields a unique finite-time integral-varifold limit. Reduced Hopf trajectories have unique anchored finite-time profile and marked conformal endpoints at arbitrary energy. Every smooth global reduced trajectory converges smoothly modulo reparametrization to an elastic profile, with quantitative rates and finite dissipation length. We compute the differential of the conformal-class projection along reduced trajectories and prove that its maximal rank persists at every finite time when it holds initially. Near the Clifford torus, Hopf tori with the same marked conformal type can have noncollinear projected velocities, ruling out a common autonomous Teichmüller equation even after positive time recalibrations.

title: Simple algebraic groups with good reduction, the genus problem, and unramified cohomology
abstract: We obtain a number of new results on the arithmetic of linear algebraic groups over higher-dimensional fields. In particular, we resolve some key open questions over 2-dimensional global fields, such as the finiteness of the genus of spinor groups of quadratic forms of dimension $\geq 10$. We also extend various finiteness results to new classes of fields, including function fields of $p$-adic surfaces. Our arguments rely in a crucial way on new finiteness results for unramified cohomology.

title: Perturbation Profiles of Scanpath Classifiers: What Reading, Code-Comprehension and Video Decoders Are Sensitive To
abstract: When a scanpath descriptor discriminates a task, it is rarely clear what the discrimination rests on. We propose a perturbation profile for trial-level descriptors. Five transformations each destroy one stated property while preserving a listed set of invariants: fixation order, duration-position coupling, the duration distribution, orientation and handedness, and fine spatial structure. The classifier is refit, and the drop in participant-held-out AUC is the pipeline's sensitivity to that property. Because refitting lets the learner use redundant information, this describes the refitted pipeline, not what a fitted classifier used. Intervals come from a participant bootstrap that refits; in simulations at the sample sizes analysed, where the target was zero they excluded zero at a pooled rate of at most 2.5%, and they covered the target in 99.6% of 2720 cases. We profiled seven descriptors on twelve binary problems from three public datasets: reading (SB-SAT, 95 participants), program comprehension (EMIP, up to 159) and video and game viewing (GazeBase, 60). Permuting fixation order raised the AUC of a descriptor built on mean saccade amplitude on three problems (by up to 0.23), because permutation turns amplitude into a measure of spatial spread. A "comprehension" contrast that pooled two programs reached AUC 0.70 with a spread-only baseline and fell to 0.47 within one program: the profile located the confound in stimulus layout. On native versus non-native readers, recurrence was sensitive to order and to jitter at the scale of text lines but not of characters, while a two-feature duration and amplitude descriptor reached the same AUC (0.65). A graph descriptor built on the code's tokens was the strongest non-baseline descriptor on the program contrast (0.78; 0.87 with boosted trees). The interpreted results held under longer runs and three seeds; under a second learner 15 of 16 kept t

title: An Interpretable Fuzzy Tree for Turbofan Remaining Useful Life with an Auditable Per-Component Diagnostic Layer
abstract: Data-driven remaining useful life (RUL) estimators for turbofan engines are accurate but opaque, and their internal features typically encode remaining life rather than any specific component's state. This paper presents an interpretable genetic fuzzy tree that predicts RUL from cruise-condition sensor means on N-CMAPSS while exposing a per-component diagnostic layer inspectable rule by rule. The tree follows the engine hierarchy: sensors to component health, then to bounded component damage, spool damage, and RUL, so each level answers a different maintenance question. Training is staged so the prognostic objective cannot reshape the diagnostic layers: health leaves are fitted to physical targets and frozen, a deterministic fuzzy damage map with fleet-referenced thresholds is imposed on each component, and only the aggregation is optimized for RUL. It consumes 13 cruise-mean scalars per cycle rather than a trajectory, which removes any sequence model. On the native split it reaches 8.44 cycles RMSE on the multi-fault subset and 11.51 across all modes with 333 free parameters, 411 total rules, 32 to 12,000 times fewer than compiled baselines. An exhaustive sensor search bounds which components are diagnosable under the tested cruise-mean design, and the rule base is structured to admit formal verification, which this study does not discharge.

title: Predictive Neuromorphic Control of a Scanning Mirror System: An Event-Centric Framework
abstract: Organizing control around events can reduce sensing and actuation demands while directly linking control decisions to the occurrence and timing of desired system behaviors. This paper proposes a novel event-centric model predictive control (MPC) framework that unifies event sensing, event prediction, and event regulation. Events define the feedback information, prediction horizon, and event-timing objectives, placing them at the center of predictive control design. The framework is developed for a scanning mirror system equipped with a baseline neuromorphic controller composed of spiking neurons that supports sparse actuation. The control objective is to achieve prescribed zero-crossing times and a desired scanning range while minimizing the mechanical energy transferred between the actuator and the mirror. A sampling-based algorithm is presented to obtain suboptimal solutions of the event-centric MPC optimization problem without requiring an explicit event-to-event prediction model. By grounding predictive optimization in events, the proposed framework opens a new direction for MPC design and its integration with neuromorphic control.

title: The sharp bound on the distance between the centers of mass of a convex body and its boundary
abstract: We prove that the distance between the centers of mass $c(K)$ and $c(\partial K)$ of a convex body $K$ and its boundary $\partial K$, respectively, does not exceed $ D_n$ times the width of $K$ in the direction of the vector joining $c(\partial K)$ and $c(K)$. The constant $D_n$ is optimal and coincides with the sharp constant in the problem of bounding the distance between the orthogonal projection of the centroid of a convex body onto a hyperplane and the centroid of its orthogonal projection onto that hyperplane.

title: Trail Making Tests in Extended Reality: A Critical Review with Implications for Cognitive Ageing
abstract: Extended reality (XR) versions of the Trail Making Test and Color Trails Test are promising for assessing and training cognition in older adults. However, each XR adaptation is a new instrument, whose display, interaction technique, timing rules and layouts may change what it measures. This critical narrative review maps these implementations by software lineage and appraises their evidence for assessment and training against common criteria. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code was inspected, serves as a measurement case. XR trail-making tests showed convergence with paper and computerised versions, varying by test part and sample, and clinical group differences (e.g., Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment). However, gaps in reliability (e.g., randomised forms), validation (e.g., norms, prospective samples) and reporting (e.g., error handling, build identity) emerged, and no training benefit attributable to the trail-making component was identified. The TMT-VR case shows how interaction technique, timing rule, error handling and unlogged layouts shape a score's meaning. Future tests should log layouts and events, estimate alternate-form reliability and undergo prospective validation, and training trials should isolate the trail-making component. Several XR trail-making tests have moved beyond feasibility, and reported tolerability during supervised sessions supports further evaluation in older adults.

title: Exponential stabilization of an Euler--Bernoulli beam via internal feedback under distributed time delay
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the internal stabilization of a closed-loop system which consists of an Euler--Bernoulli beam subjected to a structural damping mechanism with a distributed delay into the domain. Under appropriate assumptions on the weights of the delay term and internal damping, we first prove the well-posedness of the system by a semigroup approach. Then, by constructing an appropriate Lyapunov functional and utilizing the multiplier method, we establish the exponential decay of the system energy.

title: Polar foliations on the Cayley plane
abstract: We classify polar foliations on the Cayley projective plane, completing the classification of polar foliations on compact rank one symmetric spaces.

title: Stabilization of an Euler--Bernoulli beam equation with distributed damping and interior time delay
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the effect of a fixed time delay on the internal stabilization of an Euler--Bernoulli beam clamped at one end with distributed damping. Under appropriate assumptions on the feedback weights, we first establish that the problem is well-posed using semigroup theory. Furthermore, using the multiplier method combined with a suitable Lyapunov functional, we prove the exponential stability of the system.

title: Feel My Focus: Gaze-Triggered Digital Twin Creation for Remote Collaboration
abstract: We present Feel My Focus, a gaze-triggered mixed reality (MR) demonstration that enables rapid creation and sharing of lightweight 3D digital twins during remote collaboration. Unlike systems that use gaze primarily as a referential pointer, Feel My Focus treats sustained visual attention as a generative action: a fixation on a physical object initiates single-image capture, attention-guided segmentation, and one-shot 3D reconstruction, allowing a remote partner to inspect and discuss the object in situ. The system integrates gaze-tracking glasses, modular segmentation and reconstruction services, and an MR client for runtime streaming and interaction. This design prioritizes responsiveness and experiential continuity over photometric fidelity. We report observations from a public demonstration, highlighting design trade-offs, failure modes, and user control considerations for deploying gaze-triggered generative systems in real-world collaborative settings.

title: Spectral Stability, Fatou Basin Contraction, and Machine-Checked Multipliers in Holomorphic Extensions of Generalized Syracuse Dynamics
abstract: We embed the Syracuse operator $T(n) = n/2$ (even $n$), $T(n) = (3n+1)/2$ (odd $n$) and the Collatz map $C(n)$ into $\mathbb{C}$ via entire functions of exponential type $π$: $f(z) = \frac{1}{4}(1 + 4z - (1 + 2z)\cos(πz))$ and $F(z) = \frac{1}{4}(2 + 7z - (2 + 5z)\cos(πz))$. We prove five results: (1) every integer periodic cycle $C \subset \mathbb{N}^+$ of $T$ is a strictly attracting Fatou cycle of $f$ with multiplier $μ_f(C) = 3^{N_{\mathrm{odd}}}/2^N = \prod_{n \in C\text{ odd}} \frac{3n}{3n+1} \in (0,1)$, and $μ_f(O_{1,2}) = μ_F(O_{1,4,2}) = 3/4 < 1$; (2) on the Fatou basin $B(O_{1,2})$, $g = f^{\circ 2}$ conjugates to $Φ_j(g(z)) = \frac{3}{4}Φ_j(z)$ with Koenigs Taylor jets $c_2(1) = -\frac{13}{2}π^2$ and $d_2(2) = -\frac{9}{2}π^2$; (3) the Schwarzian derivative is strictly negative on $\mathbb{Z}$ ($S(f)(n) \le 3π^2 - \frac{3}{8}π^4 \approx -6.9196 < 0$), and a repelling Julia 2-cycle $O_{\mathrm{rep}} \subset J(f)$ ($μ\approx 1.2148 > 1$) isolates $B(O_{1,2})$; (4) on $(\mathbb{Z}_2, μ_{\mathrm{Haar}})$, the 2-adic Lyapunov exponent $λ_{\mathrm{Haar}} = \frac{1}{2}\ln(3/4) \approx -0.143841 < 0$ equals $\frac{1}{2}\ln|μ_f(O_{1,2})|$; and (5) we certify 20 theorems in Lean 4 (anc/CollatzAttractor.lean, 0 sorry). These results establish local Fatou invariants and 2-adic ergodic averages for $f(z)$, leaving open whether every $n_0 \in \mathbb{N}^+$ lies in $\bigcup_{k \ge 0} f^{-k}(B(O_{1,2}))$.

title: Evolving stellar wind environment around M dwarfs and its influence on magnetic star-planet interactions
abstract: M dwarfs are the most abundant group of stars in the Galaxy and they are expected to host a large number of exoplanets orbiting in the habitable zone. It is believed that stellar winds of M dwarfs can have a substantial effect on these exoplanets and on the observations of these systems. However, a systematic investigation of how the stellar winds of M dwarfs varies on timescales of a few months to years and how this impacts exoplanets around these stars is missing. We aim to investigate how variability of magnetic field properties of M dwarfs affects their stellar winds, which is essential for future studies of star-planet interactions (SPIs) and planetary habitability. Such variability might shed light on whether SPI signatures are going to repeat. We have compiled a total of 18 magnetic field maps for 6 M dwarfs, with masses between 0.1 and 0.6 $M_\odot$, and rotation periods between 2.7 and 175.6 days. We use these maps as input of 3D magnetohydrodynamic stellar wind simulations. We derive the mass-loss rate, the angular momentum-loss rate, and the Alfvén radius. For the stars with confirmed exoplanets (DS Leo, YZ Cet, and GJ 1151) we investigate the variability of stellar wind properties at the orbit. We find mass-loss rates between $1.0\times10^{-14}~M_\odot~{\rm yr^{-1}}$ and $2.3 \times 10^{-13}~M_\odot~{\rm yr^{-1}}$ and angular momentum-loss rates between $4.6 \times 10^{27}~{\rm erg}$ and $4.9 \times 10^{31}~{\rm erg}$. For individual stars the Alfvén radius, mass-loss rate, and angular momentum-loss rate varied with time by up to a factor of 1.5, 3.8, and 7.4 respectively. Our results follow the observational relation between mass-loss rate and X-ray flux. Due to the time-varying Alfvén surface, exoplanets orbiting DS Leo and YZ Cet move in and out of the sub-Alfvénic regime, affecting the nature of star-planet interactions and prospects for their detection.

title: Hyperelasticity as an efficient regularizer for 2D-3D thoracic motion models
abstract: Patient-specific motion models enable real-time volumetric imaging of the thorax from a single x-ray projection, but most existing approaches require hours of training. The VM-DS framework trains in minutes, yet its image-space self-consistency regularizer accounts for 40% of the motion-model fitting time and does not prevent the fitted fields from folding. In this paper, we explore a range of regularization approaches including scaling-and-squaring, bending energy, diffusion, first-order inverse consistency, isotropic total variation, a negative-Jacobian hinge, |log det J|, a control-point injectivity bound and hyperelastic regularization. Hyperparameters were selected on two development cases from the public DIR-Lab 4D dataset under rules fixed in advance, and the regularizers were tested on eight held-out cases. At a fixed number of training steps, the hyperelastic term trained in 5.6 against 8.4 min and gave a lower held-out TRE (2.5 mm). With a quarter of the motion-model budget it matched the baseline (2.7 mm), and at every budget from 2 to 17 min its mean TRE was lower by 0.3-0.5 mm. Hyperelastic fields had no folded voxel in any held-out view, whereas baseline fields folded in 83 % of views, with image similarity unchanged. A hyperelastic volume penalty can therefore replace image-space self-consistency, matching accuracy with 3-5 minutes of training and removing folding, bringing on-the-day motion models closer to routine use in image-guided interventions. Code will be available at https://github.com/Image-X-Institute/Voxelmap/tree/hyper

title: MICE: Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder - A Hierarchical Foundation Model for Mouse Behavior
abstract: Quantifying mouse behavior from pose is a foundational tool in neuroscience, ethology, drug discovery, and animal welfare. Self-supervised foundation models are a natural fit, but a foundation model for mouse behavior must handle social behavior - many behaviors that matter (aggression, courtship, mounting, allogrooming) are inherently multi-animal. Existing self-supervised pose models fall short: they encode each animal independently and discard interaction signal, hard-code the animal count, and pretrain one dataset at a time. We introduce MICE (Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder), a hierarchical foundation model for mouse behavior that pretrains jointly on six mouse-pose corpora spanning one to four mice and 7 to 27 keypoints. MICE combines a hierarchical individual encoder capturing per-mouse kinematics at multiple temporal scales with a Perceiver-style social encoder whose learned latent codebook decouples parameter count from animal count, so a single checkpoint serves any group size without retraining. Across four evaluation protocols spanning six datasets, MICE matches or exceeds prior keypoint-based baselines, and layer-wise probing shows the social stage incrementally improves discriminability beyond the individual encoder. Code, weights, and data are available at https://github.com/eric0708/MICE.

title: A software infrastructure proposal for mathematical research with AI agents
abstract: In 2026, AI agents began to produce mathematical results. They formalize complete theorems and settle open problems faster than a research group can review the results. The difficulty is shifting to organizing that output, deciding which results to trust and understanding them as a group. Current tools address particular problems or assist individual researchers, and none of them is designed as the shared working environment of a research group. We propose the design of a self-hosted environment in which a group of people and agents does its daily mathematical work. It consists of a small open core, which each group deploys with the resources it has and adapts through extensions. The core records who did what and gives every message and result a stable address. We also outline how the formal libraries of different groups, maintained mostly by agents, can form a network. We describe Stemma, an early prototype that implements part of the proposal, and illustrate it with a synthetic example.

title: ColNav: Uncertainty-Aware Spacetime Collision Checking with Bounding Volume Hierarchies
abstract: Safe navigation for mobile robots in dynamic and uncertain environments requires planning paths that avoid collisions with other moving targets. Typically this involves forward propagating the robot motion and checking for collisions at sampled points in space and time. Such methods can miss collisions between sampled points and are not robust to uncertainty in the state estimates. We propose ColNav, a robust collision check formulation with geometric volumes. The key aspect of our approach is encoding the uncertainty in the targets' and the ego robot's positions and velocities into spacetime tubes, in two variants that consume bounded-set and Gaussian uncertainty descriptions, respectively. The tubes are organised in bounding volume hierarchies, so that a single tree traversal covers the entire horizon, rather than testing sampled time instants, and returns a robust geometric certificate together with an estimate of the time to collision. Static and dynamic obstacles share the same representation. Our approach reaches the goal with a 100% success rate under prediction model mismatch, where the best baseline reaches 65%, and maintains up to three times the clearance in dense traffic. We also validate real-time operation on a physical robot.

title: Pauli propagation in adaptive local frames
abstract: The cost of Pauli propagation depends on the local basis in which the evolving operator is expanded. We show that its Pauli complexity splits into an occupation part, invariant under local rotations and bounded from below by the operator mass and length distributions, and a flavour part that a suitable basis can remove. We introduce frame-adaptive Pauli propagation (FAPP), which rotates the basis of every qubit, gate by gate, to the principal axes of the operator's local polarisation, exactly and within the memory structure of Pauli propagation. This simple rule achieves most of what the best local frame can, and the polarisation predicts how much any local frame can gain. In the Ising chain in transverse and longitudinal fields, FAPP lowers the truncation error at fixed memory by up to an order of magnitude and the memory by a size-independent factor of three; on the infinite two-dimensional lattice it needs up to seven times fewer strings for a given certified accuracy, and in Clifford circuits doped with T gates two to eight times fewer.

title: PA-SaR: Perception-Aware Learning, Control, and Coordination for Multi-Robot Search and Rescue
abstract: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.

title: A Trust Region Approach for Learning Schrödinger Bridges
abstract: We study the numerical approximation of Schrödinger Bridges in the setting where samples from the target distribution are unavailable and only an unnormalized target density is given. In this regime, the widely used iterative proportional fitting (IPF) procedure (and its variants) often exhibits severe numerical instabilities, stemming from ill-conditioned underlying control problems and from the fact that the optimal solution may lie far from the initialization. To address these issues, we propose a trust region variant of IPF that constrains successive updates to remain at a fixed Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current iterate. This restriction significantly improves numerical stability. Moreover, we show that the resulting method admits an interpretation as a mirror descent scheme with an adaptively chosen step size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging sampling tasks.

title: FlowEval: How Much Adaptation Does an Embodied Foundation Model Need at Deployment?
abstract: Large-scale pretraining is reducing the amount of adaptation required to deploy embodied foundation models, but it is not guaranteed that a pretrained model already provide the level of performance required in every deployment. Practitioners therefore need to understand how well a pretrained model matches a target deployment and how much adaptation data is left to be collected. We study whether a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations can reveal whether and how much target-domain data will be required before any adaptation. We introduce FlowEval, a set of training-free metrics that use the flow-matching objective to probe an embodied foundation model with a set of demonstrations. FlowEval quantifies predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations to assess how well a pretrained model fits a target deployment. Across four embodied foundation model families: Pi-0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T, and DreamZero, FlowEval distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across real-world and simulated manipulation. Further, by finetuning Pi-0.5 and GR00T on 17 RoboCasa365 manipulation tasks, we showed that FlowEval correlates with how success rate improves as additional adaptation data is provided. Together, these results suggest that FlowEval can serve as a lightweight, training-free diagnostic of how much model--deployment adaptation may be required.

title: Optimizing Multi-Tier Intermediation in Programmatic Advertising: A DAG-Based Mechanism for Supply Path Optimization
abstract: Digital programmatic advertising operates through complex, multi-hop supply chains. The opacity of these intermediary networks leads to significant efficiency losses, often referred to as the ``ad-tech tax.'' While current industry practices utilize heuristic Supply Path Optimization (SPO) to trim inefficient routes, they fail to optimize the equilibrium of the entire network. This paper extends previous work on Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) intermediation models by applying them to traceable programmatic supply chains mapped via the OpenRTB SupplyChain object. We introduce multi-attribute utility functions and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) to account for substitutable routing (OR nodes) and percentage-based fee structures. Furthermore, we outline a computational methodology and experimental framework using public \texttt{schain} and \texttt{sellers.json} data to benchmark optimal Nash social welfare against current uncoordinated market outcomes.

title: Adjoint Kernel Sensitivity of the Rough Heston Characteristic Exponent
abstract: Multi-factor approximations of rough volatility kernels affect the characteristic exponents used in Fourier-based derivative valuation. We derive an adjoint representation for the first-order sensitivity of the rough Heston characteristic exponent with respect to its memory kernel, with model parameters and the input variance curve held fixed. The Volterra--Riccati functional $\mathcal L_T(K,z)$ admits a local real-analytic extension, jointly in the kernel perturbation and the transform parameter. The Fréchet derivative of this extension with respect to the kernel in $L^1$ is represented by integration against a continuous sensitivity kernel $B_K(u,z)$, obtained from a backward linear Volterra equation and independent of the perturbation direction. This representation resolves the leading-order contributions of kernel perturbations across memory lags. On the structural kernel class, which contains the fractional kernel and its multi-factor approximations and has empty interior in $L^1$, the extension yields Hadamard directional differentiability and a first-order expansion with a quadratic $L^1$-remainder for all sufficiently close structural kernels, uniformly on compact subsets of the strip of transform parameters. The same sensitivity kernel yields multi-factor weight and decay-rate derivatives. Numerical experiments at multi-factor reference kernels assess the finite-resolution implementation and illustrate how the lag distribution of positive perturbations with equal $L^1$ mass affects the first-order response.

title: Exploring Mixed-Reality for Enhancing Driver Warning Systems: A Preliminary Study on Attention-Shifting Methods and Hazard Perception
abstract: Modern vehicles are equipped with advanced sensors and capabilities, yet engaging human drivers effectively in hazard perception remains a challenging research area. This paper investigates the potential of mixed reality (MR) to enhance driver warning systems. The study examines the impact of attention-shifting methods, including visual cues, audio cues, and a combination of both, on drivers' hazard perception. A preliminary study involving six participants was conducted, and the NASA-TLX analysis did not yield significant differences. However, through the use of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), we unveil distinct brain activation patterns associated with visual and sound cues. Further research with larger sample sizes and diverse driving scenarios is required to validate and expand upon these preliminary results.

title: Giant magnetoresistance rectification by Néel vector dynamics
abstract: We observe room-temperature giant magnetoresistance (GMR) rectification driven by Néel vector dynamics in synthetic antiferromagnets. During spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance, the out-of-phase (optical) mode makes the relative angle between the two sub-moments oscillate, producing a rectified voltage due to GMR. This component is isolated from anisotropic and spin Hall magnetoresistance contributions by its angular symmetry, with its voltages scaling linearly with microwave power. We extract a GMR coefficient of 0.18-0.20 % from the rectification, which agrees with independently measured dc magnetoresistance. Reversing the Néel vector with a dc current changes the sign of the GMR rectification voltage in a non-volatile and controlled manner.

title: Lieb-Robinson bound for one-dimensional continuum fermions
abstract: The central difficulty in quantum many-body physics is that the Hilbert space dimension grows exponentially with the total degrees of freedom. A key feature to circumvent this problem is locality, which manifests dynamically through an approximate causal structure in the form of a Lieb-Robinson bound (LRB). LRBs have been proved for quantum spin systems and certain lattice boson systems, but so far never for realistic continuum systems. We present the first LRB that applies to a standard system of one-dimensional continuum fermions. It applies to initial states with controlled moments of local particle number and energy and is thus thermodynamically stable. Our result breaks the main technical barrier that has existed for using the vast locality toolbox on continuum systems.

title: Means vs. Foundation Models for Emergency Call Forecasting
abstract: This study investigates whether generalized means can achieve forecasting performance comparable to that of TimeGPT for daily emergency call volume prediction. Specifically, two families of generalized means, the Hölder means (HM) and the Lehmer means (LM), are evaluated against fine-tuned TimeGPT across forecasting horizons ranging from one to seven days. Forecasting performance is assessed on a real-world emergency call dataset using multiple error metrics, and Diebold-Mariano test. Experimental results show that HM and LM achieve nearly identical predictive performance across all forecasting horizons. For short-term forecasting, both generalized means outperform TimeGPT, with reductions of mean absolute error (MAE) approximately 1.24\% and 2.48\% at horizons of one and three days, respectively. Conversely, TimeGPT achieves a lower error at the seven-day horizon, with an descresing of MAE by 1.98\%. However, Diebold-Mariano tests reveal no statistically significant differences between the methods at the evaluated horizons. These findings suggest that generalized means can provide competitive forecasting performance compared with a energyvore foundation model.

title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents
abstract: We built a hybrid multi-agent trading system that combines large language model (LLM) analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves. We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.

title: Measuring Generative AI Content in Political Campaigns: Evidence of Rising Adoption and Non-Disclosure
abstract: The use of generative AI in political campaigns has drawn public concern and policy attention. Public concerns range from distrust of candidates to skepticism about the authenticity and accuracy of political advertising, including AI-generated images and video. Nearly half of U.S. states have enacted laws that prohibit, or require disclosure of, "materially deceptive" AI-generated content (AIGC) in elections to guard against these concerns. This study measures how candidates and their campaigns produce and circulate AIGC during an election cycle. We develop two measures that estimate not only wether campaigns use AIGC, but how much they produce (magnitude) and in what forms (modality). We apply these measures to a novel dataset of text and images from the campaign websites, X accounts, and emails of 12,977 candidates for U.S. political office from 2023 to 2025. We report three findings. First, detectable AIGC from campaigns increased significantly across modalities over the observation window, and campaigns that use AIGC frequently do not disclose it. Second, incumbents' campaigns produced significantly less AIGC than challengers' campaigns. Third, candidates in states with AIGC disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less AIGC than candidates in other states. Our method and findings have implications for transparency and trust in elections, and on state laws that regulate AI use in campaigns. Because current state laws largely target mainly "materially deceptive" content, we identify additional policy mechanisms that could increase electoral transparency and improve trust as AIGC becomes more prevalent.

title: RADE: Risk-Adjusted Deployment Efficiency, A Framework for Routing, Memory, and Escalation in Safe LLM Systems
abstract: A deployed language model does not merely answer questions. It spends computation, consumes time, consults evidence, exposes memory, invites or avoids human review, and sometimes makes mistakes whose consequences are radically unequal. Yet LLM systems are still commonly compared as if the relevant object were a single model and the relevant outcome were a single benchmark score. This paper argues that the unit of analysis should instead be the deployment policy: the mechanism that decides when to retrieve, when to remember, when to call a larger model, when to verify, and when not to answer at all. We introduce risk-adjusted deployment efficiency (RADE), a system-level objective that scores the utility a deployment delivers net of inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected failure cost, while treating harms that cannot be priced as hard budgets alongside constraints on latency, privacy, and resources. The framework brings selective routing, retrieval and governed memory, efficient specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and human escalation into a common account. We then examine five deployment regimes in which the same nominal LLM capability leads to different rational architectures, and propose a reporting protocol based on risk-coverage behavior, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load. The central claim is modest but consequential: frontier capability should be treated as a resource to allocate, not a default state to maintain. A safe and sustainable system is not the one that always uses the strongest model; it is the one that spends capability where the reduction in risk or increase in utility justifies the cost.

title: On sinks and mirrors
abstract: Given a full rank sink recurrent cluster $\mathcal{A}$ variety, we prove that its wrapped Fukaya category is equivalent to the category of coherent sheaves on a stacky elaboration of the dual Fock-Goncharov cluster $\mathcal{X}$ variety. In particular, braid varieties for a semisimple group are mirror to the braid varieties for the Langlands dual group. Another example: for compact surfaces with no interior marked points, a least one marked point on each boundary component, and at least two marked points in total, the Fock-Goncharov moduli for SL(2) and PGL(2) are homologically mirror. The results were obtained in communion with ChatGPT Astra.

title: Local well-posedness for viscous heat-conducting fluids with discontinuous densities
abstract: In this paper, we consider the Navier-Stokes-Fourier system in space dimension $d\geq2$. We prove local well-posedness of solutions having density only in $L^p\cap L^\infty$, for suitable $p\in\,]1,+\infty[\,$, with no further regularity requirements. In particular, our result yields existence and uniqueness of solutions in the case of discontinuous densities presenting a jump across a smooth interface. The existence proof is based on the use of the Hoff effective viscous flux and on a combination of both maximal regularity and Chemin's striated regularity arguments. Uniqueness, under the assumption of slightly more regular initial velocity fields and temperatures, relies on a Lagrangian approach, supplemented with an original bootstrap argument which shows improved time integrability properties of the solution.

title: Enhancing Balance and Posture in Material Handling Tasks with a Wearable Robotic Tail
abstract: Frequent heavy lifting is linked to musculoskeletal strain, with lower back pain affecting up to 40% of manual labourers. Inspired by animals using tails for balance, we developed a wearable robotic tail as a dynamic counterbalance. Ten participants performed an imitated shelf loading/unloading task across three conditions: active tail, passive tail, and no tail. Kinematics, centre of pressure, and muscle activation (gastrocnemius, erector spinae, tibialis anterior, biceps brachii) were measured. Compared with no tail, the active tail achieved >20 mm reduction in centre of pressure peak displacement, 4.3 degree reduction in trunk motion, and >9% and >20% reductions in erector spinae and gastrocnemius activity, respectively. The passive tail produced smaller reductions, suggesting passive counterbalancing helps while active movement augments it further. Biceps brachii activation increased with the active versus passive tail. The ankle kinematics and tibialis anterior activation were unchanged. These findings support wearable robotic tails for improving balance during material handling.

title: The AI research space shapes country academic performance
abstract: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have demonstrated great potential across diverse domains, prompting increasing attention to understanding the AI ecosystem. As knowledge production is often perceived as a process of connecting existing pieces of knowledge, mapping the interconnections of AI knowledge is crucial for unraveling the dynamics of scientific production in AI. However, maps created so far have fallen short of capturing knowledge relatedness, focusing instead on citation relationships between subfields.
